title: Public Transit Time and Fare Design: Ridership Maximization Under Income Disparity
affiliations: Indiana University - Kelley School of Business and Cornell University

detail.title: Public Transit Time and Fare Design: Ridership Maximization Under Income Disparity
detail.abstract: Amid the prolonged public transit ridership decline, we study how a ridership-maximizing transit agency serving areas spatially segregated by income should set area-specific fares and travel times when facing constraints on operating budget and policy complexity. We develop a bilevel model that captures the interaction between the transit agency's decision and riders' transportation mode choice, which is governed by a micro-founded time-money allocation model that links income to value of time. We compare four policies motivated by contemporary practices in large U.S. transit systems: no differentiation (ND) with uniform fare and time; price differentiation (PD) which only allows fares to differ by income area; time differentiation (TD) where only travel times differ; or full differentiation (FD) that allows both to differ. Our analysis proceeds in three steps. First, we characterize the optimal fares and travel times under each of the four policies and how these decisions vary across income areas. Under FD, we further characterize the optimal incremental budget allocation rule. Second, combined with calibration to Chicago data, we offer practical insights on the ridership loss and distribution change of single-lever policy (TD and PD) relative to FD. Third, we examine how total budget and income disparity level affect the optimal fares, travel times, absolute and incremental budget allocation for each of the four policies. Taken together, our analysis guides when to prioritize price versus time differentiation and how to sequence reforms from ND toward FD via PD or TD, highlighting potential Title VI equity concerns along the trajectory.

detail.title: Moral Philosophy and Archetypes in the Symbolic Cohesion of the Shepherdess’s Tale
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the moralizing value of Rafael Pombo’s tale La Pastorci­ta within the Colombian cultural tradition, interpreting the story as a symbolic device of social regulation. Through an ethical and political reading, the text explores how fear, threat, and the feared figure function as pedagogical mechanisms guiding individual behavior toward the preservation of collective order. By linking excerpts from the tale with the theories of Thomas Hobbes and Niccolò Machiavelli, the study demonstrates how the pedagogy of fear becomes legitimate when oriented toward the common good and social stability. The analysis argues that the tale operates as a modern myth that translates abstract norms into effective narrative images, reinforcing values of obedience, responsibility, and communal cohesion.

title: Real-Time Micro-Fulfillment Orchestration in Omnichannel Retail Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework

detail.title: Real-Time Micro-Fulfillment Orchestration in Omnichannel Retail Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework
detail.abstract: Micro-fulfillment centers (MFCs) have emerged as a response to growing e-commerce demands, yet their integration into omnichannel retail networks creates order routing challenges that traditional optimization struggles to solve efficiently. This paper introduces a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework designed for adaptive order allocation across heterogeneous fulfillment nodes: MFCs, dark stores, and conventional distribution centers. Built on a Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) architecture, the framework allows individual agents to make rapid local decisions while preserving coordination at the network level. Computational experiments indicate a 23% reduction in fulfillment time, 18% lower per-order costs, and SLA compliance reaching 94.2% versus 91.2% for the strongest baseline. Performance remains stable across different network sizes and under varying demand conditions. These results suggest that decentralized AI approaches can effectively handle the dynamic nature of modern retail fulfillment.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the moralizing value of Rafael Pombo’s tale Juan Matachín within the Colombian cultural context, interpreting it as a narrative device for ethical and social regulation. Through an interdisciplinary approach combining literary analysis, moral philosophy, and political theory, the study explores the figure of the “anti-villain” as an ambivalent agent who, through fear, seeks to preserve the common good, social order, and harmony with nature. Drawing on Hobbes’s and Machiavelli’s reflections on fear as a foundation of order, the analysis shows how symbolic terror operates pedagogically to deter harmful behavior and reinforce communal norms. The tale is thus understood as more than children’s literature, functioning as a cultural archive that embeds collective values, mechanisms of social control, and an implicit ethic of ecological protection and community cohesion in the Colombian imaginary.

title: Media As Translator: Deconstructing Ophelia in the Era of Taylor Swift
affiliations: Guruvayurappan College

detail.title: Media As Translator: Deconstructing Ophelia in the Era of Taylor Swift
detail.abstract: This paper examines the significant role of media as a translator of meaning, focusing on how classical literary texts and figures are reinterpreted within the digital culture, enabling the translation of experience into new forms. It meditates on how the media participation, like interactive media and music video, critically interpreted and received the work. And how the representation of female agency and identity has changed today. Using Shakespeare’s Ophelia from the 17th century and the popular pop persona of Taylor Swift from the 21st century as a comparative framework. This research examines how Modern Digital media, through music videos, social platforms, and interactive media, reshape and subvert traditional narratives, such as patriarchy, into contemporary discourses of female agency and identity. By analyzing the tragic Portrayal of Ophelia in Hamlet and contrasting it with Taylor Swift’s self-represented narrative of recovery, empowerment, resistance, and self-authorship, the research paper enlightens how the subjectivity of female experience transforms under media. This is woven to the notion of Marshall McLuhan’s ₋ media as an extension of human perception, permitting translation of experience into new forms. This interdisciplinary inquiry reveals how traditional conservative literary texts are renegotiated and reconstructed into a cultural framework. This flips the gender dynamics and presents a reclamation of voice through participatory media. This analysis proclaims the urgency and necessity of understanding media not as a static document but as a performative and informative agent with political stakes in narrative representation.

title: Machiavellian Marketing vs Empathy-Based Marketing: A Comparative Analysis for Influence in Modern Economies

detail.title: Machiavellian Marketing vs Empathy-Based Marketing: A Comparative Analysis for Influence in Modern Economies
detail.abstract:
Empathy based marketing has emerged as a dominant ethical framework in contemporary marketing discourse, emphasizing authenticity, trust, and emotional alignment between brands and consumers. This paper argues that such approaches reflect a legacy persuasion model increasingly misaligned with algorithmically mediated markets. In environments defined by attention scarcity, platform gatekeeping, and information asymmetry, influence operates less through mutual trust and more through control of perception. 

This study introduces Machiavellian Marketing as a post persuasion framework oriented toward perception engineering, narrative dominance, and strategic inevitability. Drawing on behavioral psychology, sociological theory, and observable platform dynamics, the paper contrasts empathy based marketing's moral assumptions with the structural realities of algorithmic influence. The analysis demonstrates that modern markets systematically reward psychological legibility and narrative control over ethical intent alone. Machiavellian Marketing is therefore positioned not as a rejection of human psychology, but as a pragmatic response to how influence functions under algorithmic conditions.

detail.abstract: Partner alliances have become an increasingly important go-to-market (GTM) strategy in the SaaS industry as vendors seek scalable alternatives to direct sales. Despite this trend, only a limited number of firms succeed in achieving sustained partner-led growth, while many struggle with partner disengagement, declining activity, or the eventual abandonment of partner programs. These failures are commonly attributed to execution-related factors such as insufficient partner capability, lack of motivation, or market-specific constraints. This paper argues that such explanations address symptoms rather than root causes. It proposes that the effectiveness of partner alliances is primarily determined by how the triadic relationship among Vendor, Partner, and Customer is structurally designed. This study introduces the Lever-Based GTM Model, which applies the principle of leverage from classical mechanics to analyze go-to-market systems. Within this framework, the Vendor is conceptualized as the point of force, the Partner as the fulcrum, and the Customer as the point of action. The model analyzes three dominant GTM approaches-Sales-Led Growth (SLG), Product-Led Growth (PLG), and OEM/Implementation-along two structural dimensions: Relational Distance and Force Direction. The central contribution of this paper is a structural explanation of recurring failures in partner-led growth, reframing them as predictable outcomes of relational misalignment rather than execution deficiencies. By shifting the analytical focus from tactics and incentives to structural configuration, this framework offers a unified lens for understanding why similar partner strategies produce divergent outcomes. The paper further applies the model to patterns observed in the Japanese SaaS market, suggesting that many challenges attributed to cultural factors instead reflect gaps in shared structural understanding.

title: The Influence of National Identity on Consumer Preferences Between Local and Global Skincare Brand

detail.title: The Influence of National Identity on Consumer Preferences Between Local and Global Skincare Brand
detail.abstract: This study assesses the influence of national identity on consumer preferences between local and global skincare brands among residents of Valenzuela City, Philippines, in response to globalization challenges and the push for consumer nationalism in the beauty sector. Although skincare consumer behavior has been widely studied globally, limited focus has examined how national identity through marketing mix elements influence preference between local and global brands in the Philippine market. To address this gap, the study explored demographic profiles, national identity's extent of influence via the 4Ps (product, price, place, promotion), identify consumer preference through (personal identity, social identity, social categorization, distinct social group), and their relationships. Employing a quantitative correlational design, researchers surveyed 200 purposively selected respondents aged 18 and above using a structured four-point Likert-scale questionnaire, analyzed through frequencies, weighted means, and Pearson correlations. Findings indicated moderate to strong positive influences and significant relationships across variables, rejecting the null hypothesis, with promotion and place as primary drivers local brands excelling in cultural pride and affordability, global ones in innovation and prestige. Grounded in Social Identity Theory, the study concludes that national identity enhances local appeal yet demands targeted strategies for market gains, providing guidance for brands, and future research on sustained dynamics in the Philippine skincare industry.

title: Enhancing the Wisdom of AI-Assisted Crowds: Theory and Experimental Evidence
affiliations: Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Operation & Decision Technologies,  and INSEAD - Technology and Operations Management

detail.title: Enhancing the Wisdom of AI-Assisted Crowds: Theory and Experimental Evidence
detail.abstract: Accurate forecasts are critical for financial and business decision making. Such forecasts may be generated by human experts or by artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. A decision maker can benefit from the distinct advantages that each source may offer by providing AI assistance to the experts, allowing them to augment the information contained in the AI forecast by incorporating their own knowledge about the variable of interest. When multiple experts are available, accuracy can be further improved by utilizing the wisdom of crowds, forming a consensus by averaging each of their AI-assisted forecasts. However, the potential accuracy of a crowd of AI-assisted forecasters may be limited by two structural features. First, because the AI assistance is valuable to each expert at an individual level, the opinion of the AI can end up being overrepresented in the crowd's consensus. Second, the experts may fail to appropriately utilize the AI assistance when forming their forecasts, either under-or overemphasizing the information it provides. Using a stylized Bayesian model of information aggregation, we develop a procedure that can recover the most accurate consensus forecast given all information collectively observed by the AI technology and every expert in the crowd. This procedure works by pivoting the average AI-assisted forecast either toward or away from the crowd's average initial forecast. We test the performance of the proposed aggregation method in three laboratory experiments and find that it provides superior accuracy than the unassisted crowd of forecasters, the AI technology on its own, and the AI-assisted crowd.

detail.title: Lawyers' Client-Inclusive Negotiations: The "New Mediation"?

detail.abstract: When proponents initially urged the courts to institutionalize mediation for the resolution of general civil cases, they argued that the procedure would be superior to trial—and also to lawyers’ settlement negotiations—in terms of parties’ exercise of self-determination, satisfaction with outcomes, and opportunity for voice. These claims, however, rested on certain assumptions, particularly regarding the implementation of mediation and lawyers’ settlement negotiations. In mediation, the parties were to take center stage, with the mediator assisting them by facilitating their communication and negotiation so that they could reach a customized resolution. Lawyers’ settlement negotiations in general civil litigation, meanwhile, were assumed to be lawyeronly affairs that excluded the clients. Since then, scholars and other observers have often written about how much mediation has evolved. In the contemporary legal landscape, one of the models used frequently in the courts (and by private providers as well) is an evaluative, lawyer-and-caucus-dominated procedure. The evolution of lawyers’ practice in settlement negotiations has not received commensurate attention. Data has begun to suggest, however, that a substantial percentage of these negotiations may include the clients. We propose that this “client-inclusive” approach to lawyers’ settlement negotiations might outperform—or at least match the performance of—the lawyer-dominated evaluative model of mediation, using many of the same criteria initially used to promote mediation. Paradoxically, just as arbitration has evolved into the “new litigation” and mediation has become the “new arbitration,” lawyers’ client-inclusive negotiations could represent the “new mediation.” If this is so, courts should also evolve by considering the use of “client-inclusive” negotiations to satisfy judicial orders to participate in mediation and law schools should prepare students to competently implement this procedure.

title: The Paradox of Governance Calibration at Machine Speed: Why Human Intervention Cannot Meet the Decision Moment

detail.title: The Paradox of Governance Calibration at Machine Speed: Why Human Intervention Cannot Meet the Decision Moment

detail.abstract:
Organizations across sectors are under growing pressure to deploy artificial intelligence rapidly while governing its use rigorously and remaining accountable for outcomes. Over the past several years, AI governance has evolved in material ways. What began as largely retrospective oversight—policy review, documentation, and periodic audit—has moved toward operational observability. Many organizations now operate with near-continuous visibility into live AI systems, supported by sandboxes, controlled pilots, detailed logging, and post-incident reconstruction.

These advances are not cosmetic. They have improved transparency, reduced certain classes of risk, and made accountability more concrete. Governance today is closer to execution than at any previous point.

Yet as governance has moved closer, a persistent unease has emerged.

Across an increasing number of operational domains, AI systems now make decisions at machine speed—optimizing, adapting, and acting in milliseconds within delegated bounds. In these environments, governance mechanisms continue to operate on human timescales. Even where systems are observable in near-real time, intervention typically requires confirmation, escalation, and authorization. By the time these processes complete, decisions have already executed—often repeatedly and at scale.

This paper argues that the resulting tension is not a failure of governance, intent, or competence. It is a structural timing constraint. Governance happens in time, and AI decisions increasingly occur outside the window in which human intervention can reliably act.

The distinction between oversight and control is therefore central. Oversight enables organizations to observe system behavior, assess outcomes, and respond after execution. Control requires the ability to interrupt or redirect decisions before consequences unfold. As decision speed accelerates, these two functions diverge. Visibility improves, but control arrives only after the decision moment has passed.

This divergence reshapes accountability. In machine-speed systems, responsibility increasingly attaches upstream—away from individual decisions and toward the conditions under which decisions are allowed to occur. Accountability is exercised through design choices, constraints, and pre-commitments made before deployment, and through rigorous reconstruction after the fact. While these mechanisms can limit damage and support learning, they do not restore decision moment control.

The paper examines why proposals for real-time or continuous governance struggle in practice, including constraints related to authority, accountability ambiguity, scale, and system distortion. It then documents governance adaptations that do scale under these conditions, including constraint-based decision governors, explicit autonomy scoping, pre-commitment architectures, and replay-based accountability. These approaches acknowledge irreversibility as a governance condition rather than treating it as a failure.

The implications extend beyond any single organization or regulatory regime. As AI systems become more deeply embedded in operational decision flows, the challenge of governance shifts from intervention to calibration. The central question is no longer who is responsible in the moment, but when responsibility can still act.

Understanding this timing constraint is essential for regulators, boards, and leaders seeking credible governance in an era of machine-speed decision-making—without promising control that cannot be exercised in practice.

title: Dying Declaration as an Evidence

detail.title: Dying Declaration as an Evidence

keywords: Who Are not Considered as a Witness

detail.abstract: This paper examines the admissibility and evidentiary value of statements made by persons who are dead or otherwise unavailable as witnesses under Section 32 & related provisions of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and the corresponding provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. It situates these exceptions within the general rule favouring direct oral evidence given on oath and subjected to cross-examination, and explains why, in limited situations the law nevertheless accepts hearsay as relevant and reliable. The discussion begins with the legal status of dead persons and the jurisdictional basis for recognising their intentions and statements even after the extinction of legal personality. It then analyses the requirements for invoking Section 32, including death, absence, incapacity, or unreasonable expense or delay in securing attendance, and emphasises the need to first prove these foundational facts. The core of the paper is a doctrinal and case-law based analysis of the specific categories of statements covered: dying declarations relating to the cause of death or the circumstances of the transaction; statements made in the ordinary course of business; declarations against pecuniary or proprietary interest; opinions on public rights, customs or matters of general interest; declarations as to relationship; and documents relating to transactions relevant to custom or right. The paper further addresses statements expressing collective feelings relevant to a matter in issue and explains the conditions under which former testimony becomes relevant in subsequent proceedings under section 33. Through leading English and Indian decisions, it evaluates when dying declarations are treated as complete, how courts assess their liability, and how far such statements alone can sustain conviction in criminal trials.

detail.abstract: Despite widespread experimentation, most organisations struggle to translate artificial intelligence initiatives into sustained operational or economic value. Public commentary frequently attributes these difficulties to leadership failure, cultural resistance, or generic transformation challenges. Drawing primarily on Gartner's AI/Human Readiness research and MIT NANDA's empirical analysis of enterprise AI deployments, this paper argues that early AI outcomes are constrained instead by a small number of AI-specific execution gaps that systematically recur across organizations regardless of sector or AI use case. These gaps arise from structural mismatches between probabilistic, learning-based systems and organisational designs optimised for deterministic processes and linear accountability. The paper identifies and operationalises these gaps, outlines how they manifest in practice, and highlights concrete signals associated with improved outcomes in the first 6-18 months of implementation.

English Abstract: Blockchain technology, which gained widespread attention with the emergence of Bitcoin in 2008, constitutes an innovative technological infrastructure with the potential to profoundly transform economic, business, and legal systems. This technology enables the recording, verification, and storage of information in a decentralized, secure, and immutable manner, without reliance on a central intermediary. Alongside cryptocurrencies, additional key applications have emerged, including smart contracts and Initial Coin Offerings (ICOs), which present significant legal and ethical challenges.

This paper examines the foundational principles of blockchain technology, including decentralization, transparency, immutability, and consensus mechanisms, and analyzes its primary applications from a legal perspective. It further explores the legal issues arising from the implementation of smart contracts, cryptocurrency trading, and ICOs, highlighting the tensions between autonomous technological frameworks and traditional legal doctrines such as contract law, securities regulation, and financial oversight.

Finally, the paper provides a comparative review of legislative and regulatory responses adopted in various jurisdictions, with a particular focus on the United States, and examines the regulatory landscape in Israel. The study identifies a legal gap that necessitates regulatory adaptation and emphasizes the need for a balanced legislative framework that promotes technological innovation while safeguarding public interests, legal certainty, and the rule of law.

detail.abstract: This study focuses on the higher education of Muslim (Meitei Pangal) women in the Thoubal District of Manipur. The primary objective is to identify the challenges faced by Muslim women pursuing higher education in this specific district. The research employed a descriptive survey methodology, selecting a total of 45 Muslim women for interview from various higher educational institutions in the district through Simple Random sampling. The researcher utilized self-developed questionnaires for data collection, gathering information from both primary and secondary sources. The collected data underwent analysis using statistical techniques to derive percentages. The study's findings revealed that 85% of the respondents encountered financial difficulties. Additionally, 92% of the participants expressed that the distance to various educational institutions from their residences was considerable. These findings provide a comprehensive overview of the status of Muslim women in higher education within this particular district of Manipur. Furthermore, it is anticipated that the outcomes of this study will catalyze positive qualitative changes in the realm of education, particularly benefitting Muslim women in the district.

title: A Model of Artificial Jagged Intelligence
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: A Model of Artificial Jagged Intelligence
detail.abstract: Generative AI systems often display highly uneven performance across tasks that appear "nearby": they can be excellent on one prompt and confidently wrong on another with only small changes in wording or context. We call this phenomenon Artificial Jagged Intelligence (AJI). This paper develops a tractable economic model of AJI that treats adoption as an information problem: users care about local reliability, but typically observe only coarse, global quality signals. In a baseline one-dimensional landscape, truth is a rough Brownian process, and the model "knows" scattered points drawn from a Poisson process. The model interpolates optimally, and the local error is measured by posterior variance. We derive an adoption threshold for a blind user, show that experienced errors are amplified by the inspection paradox, and interpret scaling laws as denser coverage that improves average quality without eliminating jaggedness. We then study mastery and calibration: a calibrated user who can condition on local uncertainty enjoys positive expected value even in domains that fail the blind adoption test. Modelling mastery as learning a reliability map via Gaussian process regression yields a learning-rate bound driven by information gain, clarifying when discovering "where the model works" is slow. Finally, we study how scaling interacts with discoverability: when calibrated signals and user mastery accelerate the harvesting of scale improvements, and when opacity can make gains from scaling effectively invisible.

detail.abstract: This paper exploits that the Covid-19 pandemic came as an unexpected shock that temporarily reduced the ratio of vacancies to seekers. We use this unique setting to understand the importance of job opportunities for the impact of unemployment on workers’ careers. Compared to individuals who became unemployed under more benign conditions, we find greater and lasting adverse effects on earnings. We provide evidence that lower job opportunities lead unemployed individuals to take up jobs that are further down the occupationspecific wage distribution. Finally, we substantiate the importance of job prospects by using exogenous variation in the pandemic’s effect on occupations.

title: Liquidity, Government Bonds, and Sovereign Debt Crises

detail.title: Liquidity, Government Bonds, and Sovereign Debt Crises
detail.abstract: This paper studies the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis through the lens of funding liquidity in government bonds. Using newly collected data on repo haircuts from LCH Clearnet Ltd, the paper identifies liquidity shocks with a high-frequency structural VAR, separately from sovereign risk shocks, and shows that reductions in funding liquidity substantially increased yields on peripheral government bonds. To explain these effects, a general equilibrium model with financial frictions reproduces the empirical dynamics of a liquidity shock, capturing the rise in bond returns, the flight-to-liquidity, and the contraction in aggregate activity during the crisis. The model further highlights how liquidity and sovereign risk interact, generating a feedback loop that amplifies market stress. Evidence from the COVID-19 pandemic, including ECB haircut reductions, corroborates the role of this funding liquidity channel.

detail.abstract: The continuous rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) concentration is one of the most critical drivers of global climate change, necessitating the development of innovative technologies for both carbon capture and utilization. While conventional carbon capture approaches primarily focus on sequestration, limited attention has been given to systems that simultaneously remove CO₂ from ambient air and convert it into value-added materials. This research presents the design and development of Aegis-1, a prototype-scale integrated machine capable of capturing atmospheric CO₂ and converting it into oxygen and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) through a two-stage process involving chemical absorption and carbonate electrolysis. In the first stage, Aegis-1 employs a direct air capture mechanism using an aqueous monoethanolamine (MEA) solution promoted by piperazine (PZ) to selectively absorb CO₂ from ambient air. The use of the MEA-PZ blend enhances absorption kinetics, reduces residence time, and improves operational efficiency compared to conventional amine systems. The CO₂-rich solution is subsequently thermally regenerated to release high-purity CO₂ gas, enabling continuous cyclic operation. In the second stage, the released CO₂ is electrochemically converted using a molten carbonate electrolyte, where carbonate electrolysis produces solid carbon in the form of carbon nanotubes at the cathode and pure oxygen gas at the anode. The Aegis-1 system represents a novel integration of direct air capture with electrochemical CO₂ conversion, offering a pathway for negative-emission technology coupled with nanomaterial production. This paper discusses the working principles, chemical reactions, system architecture, and expected performance of the prototype, along with its environmental and techno-economic significance. Although the current work focuses on design and feasibility analysis, the proposed approach demonstrates strong potential for scalable carbon utilization, contributing to sustainable climate-mitigation strategies and advanced material manufacturing.

title: Multi-Scale Information Dynamics in Economic Systems: A Framework for Risk Management and Hedged Options Strategies

detail.title: Multi-Scale Information Dynamics in Economic Systems: A Framework for Risk Management and Hedged Options Strategies
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for understanding economic systems through multi-scale information dynamics (MSID). We propose that economic agents do not merely respond to information but actively produce it, and that economic meaning emerges from integrated information flows across multiple scales (individual, market, institutional, cultural). We formalize this framework using information theory (transfer entropy, mutual information) and develop an Economic Meaning Index (EMI) that quantifies the degree of information integration across scales. Using real-world financial data from 2008-2023, we demonstrate how EMI predicts regime changes and crisis periods more effectively than traditional volatility measures. We validate our framework through agent-based modeling simulations and show its practical application in hedged options strategies and risk management. Our results suggest that risk management should shift from volatility-based approaches to meaning-based approaches, where risk is understood as the degradation of cross-scale information coherence rather than mere price fluctuations.

Despite significant progress in renewable energy deployment, energy efficiency improvements, and emission control policies, these mitigation strategies remain insufficient to address the large volume of CO₂ already accumulated in the atmosphere. Consequently, active carbon dioxide removal technologies have become an essential component of long-term climate stabilization efforts. Direct Air Capture (DAC) has emerged as a promising approach capable of extracting CO₂ directly from ambient air, independent of emission sources. This paper presents a conceptual and prototype-based assessment of Aegis-1, a modular Direct Air Capture and Carbon Utilization machine designed to process ambient air, selectively capture CO₂, and convert a fraction of the captured carbon into carbon nanotubes (CNTs). Unlike conventional DAC systems that primarily rely on underground geological storage, Aegis-1 integrates carbon utilization pathways to ensure permanent carbon fixation while simultaneously generating value-added materials. The remaining captured CO₂ that is not used for CNT synthesis is directed toward stable and long-term utilization routes such as mineralization and solid material integration, preventing its re-release into the atmosphere. The study evaluates the projected air processing capacity of the Aegis-1 system, hourly CO₂ capture potential, carbon conversion rates, and secondary CO₂ utilization strategies. Furthermore, the potential impact of large-scale deployment of such systems on atmospheric CO₂ reduction and global warming mitigation is analyzed. By combining direct air capture with durable carbon utilization, Aegis-1 demonstrates a hybrid climate-technology framework that aligns environmental sustainability with industrial and economic feasibility, particularly in the context of emerging economies.

This research paper proposes a technology-driven and business-oriented climate-tech manufacturing framework focused on capturing carbon dioxide and converting it into stable, non-emissive carbon-based materials. Unlike conventional carbon utilization pathways that involve fuels or short-lived products, which eventually release carbon back into the atmosphere, this approach ensures permanent carbon locking at the material level. From a business perspective, the model establishes revenue generation through the commercialization of durable carbon-based products rather than reliance on carbon credits or policy-driven incentives. These materials can be integrated into manufacturing, construction, and advanced material applications, creating direct market demand while simultaneously delivering environmental benefits. This alignment of climate impact with industrial value creation enhances the financial sustainability and scalability of carbon capture technologies. The study integrates technical feasibility with market dynamics, cost structure, and revenue mechanisms to evaluate the overall viability of the proposed framework. By bridging chemical technology, manufacturing innovation, and business strategy, the model demonstrates how climate-tech solutions can transition from experimental concepts to commercially viable enterprises. The proposed framework is particularly relevant for emerging economies, where industrial growth and climate responsibility must progress in parallel.

title: From Mobilization to Management: The 1989 Tiananmen Crisis as a Structural Turning Point

detail.title: From Mobilization to Management: The 1989 Tiananmen Crisis as a Structural Turning Point
detail.abstract: This paper argues that China's post-1989 democratic impossibility is best explained not by ideology but by the elimination of social organizational capacity. The mobilization of the 1980s was not the product of an emerging civil society, but a residue of the CCP's movement-based governance, intensified by the Cultural Revolution. The early reform era (1978-1989) remained institutionally indeterminate; Tiananmen escalated within this space and activated leaders' Cultural Revolution-shaped fears of organized mass politics and systemic disorder. After 1989, the regime retained democratic language yet redefined society as an object of management and pursued de-organizationalization, dismantling horizontal networks and removing the societal foundations required for democratization.

The analysis reveals that over 25% of the road network is vulnerable to inundation. Furthermore, a mitigation strategy targeting the top five high-impact sinks was simulated, demonstrating that localized detention interventions could significantly enhance network resilience.

detail.abstract:
What is the core question? Why do humans treat Artificial Intelligence and transgender subjects with similar skepticism? This paper asks why we demand these groups "prove" their internal experience (consciousness or gender) in ways we never demand of "natural" biological humans.

How is it analyzed? Instead of treating this as a philosophical mystery (the "Hard Problem"), this paper treats it as an economic calculation. Using Game Theory and the concept of "Homo Economicus," it models the interaction between a Human Observer and a Non-Normative Subject.

What are the findings? The paper defines a new concept called "Ontological Arbitrage." It finds that denying recognition to AI or trans subjects is a "Nash Equilibrium"—a stable strategy where the observer maximizes their own social status by treating the Other as an object.

What is the solution? The paper concludes that simple logic cannot solve this; it requires an ethical shift toward "Radical Asymmetry" (caring without expecting a return), drawing on the philosophy of Emmanuel Levinas.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how planetary gravity affects urban agglomeration by altering transportation and construction costs. Extending a reduced-form New Economic Geography framework, we model gravity as an exogenous parameter that scales congestion and infrastructure costs within cities. The model predicts a gravity-dependent upper bound on sustainable city size. Applying the framework to Mars as a case study, we show that lower gravity relaxes congestion forces, allowing larger urban agglomerations than on Earth, despite harsher environmental constraints. The analysis highlights gravity as a fundamental physical determinant of spatial economic structure and provides a new lens for evaluating extraterrestrial settlement and urbanization.

title: Structural Diffusion and Long-Run Growth A Partial Differential Equation Framework

detail.title: Structural Diffusion and Long-Run Growth A Partial Differential Equation Framework
detail.abstract:
Most formal growth models describe long-run dynamics within low-dimensional aggregate state spaces, relying on ordinary differential equations (ODEs) to capture accumulation processes. While effective for medium-horizon analysis, such approaches face conceptual limitations when growth is shaped by slow structural evolution, diffusion, and persistent heterogeneity.

This paper introduces a partial differential equation (PDE) framework for modeling long-run growth, treating structure as a continuous state dimension rather than a discrete regime. The framework decomposes dynamics into local accumulation, structural diffusion, and interaction effects, providing a unified formal language for representing gradual structural change and path dependence. An illustrative specification demonstrates how nonlinear diffusion–accumulation interactions can generate persistent structural gradients and heterogeneous convergence patterns, including endogenous growth slowdowns.

The contribution is methodological rather than empirical. By explicitly modeling diffusion in structural space, the framework expands the analytical toolkit available for studying long-horizon economic development and structural transformation.

detail.abstract: We explore the intersection of shareholder activism and antitrust regulation. Congress established antitrust laws to address monopoly behavior, stifled competition, and economic concentration. However, antitrust regulation has had unanticipated impacts. In this paper, we show that the premerger notification requirements of the Hart-Scott-Rodino ("HSR") Act affect the behavior of activist investors. Exploiting the HSR notification threshold, we provide causal evidence that activists are less likely to target firms when a "toehold" position would trigger HSR disclosure requirements prior to a Schedule 13D filing. Contrary to some suggestions by policymakers, we find no evidence that activism increases industry concentration. Instead, concentration appears to decrease after activist intervention. Our results support policy changes to the HSR premerger notification rules, including its threshold and investment-only exception.

detail.title: Rising Cost of Living and Inflation: A Situation Analysis & Way Forward
detail.abstract: Bangladesh has been experiencing persistent inflation and a rising cost of living, particularly since 2022, impacting both urban and rural communities. The prices of essential goods-such as food, fuel, transportation, housing, and utilities-have risen sharply, placing significant pressure on lowand middle-income households. For instance, the price of staple foods like rice, edible oils, and vegetables has increased by double digits, while fuel and transportation costs have surged, making daily life more expensive for ordinary families (Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics, 2024; Bangladesh Bank, 2024). The IMF (2024) and World Bank (2023) highlight that global factors, including rising commodity prices and supply chain disruptions, have further amplified domestic inflationary pressures. However, the problem is not purely economic. Domestic governance and institutional capacity play a central role in shaping the country's ability to manage inflation. Khaled (2010, 2015, 2022, 2024, 2025) emphasizes that weak strategic management, poor coordination across government agencies, inconsistent reform implementation, and limited oversight have undermined the effectiveness of policy measures. As a result, citizens-especially those in low-income households-bear the brunt of rising costs, often having to cut back on nutritious food, healthcare, and education. This report argues that inflation in Bangladesh is both an economic and a governance challenge. Strengthening institutional capacity, improving fiscal and monetary coordination, and implementing strategic, citizen-focused reforms are essential to protect vulnerable households and ensure broader economic stability.

detail.abstract: This paper focuses on analysis of the origins, political bacground and social consequences of the “LGBT-free zones” resolutions adopted by numerous local governments in Poland starting from 2019. The following motions carried significant symbolic and practical implications mostly by legitimizing exclusionary attitudes toward sexual and gender minorities. Using legal analysis, policy documents, NGO reports and contemporary political discourse this study situates the phenomenon within Poland’s within broader context of rising conservative identity politics. The findings show that the resolutions intensified polarization, normalized discriminatory rhetoric and contributed to the stigmatization of LGBT+ communities. The paper also examines the strong international response, particularly from the European Unionm, which used its political instrument to pressure municipalities to withdraw the resolutions by 2025. The study concludes by outlining policy recommendations aimed at preventing similar forms of institutionalized discrimination, emphasizing the need for legal safeguards and equality strategies.

detail.abstract: The security of cloud networks is becoming increasingly critical as more organizations transition to cloud-based infrastructures. Traditional security models often struggle to handle the complexity and scale of modern cloud environments, making them vulnerable to a range of cyber threats. The integration of Cognitive Artificial Intelligence (AI) with Zero-Trust models presents a promising solution for advanced threat detection and enhanced security in cloud networks. Cognitive AI uses machine learning, behavioral analytics, and anomaly detection to understand and predict potential security risks, while Zero-Trust frameworks continuously verify and validate access requests regardless of their origin. This paper explores the synergy between Cognitive AI and Zero-Trust security models in cloud environments. It examines how these technologies can work together to detect and mitigate advanced threats in real-time, improve the security posture of cloud networks, and offer proactive defense strategies. The effectiveness of this integrated approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments focused on identifying and responding to simulated cyberattacks.

detail.abstract:
Modern asset theory provides robust tools for evaluating liquidity, risk, and expected return across standardized financial instruments. These tools are less effective when applied to assets whose economic relevance depends materially on continuity across ownership regimes, legal structures, and cultural recognition over extended time horizons. Such assets -here referred to as cultural assets - include, but are not limited to, heritage real estate, art collections, vineyards, archives, historically embedded enterprises, and other assets whose persistence cannot be evaluated through liquidation-based or performance-centric models alone.

This paper introduces Cultural Asset Economics, a structural analytical framework developed to evaluate the long-horizon survivability of culturally embedded assets. The framework does not predict returns, optimize portfolios, or rank assets by performance. Instead, it isolates and compares non-financial structural dimensions, often observed informally but rarely analyzed explicitly, that condition whether an asset can retain functional integrity across decades, ownership transitions, and jurisdictional regimes.

We argue that systematic allocation error arises not from informational inefficiency but from analytical incompleteness: critical structural variables affecting durability, ownership continuity, and intergenerational transfer are routinely excluded from formal analysis and treated only informally in practice. To address this gap, we introduce three primary analytical lenses: the Cultural Asset Durability Index (CADI), the Ownership Friction Index (OFI), and the Generational Transfer Risk Index (GTRI), along with two secondary extensions addressing yield extraction and exit flexibility.

The framework is explicitly comparative rather than predictive, structural rather than behavioral, and designed for decision support rather than optimization. While inherently context-dependent and imperfect, this lens provides a necessary complement to financial analysis when evaluating assets whose economic life spans ownership successions rather than market cycles.

title: Ashokan Pillar Edicts and Contemporary Public Art: A Comparative Semiotic Study of Monumentality and Authority

detail.title: Ashokan Pillar Edicts and Contemporary Public Art: A Comparative Semiotic Study of Monumentality and Authority
detail.abstract: This paper presents a comparative analysis of two historically distant yet functionally comparable systems of public visual communication: the Ashokan Pillar Edicts of the third century BCE and contemporary public art practices of the late twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Drawing on historical analysis, art theory, and sociopolitical semiotics, it examines how both forms operate as public markers designed to shape ethical behavior, organize shared space, and articulate authority. The study argues that the Ashokan pillars represent a monosemic, centralized model of monumental communication, in which ethical governance was disseminated through durable materials, codified symbolism, and imperial authorship. In contrast, contemporary public art is shown to function through polysemic, dialogic, and often ephemeral modes that prioritize participation, contestation, and negotiated meaning. By contrasting these two visual regimes, the paper demonstrates a broader historical shift in the relationship between power, art, and publics: from top-down ethical instruction aimed at imperial cohesion to bottom-up critical engagement oriented toward social equity and democratic negotiation. This comparison reframes monumentality not as a stable artistic category, but as a historically contingent strategy of public communication shaped by changing political and ethical conditions.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a Hybrid Commodity–Financial Instrument (CFI) Basket as a diversified monetary anchor designed to strengthen long-run stability for economies reliant on single-anchor exchange-rate regimes. Building on Frankel’s “currency-plus-commodity” concept, the hybrid-CFI model combines real commodities (such as energy, metals, and key agricultural goods) with liquid financial instruments, including Sukuk, short-term sovereign bills, and high-grade bonds, to integrate intrinsic-value stability with liquidity and operational flexibility. Because each unit of currency can, in principle, be fully backed by tangible real assets or high-quality instruments under an explicitly defined reserve and valuation framework, the hybrid-CFI model provides a pathway toward a base-money full-reserve framework. This pathway is conditional on complementary regulatory design that reduces leverage-driven instability inherent in fractional-reserve systems. The paper outlines three possible configurations, examines institutional and technical requirements, and presents a sequenced transition path that avoids destabilizing expectations. It also highlights the role of AI in forecasting, monitoring, and communication during regime change. Overall, the hybrid-CFI structure offers a credible “Plan B” for economies seeking greater resilience and a gradual transition toward a real-value, ethically grounded monetary architecture aligned with Islamic Economic System (IES) principles.

title: Listening: A Negotiator's Playbook

detail.abstract:
As negotiators, we focus extensively on expressing our own thoughts, preferences, and goals. We prepare what we want to say to the other party before the negotiation; we engage in verbal expression during the negotiation; and then we might reflect on what words or phrases we used (or should have used) after the negotiation. In sum, our own expressive speech—the output side of communication—consumes our mental energy. What is often lost in our preparation, interaction, and reflection is the pivotal role that listening plays during the negotiation process. Listening is not just a nice thing to do (although it is that too). A high-quality listener is positioned to benefit, as listening engenders a positive feeling between the parties such that their relationship is strengthened and more information will be revealed. This note presents a framework to develop and apply listening skills throughout the stages of negotiation. It uses insights from interviews with several professionals: a hostage negotiator, a psychologist, and a chaplain, all of whom rely on listening to do their work well. Though operating across distinct contexts, the advice and experience presented here point toward a coherent conclusion: Listening is not passive. It is a deliberate practice built upon developing curiosity, unlocking insights, and implementing commitments.

detail.abstract: Adapted Portfolio Theory (APT) is a new investment framework designed for environments of persistent inflation and structural currency debasement of 7-14% per annum in developed economies. It redefines risk as the probability of permanent loss of purchasing power, embeds inflation and debasement explicitly in the optimization process, employs regime-dependent covariance matrices, and enforces a dynamic Minimum Portfolio Hurdle Rate (MPHR) of 19-26% nominal CAGR (mid-point 22-23%) so that portfolio returns systematically exceed the combined forces of monetary erosion. title: Radical Left in a Globalized Conflict: Ideology, Media, and Local Politics in the Ukraine War

detail.title: Radical Left in a Globalized Conflict: Ideology, Media, and Local Politics in the Ukraine War
detail.abstract: The ongoing Ukraine war has reshaped not only global geopolitics but also the ideological configurations of the radical left across Europe and beyond. This research investigates how radical left movements interpret, frame, and respond to the conflict through the interplay of ideology, media, and local politics. The study addresses a central question: How does the radical left navigate the Ukraine war amid competing narratives of anti-imperialism, sovereignty, and global solidarity? Situated within the broader context of globalization and digital communication, it examines the ideological tensions between opposing NATO expansion and condemning Russian aggression, revealing deep internal fragmentation within leftist discourse. Using qualitative content analysis, the research draws upon political statements, social media posts, and activist publications from radical left parties, movements, and independent media outlets in Europe and the Global South. It also employs discourse analysis to trace how transnational ideological currents are localized through municipal politics, protests, and grassroots mobilizations. The analysis reveals a pluralistic ideological landscape within the radical left. While some groups frame the war as a manifestation of Western imperialism, others highlight Russia's expansionist violence and advocate international solidarity with Ukraine. Media plays a decisive role in shaping these positions-digital platforms function simultaneously as tools of transnational solidarity and arenas of ideological contestation. Local political actors reinterpret global narratives through the lens of domestic struggles, generating diverse forms of activism and dissent. The study concludes that understanding the radical left in the Ukraine war requires a multi-scalar perspective that connects global ideological debates with local political practices. It demonstrates that radical left actors operate within complex ethical and strategic dilemmas, reflecting the broader challenges of leftist politics in an era of globalized conflict.

This case focuses on a cloud-based software company's efforts to reduce its greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. While the company has already taken steps to achieve this goal—purchasing renewable energy and reducing electricity usage, for example—it will not reach its target of reducing 50% of these emissions by 2030. An internal sustainability council has recommended the purchase of carbon credits, which would have an annual price tag of approximately $8 million. Company leadership is aware that the use of carbon credits is complicated and has both positives and negatives. Many companies that have adopted this approach have, for example, been accused of “greenwashing,” or making claims about sustainability results despite those results being questionable. If the company opts for the carbon credits route, how will it ensure that this approach is truly effective, with tangible results and responsible, honest players throughout the process? Should the purchase be publicized (with the risk of a “greenwashing” accusation), or should it be kept under the radar? This case explores the background, technology, logistics, and complexities of carbon credits, as well as potential other strategies for reducing GHG emissions.

Excerpt

Carbon Credit Markets

You are executive vice president and chief impact officer at Vercelio, a cloud-based software company headquartered in Palo Alto, California. In this role, you oversee the company's global sustainability efforts. The company provides, among other products, customer relationship management applications, with a focus on sales, customer service, and e-commerce. Vercelio's platform utilizes IT, sales, marketing services, and commerce to connect its customers' data across systems, applications, and devices.

Vercelio has committed to reducing its greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 50% by 2030 and has made many changes, from purchasing renewable energy to reducing electricity usage, in pursuit of this commitment. Most of the quick and easy changes have already been made, and it is clear, according to a carbon-analysis consultant the company hired to assess its carbon footprint, that Vercelio will not reach its goal.

You have just met with members of your sustainability council. After much research, the council has recommended that Vercelio buy carbon credits to reach its 2030 goal. As you consider the proposal, you are aware that the topic of carbon credits, also called carbon offsets, is a somewhat controversial one. You are completely aligned with Vercelio sustainability goals but nevertheless understand that taking this step involves both positives and negatives. Many companies that have adopted this approach have, correctly or not, been accused of “greenwashing,” or making claims about sustainability results despite those results being questionable.

The carbon credits Vercelio is considering purchasing will have an annual price tag of approximately $8 million. If you decide to make the purchase, how will you ensure that this approach is truly effective, with tangible results and responsible, honest players throughout the process? Will you publicize the purchase or keep it under the radar? Perhaps you should invest elsewhere. As you look over your team's proposal, you jot down notes in an attempt to understand the complexities of the carbon credit market.

detail.abstract:
The slope and position of the US Treasury yield curve are of fundamental importance to households, investors, banks, and governments. This note explores the determinants of the slope and position, focusing on the short end (pinned down by monetary policy rates) and long end (determined by additional macro-finance factors).

Excerpt

The Position and Slope of the Yield Curve

In mid-2019 the US Treasury yield curve inverted (Figure 1), causing some excitement as yield-curve inversions had preceded every US recession within the past 50 years. Then, after having been upward sloping in 2020 and 2021, the US yield curve shifted up and inverted in 2022, precipitating the failure of Silicon Valley Bank, and stayed inverted for 2 years. But what determines the position and slope of the yield curve?

Figure 1. US Treasury yield curves at four points in time.

Source: Created by author.

0. What Is the Treasury Yield Curve?

We'll focus on the US Treasury yield curve, which plots the yields of US Treasury securities with maturities ranging from one month to 30 years. Figure 1 shows the yield curve as of four points in time: 2010Q4 (dashed line), 2019Q3 (thin solid line), 2022Q4 (thick black line), and 2024Q4 (thick orange line). In 2010Q4 the yield curve was upward sloping and quite steep—longer-term interest rates (for example, on the 10-year or 30-year Treasury bonds) were much higher than short-term interest rates (e.g., on the three-month Treasury bill). In contrast, in 2019Q3 the yield curve was inverted, at least through 10 years, and overall was quite flat. The yield curve was upward sloping in 2020 and 2021 (not shown) because the Fed decreased the short end to zero and the long end didn't move much. Then in 2022 it quite dramatically shifted up and inverted.

title: Empirical or Simulated? Revisiting Training Data Assumptions in Learning-Based Quantum Error Mitigation
affiliations: Lancaster University

detail.title: Empirical or Simulated? Revisiting Training Data Assumptions in Learning-Based Quantum Error Mitigation
detail.abstract: Machine-learning quantum error mitigation (ML-QEM) offers a practical route to reduce noise on NISQ hardware by replacing repeated circuit sampling with a model trained to infer ideal expectation values. However, existing studies differ on how training data are obtained, with some relying on classically simulated noise models and others using data measured from real quantum processors, often without justification of the choice. This work provides the first systematic investigation of how the balance between simulated and empirical training data influences ML-QEM performance. Random circuits of two to five qubits were executed both on the 133-qubit IBM Torino device and its corresponding noise simulator to produce matched datasets containing identical circuits and measurement statistics. Random-forest regressors were trained on five data regimes, ranging from purely simulated to purely hardware-generated training data, while keeping all other experimental factors constant. Performance was assessed through prediction error on platform-independent hardware-based test circuits, with robustness checks conducted using alternative models and resampling analyses. The results show that the models trained exclusively on simulated data achieve mitigation accuracy statistically indistinguishable from those trained on mixed or fully empirical data for the tested circuits. Inclusion of hardware data yields no measurable performance gain. These findings indicate that, for the benchmark families and models tested on IBM computers, the additional cost of generating hardware training data does not translate into improved mitigation effectiveness. The study therefore provides some support for simulator-only training as a justified and costefficient strategy for ML-QEM development, providing an empirical basis for data-source selection.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Imperial Self-Realization Loop (ISR) as a structural model for understanding how large republics drift into, and then become trapped by, imperial arrangements. Rather than treating empire as the product of singular decisions or ideological missions, ISR conceptualizes empire as a recurring response to internal distributional tensions. When core actors in a republic capture disproportionate rents from external circuits, while peripheral groups bear a growing share of the costs and human risks, political elites are incentivized to seek further resources "outside" rather than confront distributional conflicts "inside." Each successful round of expansion and externalization appears to stabilize the system, but also generates new obligations-to veterans, dependent regions, and rent-seeking coalitions-that raise the long-run costs of retrenchment. Over time, the republic's material and institutional skeleton acquires an imperial character, even as republican forms and self-descriptions persist. Using Rome and the contemporary United States as primary cases, the paper develops ISR in three steps. First, it introduces a simple distributive vocabulary of core rents, peripheral returns, and imperial costs, and formalizes ISR as a four-move loop: smallholder or middle-strata erosion, external expansion as compensatory strategy, domestic buy-offs funded by imperial rents, and the accumulation of new obligations that require further expansion. Second, it reconstructs Rome’s transition from a smallholder republic to an empire whose internal stability depended on latifundia, urban grain distributions, and provincial extraction. Third, it analyzes the American loop, focusing on the global security architecture, globalization, deindustrialization, the Pentagon spiral, and the entanglement of welfare and regional economies with imperial infrastructures. The paper concludes by introducing the “restructuring personality” as a leadership type selected by laterepublic ISR configurations, and by reflecting on the normative stakes: whether contemporary republics can develop mechanisms of conscious repricing—periodic reconsideration of who pays and who benefits—before late-republic crises force the issue through disruption.

This paper introduces Project AURELIUS, a next-generation operational doctrine designed to counter illicit financing networks that no longer transact through traceable monetary systems. Current counter-terrorist financing (CFT) architectures remain optimized for bank-linked flows, yet the most resilient threat actors now operate through Barter-Based Terrorist Financing (BBTF), in which commodities such as oil, gold, timber, and mining concessions function as the unit of account, medium of exchange, and store of value.

The doctrine fuses (1) commercial satellite sensing and SAR detection of commodity flows, (2) graph-analytic mapping of shell networks and tokenized asset conduits, and (3) survivor-centric natural language processing to capture ground-truth risk signals at the human layer.

Case typologies including ISIS oil swaps and Sahel gold extraction linked to armed actors illustrate how BBTF economies bypass SWIFT, crypto ledgers, and classical AML thresholds

To prevent misuse, the doctrine embeds a Double-Lock oversight regime combining executive authorization and independent judicial method review, alongside explicit prohibitions on domestic political surveillance, economic espionage, and refugee-data repurposing.

The paper concludes that democratic states must migrate from currency-centric visibility to commodity-centric economic radar in order to sustain deterrence in an era of digitized barter and sanctions-resistant extractive networks.

title: Extreme Value Theory Applied to Twin Primes and Sophie Germain Prime Distributions: A Comparative Statistical Analysis

detail.title: Extreme Value Theory Applied to Twin Primes and Sophie Germain Prime Distributions: A Comparative Statistical Analysis
detail.abstract: We present the first comprehensive application of Extreme Value Theory (EVT) to twin primes and Sophie Germain prime distributions, extending our previous work on prime gaps (https://ssrn.com/abstract=5495027). Through rigorous statistical analysis of the first 1,000,000 primes, we identify 86,027 twin prime pairs and 44,842 Sophie Germain primes, revealing fundamentally different extreme value behaviors compared to general prime gaps. Our analysis demonstrates that twin prime gaps exhibit GEV shape parameter ξ twin = 0.089 ± 0.012 (lighter-tailed than general gaps), while Sophie Germain prime gaps show ξ SG = 0.156±0.015 (heavier-tailed), both displaying Fréchet-type extremes. Twin prime gaps violate Cramér's bound in 26.05% of cases (maximum ratio 7.79), while Sophie Germain gaps exceed it in 28.45% (maximum ratio 6.40), contrasting sharply with general primes (0.003% violations). We establish that twin prime gaps are predominantly multiples of 6 (100.00%), confirming theoretical predictions, with mean gap 180.01 and mean Cramér ratio 0.7558. Sophie Germain primes demonstrate density ρ SG = 0.0448 ± 0.0003 and mean gap 172.67. Shapiro-Wilk tests conclusively reject normality for all three distributions (p < 10-55), validating the necessity of EVT methodology. Our comparative Q-Q analysis reveals distinct tail behaviors across prime classes, providing the first empirical framework for understanding extreme events in special prime sequences.

detail.abstract: Using longitudinal data from the Gallup Panel covering more than 30,000 U.S. employees surveyed from 2023 to 2025, I document heterogeneous adoption of generative AI and its "organizational transmission" within firms. First, I show that the share of active (occasional) AI users grew from 9% to 24% (10% to 23%). I subsequently document these patterns by organizational class of work, organizational hierarchy, income, industry, and occupation. Second, I show that perceived strategic clarity is the dominant correlate of frequent adoption: employees in clear-strategy organizations are roughly 26 percentage points more likely to report frequent use. Strategic clarity itself is tightly linked to managerial communication and credibility, including meaningful feedback and trust in leadership. Third, exploiting within-person variation, income-by-time controls, and a job-switcher design, I show that the relationship between AI use and worker outcomes is strongly contingent on organizational context. Frequent AI use is associated with substantially higher engagement and job satisfaction and with markedly lower burnout when organizations communicate a clear AI strategy, while these benefits are muted or reversed in low-clarity environments. These results are consistent with the predictions from a stylized theoretical model whereby workers are more likely to adopt and experiment with AI when they experience psychological safety.

title: The Development of Domestic Bond Markets

detail.title: The Development of Domestic Bond Markets
detail.abstract: This paper documents the importance of government debt in facilitating the development of corporate bond markets. Using micro-level data from Brazil, I exploit variation in the supply of government bonds at different maturities to estimate the causal effect of additional government debt outstanding on firm issuance decisions. I find that at early stages of development, government debt complements corporate debt, implying that additional government debt outstanding at a given maturity causes firms to issue more. These effects ultimately increase long-term debt issuance and investment across firms, with stronger responses from companies with higher asset duration. However, as markets mature and government debt levels rise, I document a shift from complementarity to substitution. This evidence can be rationalized through government debt reducing corporate pricing uncertainty by providing pricing benchmarks and facilitating price discovery in bond markets.

detail.abstract: Modern industrial civilization, which began with the Industrial Revolution, is considered an unprecedented peak in human history in terms of technological progress, population growth, and material abundance. This civilization was built on the implicit assumption that economic growth can continue forever, that natural resources are inexhaustible, and that human ingenuity can overcome any challenge we face [ ]. However, the second quarter of the twenty-first century is witnessing an accelerating erosion of this premise, as a set of interconnected crises begins to threaten not only our stability but the very existence of industrial civilization as we know it. The challenges we face are no longer separate; the economic crisis cannot be separated from the energy crisis, and both cannot be separated from the geopolitical conflict over resources, all of which are exacerbated by climate and social changes. This interconnectedness is what is called the "Integrated Catastrophe Theory," which suggests that the world is approaching a critical tipping point that could lead to a major civilizational decline by the year. This chapter aims to analyze the four main dimensions of this integrated crisis: economic, geopolitical, scientific/technical, and social, and how each interacts to accelerate the pace of decline.
