Using census data, we document large average gains on all outcomes, alongside substantial heterogeneity by race and gender. On average, Black men exhibit smaller schooling gains than white men but larger employment and earnings gains. Among Black men (and women), we identify a pronounced gradient in gains linked to systemic racial discrimination in the pre–Civil Rights era: individuals born in more discriminatory Jim Crow states realized much smaller gains than those born in less discriminatory states. There is no similar gradient among white Americans. Women of both races exhibit smaller education and earnings gains than men on average, consistent with cultural and institutional barriers to women's work. Our findings highlight the role of opportunities in shaping the extent to which investments in early-life health translate into longer run economic gains.

title: Institutional Trust as a Lever to Integrate Iraq's Informal Economy

detail.title: Institutional Trust as a Lever to Integrate Iraq's Informal Economy
detail.abstract:
This study examines the critical role of institutional trust as a strategic lever for integrating Iraq’s large and persistent informal economy into the formal economic system. Although the informal sector provides livelihoods for millions of Iraqis, its detachment from state oversight stems largely from low public confidence in governmental institutions, complex regulations, and a historical legacy of instability.

The paper analyzes the key determinants of institutional trust,including the quality of public services, transparency of policymaking, bureaucratic efficiency, and the performance of regulatory bodies—and explains how low trust discourages workers and firms from registering or complying with taxation and formal regulations.

Furthermore, the study proposes a practical framework showing how trust-building policies,such as administrative simplification, digital transformation, targeted tax incentives, and strengthened accountability mechanisms ,can convert trust from a social concept into an economic tool. This transformation reduces compliance costs, increases productivity, broadens the tax base, and enhances long-term state stability.

title: Digital Interfaces, Trust, and the Healing Relationship in European-American Clinical Care

detail.title: Digital Interfaces, Trust, and the Healing Relationship in European-American Clinical Care

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Digital tools such as electronic health records (EHRs), telemedicine, and decision-support systems have become prevalent in healthcare systems across Europe and the Americas. While these systems improve care coordination and documentation, they also introduce significant challenges for both clinicians and patients. This article examines the impact of screen use on clinician physiology, cognition, emotion, and the clinician-patient relationship. Drawing on established frameworks, we analyze cognitive overload, physical strain, burnout, and moral distress among clinicians, as well as misinformation, anxiety, and inequity among patients. The use of screens during clinical encounters can diminish eye contact and attention, thereby undermining narrative listening and presence, which are essential to effective care. Such changes risk eroding the trust necessary for treatment adherence, patient satisfaction, and effective health governance. We argue that digital systems should support, rather than supplant, healing relationships. To this end, we recommend user-centered EHRs, ambient documentation, preservation of clinical rituals, responsible data governance, and digital literacy initiatives. Healthcare innovation must uphold the core values of medicine: presence, compassion, understanding, and trust.

title: Strategic ESG Orientation and Financial Resilience in Emerging Markets
affiliations: , Copperbelt University and City University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Strategic ESG Orientation and Financial Resilience in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: This study introduces a diagnostic ESG orientation typology (Strategic, Transitional, and Compliance) to demonstrate ESG orientation, which represents the extent to which ESG practices are internalized and institutionalized within the organization, beyond an ESG disclosure score. It then seeks to establish the link between ESG orientation and financial resilience within Zambia's agro-food sector. It thus enables context-specific conclusions beyond generalized ESG disclosure scores for emerging markets. Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, based on a sample of 55 firm-year observations (2014-2024) of five listed agro-food sector firms, the firm-level analysis applies a fixedeffects panel regression of the quantitative sample. The qualitative classification of ESG orientations is guided by a structured coding framework that applies ISO IWA 42:2024 ESG principles when analysing the texts of the firms' annual reports. Strategic ESG firms (characterized by board sustainability responsibility, longhorizon environmental investments and stakeholder engagement) were financially more resilient (in terms of ROA) than Compliance or Transitional firms. The typology offers explanatory power by connecting depth of ESG integration to profitability trajectories and proves the narrowness of ESG ratings disconnected from strategic framing. This study, unlike extant studies focusing on ESG score levels, conceptualizes ESG as an organizational orientation and proposes an ISO-aligned qualitative classification system that is applicable to emerging markets. This research extends previous studies by providing a typological lens through which the financial materiality of ESG can be understood in weak regulatory environments and thus provide novel diagnostic and policy utility.

title: Stereotypes, Financial Literacy, and Confidence: An Information Provision Experiment
affiliations: and Jönköping University - Jönköping International Business School

detail.title: Stereotypes, Financial Literacy, and Confidence: An Information Provision Experiment

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Financial literacy is an important prerequisite for making informed financial decisions, but it remains low, especially among women and older people. Internalized stereotypes can undermine confidence and subsequently affect behavior in financial matters, leading to suboptimal decisions. This paper investigates how stereotype salience affects confidence in financial literacy. In an information provision experiment, we inform respondents about age or gender differences in numeracy to examine the impact on financial literacy, confidence, hypothetical investment and saving decisions, and demand for information and education. We find that being informed about age differences has no significant effect. In contrast, being informed about gender differences increases the confidence of male respondents through a stereotype boost, while leaving female respondents largely unaffected.

title: Examining the Economic Cost of Investment Lockups
affiliations: and UNC Management Company

detail.title: Examining the Economic Cost of Investment Lockups
detail.abstract: Investment lockups are a defining structural feature of private funds, restricting an investor's ability to redeem capital for predetermined periods. While typically justified as necessary to accommodate illiquid underlying positions, lockups impose a real economic cost by removing the ability to exit opportunistically, particularly during adverse states of the world. Following Longstaff (1995), who demonstrates that illiquidity may be interpreted as the loss of a valuable timing option, we model the forgone liquidity embedded in hedge-fund lockups as a European put struck at the fund's initial net asset value (NAV). Using a Monte Carlo framework and a geometric Brownian motion specification for NAV dynamics, we examine how this option value varies across trend returns and volatility levels. Consistent with Aragon (2007), who documents return premia associated with share restrictions, we find that lockup costs are particularly sensitive to volatility and that low-trend, high-volatility strategies impose economically significant liquidity costs. Our results provide a transparent benchmark for evaluating lockup provisions and assessing whether expected returns compensate for forgone liquidity.

title: Are Existing Preventive Measures that Regulators are Employing to Prevent Stock Market Manipulation Sufficient?

detail.title: Are Existing Preventive Measures that Regulators are Employing to Prevent Stock Market Manipulation Sufficient?
detail.abstract: Stock market manipulation remains a persistent threat to market integrity, investor confidence, and economic stability, particularly as financial markets become increasingly digitised and accessible. This dissertation examines whether the preventive measures currently employed by regulators are sufficient to deter and mitigate modern forms of stock market manipulation. Drawing on peer-reviewed academic literature, regulatory frameworks, and real-world case studies, the research evaluates the effectiveness of existing controls across four key areas: online pump-and-dump schemes, insider trading, analyst-driven persuasion, and biased credit rating practices. Case studies, notably the GameStop short squeeze and the 2008 financial crisis, are used to assess how these measures perform under conditions of extreme market stress and coordinated behaviour. While certain tools demonstrate partial success in reducing volatility and information leakage, the research identifies significant structural weaknesses, including enforcement limitations, behavioural biases, and the adaptability of manipulators.

title: D.A.S.H. II: Defeating Authoritarian Sportshandling and Post-Capture Control

detail.title: D.A.S.H. II: Defeating Authoritarian Sportshandling and Post-Capture Control
detail.abstract: Authoritarian and monopolistic actors often maintain influence in sport long after initial entry. Following ownership, sponsorship, or event access, they consolidate control through governance dependence, market design, and narrative management. This paper extends the D.A.S.H. (Defeating Authoritarian Sportswashing and Handling) framework beyond ingress to examine sportshandling-the phase of post-capture control. The study introduces the P.C.R. (Post-Capture Risk) Model, a five-question, 0-3-point scoring tool that measures narrative dominance, governance dependence, market closure, data and revenue leverage, and the availability of rights and remedies. Using comparative cases-FIFA, Major League Soccer and the U.S. Soccer Federation, the NBA, the IOC and Formula 1, and the Bundesliga 50 + 1 rule-the analysis identifies how legitimacy becomes structural power. Results show that sportshandling flourishes where closed competition, dependent oversight, and captive media ecosystems intersect. The D.A.S.H. II framework complements the original protocol by diagnosing risks that emerge after legitimacy has been laundered, offering regulators and leagues a transparent method for mapping institutional capture and resilience.

title: The Role of Trade Compliance in Strengthening U.S.–Africa Economic Relations

detail.title: The Role of Trade Compliance in Strengthening U.S.–Africa Economic Relations
detail.abstract: This paper examines the strategic role of trade compliance in strengthening U.S.-Africa economic relations. While the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) has expanded duty-free access to the U.S. market, evolving trade policies and regulatory complexities pose challenges for sustainable engagement. Compliance professionals, particularly those with cross-jurisdictional expertise in African, U.S., and maritime law, are essential to mitigating risks, ensuring lawful and ethical commerce, and fostering transparency. Their work enables U.S. companies to participate in procurement, attract investment, and uphold fair trade practices. By advancing a rules-based trading system, trade compliance contributes to economic diplomacy, competitiveness, and long-term partnership between the United States and Africa. This analysis highlights how compliance frameworks are not merely technical requirements but strategic instruments for building trust, stability, and sustainable growth in international trade.

title: Debtor Protection and Health Insurance: Evidence From Personal Bankruptcy Reform
affiliations: Prometeia - AMIF,  and

detail.title: Debtor Protection and Health Insurance: Evidence From Personal Bankruptcy Reform

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We investigate how the use of bankruptcy as an implicit health insurance varies across households, focusing on heterogeneity by asset holdings, race, marital status, and educational attainment. Using a difference-in-differences design based on the 2005 bankruptcy reform, we find that the reform modestly increased health insurance coverage among middle-income households unlikely to lose assets under Chapter 7, with stronger effects for married and less educated households. The reform primarily affected White households, suggesting racial disparities in bankruptcy use. Treated households also showed increased healthcare utilization and spending. These heterogeneous effects highlight how the reform may have deepened existing health and financial inequalities.

title: Pension Wealth and the Timing of Retirement
affiliations: Aarhus University - School of Business and Social Sciences, University of Aarhus - Department of Economics and Aarhus University

detail.title: Pension Wealth and the Timing of Retirement

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We analyze how pension wealth influences retirement timing using 25 years of Danish administrative panel data on wealth and labor market status. Exploiting early-career variation in firm-specific mandatory pension contribution rates, we study labor supply decisions from age 55 onward. Greater pension wealth accelerates labor market exit: at age 63, the elasticity is about 0.3 — an additional 100,000 DKK (15,000 USD) at age 55 reduces earnings by 1% at age 63. Effects intensify near statutory retirement age, driven by self-support and early occupational pension withdrawals. Mandatory savings raise retirement wealth but induce earlier exit, underscoring key behavioral responses for pension policy design.

title: Reverse Stress Testing Geopolitical Risk in Corporate Credit Portfolios: A Formal and Operational Framework
affiliations: University of Orleans, Square Research Center and University of Orleans

detail.title: Reverse Stress Testing Geopolitical Risk in Corporate Credit Portfolios: A Formal and Operational Framework
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a formal framework for reverse stress testing geopolitical risk in corporate credit portfolios. A joint macro-financial scenario vector, augmented with an explicit geopolitical risk factor, is mapped into stressed probabilities of default and losses given default. These stresses are then propagated to portfolio tail losses through a latent factor structure and translated into a stressed CET1 ratio, jointly accounting for capital depletion and risk-weighted asset dynamics. Reverse stress testing is formulated as a constrained maximum likelihood problem over the scenario space. This yields a geopolitical point reverse stress test, or design point, defined as the most probable scenario that breaches a prescribed capital adequacy constraint under a reference distribution. The framework further characterises neighbourhoods and near optimal sets of reverse stress scenarios, allowing for sensitivity analysis and governance oriented interpretation. The approach is compatible with internal rating based models and supports implementation at the exposure or sector level.

title: Behavioural Biases in ESG Due Diligence
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Behavioural Biases in ESG Due Diligence
detail.abstract: This research synthesises a variety of empirical and theoretical literature examining how social and cognitive biases systematically lead to the inaccurate representation of (ESG) environmental, social, and governance due diligence in private equity (PE) buyouts. We employ a variety of behavioural finance theories and gather information from an industry survey of 48 private equity (PE) deal team members, qualitative interviews with industry participants as well as case study analysis to establish that the following recurrent biases materially underrepresent ESG risks and overstate value-creation opportunities: overconfidence, confirmation bias, anchoring, availability heuristic and groupthink. Furthermore, through the enactment of quantitative analysis, we are able to show that PE deals with bias in their assessments of ESG have an average mispricing of enterprise value (EV) relative to bias mitigated benchmarks of 6%-9%. Additionally, we show that 53% of PE deals are ultimately cancelled due to the identification of material ESG issues late in the process, thus resulting in significant sunk costs and revealing the initial assessment was systematically flawed due to cognitive bias. To improve pricing precision, limit unsuspected surprises post-acquisition, and improve long-term portfolio resilience, the research provides a comprehensive debiasing framework that includes mandatory devil's advocacy protocols, multiple independent data anchor points, external specialist involvement for validation of data used and realigned incentive structures that support accurate pricing.

title: Analyzing the Relationship Between Clutch Time Usage Rate and NBA Player Efficiency
affiliations: , University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - UC San Diego and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - UC San Diego

detail.title: Analyzing the Relationship Between Clutch Time Usage Rate and NBA Player Efficiency
detail.abstract: The authors analyze the relationship between clutch time usage rate and player efficiency using National Basketball Association (NBA) regular season and clutch time data from the 2024-2025 season. The study finds insufficient evidence to conclude if players' clutch time usage rate reliably predicts a significant increase or dropoff in efficiency during clutch time situations. The study also found no evidence to support the notion that star players (players with a clutch time usage rate greater than or equal to 0.25) are significantly more or less efficient in the clutch as opposed to the general NBA population.

title: Linking Playmaking Discipline to Scoring Efficiency: An Analysis of Assist-to-Turnover Ratio and True Shooting Percentage in the NBA

detail.title: Linking Playmaking Discipline to Scoring Efficiency: An Analysis of Assist-to-Turnover Ratio and True Shooting Percentage in the NBA
detail.abstract: The authors explore the relationship between assist to turnover ratio and player efficiency using National Basketball Association (NBA) regular season data from the 2020-2025 seasons. The study finds a detectable negative linear relationship between assist and turnover ratio and true shooting percentage, however the model exhibits low explanatory power of variance. Granular position based regressions indicate that forwards are the only position group to exhibit a statistically significant relationship between variables, with guards and forwards both having positive beta coefficients.

This document, spanning 33 pages, underscores the "America First" paradigm, prioritizing national interests such as economic autonomy, border security, and hemispheric dominance. Through a comprehensive analysis, this article examines the NSS's embodiment of exceptionalism alongside its anti-exceptionalist inclinations, compares it with the strategies of the Obama and Biden administrations, traces the historical evolution of dual exceptionalism between China and the United States, assesses the interplay between presidential prerogatives and congressional dynamics, and evaluates whether the strategy reflects a genuine contraction or a strategic "dealmaking" facade. title: Who Benefits from Remote Work?
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Finance Area, NYU Stern School of Business and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School

detail.title: Who Benefits from Remote Work?
detail.abstract: We examine how remote work affects firm productivity and employment outcomes. Using an instrumental variables design based on pre-pandemic occupational remote work suitability, we find that remote work increases the productivity of startups while reducing productivity for established firms. This effect operates partially through labor market scaling: remote startups experience substantially higher hiring rates, overcoming geographical hiring constraints for talent acquisition. Our findings suggest that remote work alleviates a key disadvantage that young firms face in hiring and expanding, while established firms experience challenges in adopting remote working practices.

title: Cannabis Consumption in North American Legal Markets: Evidence from Seven Jurisdictions Across Regulatory Models

detail.abstract: This study establishes baseline cannabis consumption patterns using publicly available sales data from seven jurisdictions: six U.S. states (Florida, Oregon, Michigan, Illinois, Colorado, Washington) and Quebec's provincial monopoly system. Four jurisdictions provide Tier 1 data quality with actual dispensed weight: Florida (medical program), Oregon (recreational), Quebec (state monopoly), and Michigan (recreational, export-adjusted). Colorado and Illinois provide Tier 2 revenue data. Washington provides Tier 3 survey-based data (self-reported expenditures). Notably, consumption patterns remain consistent across fundamentally different regulatory models-private commercial markets in U.S. states versus Quebec's state monopoly retail system-suggesting that regulatory structure does not significantly affect per-user consumption levels. Price variations ranging from $3.00 to $8.00 per gram similarly show minimal impact on consumption patterns, indicating that biological and behavioral factors rather than economic variables primarily determine usage amounts. These findings have substantial implications for market sizing, cultivation capacity planning, tax revenue projections, and regulatory policy design. Accurate consumption baselines enable policymakers and industry stakeholders to develop realistic market models and avoid capital misallocation driven by inflated demand assumptions.

title: Schooling and Prosocial Behavior: Evidence from China's Compulsory Education Reform

detail.abstract: We study the causal relationship between schooling and prosocial behavior in later life by exploiting the exogenous temporal and geographical variations in exposure to the Compulsory Education Law (CEL) across different cohorts as an instrumental variable. Our findings reveal that an additional year of schooling increases the probability of charitable donations by 5.1 percentage points and increases the amount of charitable donations by 26.2%. We provide evidence that the increase in prosocial behavior is driven by improvements in cognitive skills, increased levels of openness and extraversion, as well as higher income, rather than by social pressure effects.

title: Probing Social Abstractions in GPT-2: Intentionality, Fairness, and Deception

detail.title: Probing Social Abstractions in GPT-2: Intentionality, Fairness, and Deception

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable fluency yet remain opaque in how they represent abstract, human-centered concepts. This paper investigates whether the social abstractions intentionality, fairness, and deception are encoded in structured or linearly accessible forms within GPT-2 Medium. Using probing and activation-based analyses, this paper tests whether these concepts can be linearly decoded from activations across layers. The results reveal a clear gradient of accessibility: deception, tied to surface-level linguistic regularities such as overconfident or stereotyped phrasing and common misconception templates, is robustly decodable; fairness shows weak, unstable signals; and intentionality is effectively absent in linear space. These patterns indicate that linguistic correlates are readily captured, while socially grounded reasoning remains diffuse and distributed. The consistently low separation scores across all tasks suggest that these concepts are not localized to discrete units, but instead may be distributed across high-dimensional, entangled directions in representation space. By mapping this spectrum of conceptual accessibility, this paper highlights both the promise and limits of probing as an interpretability tool and underscores the need for methods that move beyond superficial statistical cues toward causal understanding of how large language models represent and use socially meaningful abstractions.

title: The Expanding Demands for Teachers and the Limits of Training
affiliations: Jefferson-Lewis-Hamilton-Herkimer-Oneida BOCES

detail.title: The Expanding Demands for Teachers and the Limits of Training
detail.abstract: In recent years, the work of a teacher has stretched far past teaching lessons in the classroom. Teachers are now expected to step into roles that include helping with student mental health, keeping up with legal requirements, handling new technology, and guiding social and emotional learning. The problem is that most teacher training programs never prepared them for all of these added tasks. This paper looks at how that gap has grown by reviewing recent studies, changes in the law, and biblical examples that offer guidance. It points out how poor professional development, the lasting impact of COVID-19, and a lack of resources have worn teachers down and led to high levels of burnout. By reviewing how these demands developed and where schools are now, the paper shows why older models of teacher preparation no longer work. It ends by offering ways to rebuild teacher support that protect both their jobs and their personal limits, with solutions that are practical and grounded in faith.

title: Occupation-Specific Education Requirements and Occupational Silos: Evidence from CPA Licensing Rules
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Occupation-Specific Education Requirements and Occupational Silos: Evidence from CPA Licensing Rules
detail.abstract: We study the effect of licensing-induced, occupation-specific education requirements on workers' occupational mobility and earnings. We study this question in the context of Certified Public Accountants' (CPAs) licensing rules, exploiting the staggered introduction of a change in the number and composition of CPAs' educational requirements across states. We find that an increase in mandatory accounting-specific credit hours leads to more time spent in accounting jobs, less cross-occupation job switching, and a reduction in the licensing earnings premium. Supplemental analyses indicate that the effects represent a specialization of worker skills rather than a general decline in CPAs' accounting performance. The collective findings suggest that by imposing occupation-specific course requirements, licensing regimes can create less portable human capital, reducing both occupational mobility and the licensing earnings premium.

detail.abstract: Multi-agent trading systems deployed in non-stationary financial markets exhibit catastrophic behavioral drift due to credit contamination and mutual co-adaptation. We introduce TLBA (Two-Level Bias Adaptation), a structural stabilization mechanism that separates a live policy (L1) from a fixed-environment baseline (L2) and periodically cleanses L1 using L2 as a reference anchor. This structure structurally mitigates non-stationarity and credit assignment problems without relying on model complexity or AGI. Furthermore, we interpret the stabilized behavioral layer as the first hypercube of the THS (Theoretical Harmonic Structure) and propose the CEI Hypercube 5 Meta-Architecture. This architecture stacks environmental, observational, normative, and hypothetical layers atop the behavioral cube, providing a practical, quasi-AGI framework for high-dimensional financial decision-making. We validate the stability of TLBA through experiments in both moderate and extreme drift scenarios.

title: Private Credit's Public Consequences
affiliations: and Washington and Lee University School of Law

detail.title: Private Credit's Public Consequences
detail.abstract: The private credit market has become increasingly important as a source of financing for U.S. firms. While large-scale debt financing for firms has traditionally been transacted through public bond offerings or syndicated bank loans, in recent years, firms have been able to achieve requisite financing through alternative channels, particularly through syndicated arrangements by private equity firms. When firms can achieve necessary financing faster, cheaper, and with better customization, such financing is highly beneficial to firm growth and hence benefits both workers and investors in the real economy. At the same time, market innovations, while individually limited in risk, can combine to propagate the transmission of credit and financial stability risks. In particular, private credit is transferring maturity and financial risk from three markets (insurance, credit, and equity) into a financial product with limited disclosure, concentration, and long-dated liabilities that create the potential for maturity mismatch. Coupled with securitization and the introduction of new capital flows from tax-privileged retirement accounts, we detail risks in an industry with limited monitoring and the potential for significant negative externalities. We propose several policy solutions addressing these concerns, with the objective of maintaining the beneficial aspects to private credit, while mitigating downside credit propagation and financial stability risks.

detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of distributed systems, especially in cloud environments, has led to a greater need for advanced security mechanisms. Zero-Trust architectures, which assume that no entity, whether inside or outside the network, should be trusted by default, have emerged as a robust solution to mitigate security risks. However, traditional security models face challenges in dealing with the complexity and scale of modern cloud-native systems. Federated Learning (FL), a privacy-preserving machine learning technique, presents an opportunity to enhance Zero-Trust security enforcement by enabling collaborative model training without sharing sensitive data. This paper explores the integration of Federated Learning with Zero-Trust security models to enforce privacy and security in distributed systems. We discuss the advantages of privacypreserving FL in maintaining data confidentiality while enhancing the effectiveness of security measures. Experimental results demonstrate the ability of Federated Learning to improve threat detection and response times while preserving privacy across decentralized systems

title: The Foundations of Meta Solutionism

detail.title: The Foundations of Meta Solutionism
detail.abstract: This paper introduces Meta Solutionism, a solver-centric, meta-normative framework concerned with the legitimacy of problem formation prior to solution implementation. Existing problem-solving approaches across philosophy, economics, ethics, and systems design typically evaluate solutions after problems are assumed to be given, objective, and neutral. This paper argues that such assumptions obscure a critical antecedent question: under what normative conditions does a proposed solution qualify as a legitimate solution at all. Meta Solutionism addresses this gap by systematically integrating logic, ethics, and aesthetics as jointly necessary conditions for valid solution formation, rather than as separable or sequential considerations. The framework further emphasizes the epistemic role of the observer by examining how perspective, intent, cognitive constraints, and incentive structures shape both the identification of problems and the range of acceptable interventions. Drawing on bounded rationality and probabilistic reasoning, Meta Solutionism employs probability ranges and macro-micro perspective shifts as clarity-oriented tools for allocating attention under uncertainty, rather than as mechanisms for optimization. The framework is applied to illustrative cases that reflect real life dilemmas, demonstrating how technically efficient or ethically motivated interventions may nevertheless fail legitimacy when normative coherence is absent. Meta Solutionism is advanced as a pre-solution architecture that governs how problems are recognized, prioritized, and normatively framed. In doing so, the paper positions framework as a meta-normative contribution that precedes empirical optimization and reframes solution-making as an epistemically and ethically constrained activity.

title: The Gender Logic of Greed: From Defensive Assurance to Expansive Accumulation – A Class-Stratified and Gender-Comparative Study on Female Decision Patterns
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Gender Logic of Greed: From Defensive Assurance to Expansive Accumulation – A Class-Stratified and Gender-Comparative Study on Female Decision Patterns
detail.abstract: This paper constructs and validates an integrated theoretical framework: "Master Drive → Biological Vulnerability → Resource Status → Decision Pattern Differentiation." The ultimate root of global gender conflict is identified as the "Triple Loop of Group Instinct" (derived from [2]), which generates "Absolute Greed Pressure (P)". Here, "greed" is not a moral judgment but a rigid decision tendency for individuals to hedge risk and pursue value in a group context. Gender, through "Biological Vulnerability" (quantifiable indicators like reproductive risk, physical disparity), anchors the female initial decision state to "Defensive Greed": a resource acquisition behavior centered on survival assurance and risk hedging. The core thesis is that Cultural Institutions act as an "Exit Cost Regulator (C)"—the minimum cost required for an individual to maintain survival and dignity after separating from a relationship (marriage/cooperation). Through cross-cultural comparison (East Asia Low-Welfare vs. Western High-Welfare), we find that low-welfare cultures (High Exit Cost C_High) and high-welfare cultures (Low Exit Cost C_Low) exert opposite mechanisms (suppression vs. liberation) on the constant pressure P. This interaction ultimately leads to the "Logical Isomorphism" equilibrium in macro-marriage data—where different paths achieve a similar "demand satisfaction-conflict balance" state. This framework unifies contradictory female behaviors in consumption (savings vs. luxury goods) and marriage (seeking stability vs. seeking compatibility) and provides quantifiable micro-mechanisms for cross-cultural gender studies.

title: Vendor Pricing in Urban Indian Vegetable Markets: A Behavioral Interpretation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Vendor Pricing in Urban Indian Vegetable Markets: A Behavioral Interpretation
detail.abstract: This study examines the pricing dynamics of perishable vegetables in informal markets in India, proposing that observed prices reflect both rational economic factors and behavioral psychological heuristics. Classical economic theory explains perishable goods pricing primarily through supply-demand equilibrium and marginal utility, while spatial economics adds location-based price differentiation. However, field observations suggest that vendor pricing decisions show systematic deviations from purely rational models, consistent with Prospect Theory's insights about reference dependence and loss aversion.

title: Pass-Through of Tariffs to Retail Prices: A Bias-Corrected Local Projection Approach
affiliations: Florida International University (FIU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Pass-Through of Tariffs to Retail Prices: A Bias-Corrected Local Projection Approach
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the dynamic pass-through of tariff changes to 115 item-level retail prices in the United States using a novel monthly dataset spanning three decades (1995-2025). We address the critical econometric challenge of Nickell bias in long-horizon impulse response estimation by employing a bias-corrected split-panel jackknife estimator within a local projection framework. The identification strategy leverages item-specific tariff variation within a robust two-way fixed effects structure that absorbs common time-varying macroeconomic shocks, such as aggregate inflation and business cycles, while strictly controlling for unobserved time-invariant item heterogeneity. The results reveal a distinct reversal dynamic: tariff shocks are highly inflationary initially, but exhibit a statistically significant reversal in the long run, consistent with general equilibrium adjustments. While pass-through was negligible prior to 2010, the post-2010 era, characterized by broad-based protectionism, exhibits a robust, high-magnitude, and persistent transmission of tariffs to consumer prices. We also uncover critical state-dependent asymmetries, as large tariff shocks induce more sustained price adjustments than small fluctuations. These findings suggest that the inflationary costs of modern trade wars are more structurally embedded than previously understood and that standard fixed-effects estimators significantly underestimate the long-run persistence of trade policy shocks.

detail.abstract: The article examines how the principle of procedural autonomy was introduced and then incrementally modified by the Court of Justice of the EU through its self-citation practice. Doctrinal analysis of the jurisprudence of the CJEU is combined with evidence-based methods. Three conclusions are drawn. First, that the principle of procedural autonomy is anchored in the principle of sincere cooperation. Further, that the principle of procedural autonomy was introduced to the case law in 1998, by means of a silent, incremental change of a self-citation. Finally, that procedural autonomy was linked by the CJEU to the 1976 Rewe judgment, which is silent on procedural autonomy. Accordingly, this article argues that procedural autonomy should be read not as Member States' safe harbour, but as Member States' duty to ensure effective enforcement of EU law.

detail.abstract: How does the death of soldiers shape women's participation in the labor market? Using county-level census data from 1925 to 1970, I examine how military mortality during World War II affected women's labor market status in the short and medium term in the German state of Bavaria. Employing a difference-indifferences approach, I find that higher military mortality did not lead to increased female labor force participation in the postwar period. Instead, within the group of non-participants, many women shifted their livelihood from household dependence to state support or self-provision. This effect is mainly driven by war widows.

title: State-Dependent Financial Market Responses to Balance Sheet Policy Announcements

detail.title: State-Dependent Financial Market Responses to Balance Sheet Policy Announcements
detail.abstract: We document state-dependent transmission of balance sheet policy announcements during the large-scale asset purchase era. Using daily Treasury yield changes on FOMC announcement dates as publicly replicable proxies for policy-related news over 2008Q1 to 2023Q4, we show three patterns. First, announcement-day yield responses are substantially weaker when federal debt service relative to revenue is elevated, with attenuation around 60 percent in high debt-burden regimes. Second, interactions between announcement-day surprises and an expectations and uncertainty index operate primarily in low debt-service states and diminish as fiscal conditions deteriorate. Third, periods characterized by accommodative announcement-day yield movements are followed by medium-run declines in private fixed investment of approximately 2.7 percentage points over 12 to 14 quarters (95 percent CI: roughly minus 4.3 to minus 0.8 percentage points), with this pattern aligning more closely with Treasury market functioning measures than with long-term yield movements. The results reveal economically meaningful nonlinearities in announcement-day transmission that are robust across fiscal measures and market functioning proxies.

detail.abstract: Do audit studies predict actual employment outcomes? We match firms from Kline, Rose and Walters (2023)'s large-scale correspondence experiment to LinkedIn employment records. Firms discriminating more against Black applicants in callbacks employ significantly fewer Black workers: moving from a 25th to 75th percentile discriminatory firm reduces the Black share of new hires by 17%, with magnitudes suggesting downstream amplification. This relationship is stronger for employees hired during the audit period and at entry-level positions, and replicates using the exact distinctively race-and gender-coded names from the audit study. However, callback gaps do not predict post-hire outcomes: Black workers face promotion penalties across all firms, but these disparities are uncorrelated with callback gaps. These findings validate correspondence experiments as measures of hiring barriers, suggesting that targeting the most discriminatory firms could reduce aggregate hiring disparities.

title: Neurodiversity in the Workplace: A Comprehensive Examination of Organizational Practices Supporting Neurodivergent Employee Wellbeing

detail.title: Neurodiversity in the Workplace: A Comprehensive Examination of Organizational Practices Supporting Neurodivergent Employee Wellbeing
detail.abstract: The neurodiversity movement has fundamentally transformed how organizations conceptualize cognitive differences in the workplace, shifting from deficit-based models toward strength-based perspectives that recognize the value of neurological variation. This narrative review provides a comprehensive examination of organizational practices that support neurodivergent employee wellbeing, synthesizing research across autism spectrum conditions, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), dyslexia, and other forms of neurodivergence. Drawing on the neurodiversity paradigm, the social model of disability, and personenvironment fit theory-while engaging critically with tensions within and among these frameworks-the article analyzes the prevalence and characteristics of neurodivergent employees, examines workplace challenges and barriers they face, and evaluates organizational interventions with attention to evidence quality. Key findings suggest that environmental modifications, inclusive management practices, flexible work arrangements, and organizational culture change can enhance neurodivergent employee wellbeing and performance, though evidence quality varies across interventions and significant implementation challenges remain. The article critically examines tensions, trade-offs, and unintended consequences of neurodiversity initiatives, addresses structural and policy-level factors alongside organizational practices, and considers perspectives of multiple stakeholders including managers, coworkers, and neurodivergent employees themselves. Particular attention is given to technology and remote work implications, temporal dynamics across career stages, and the evolving nature of work organization. The article concludes with implications for human resource management, organizational policy, and future research directions, while acknowledging limitations of the current evidence base and the contested nature of neurodiversity as both concept and movement.

detail.abstract: This testimony analyzes the 2025 Small Business Administration "audit" of the 8(a) Program within the broader federal procurement integrity framework, emphasizing that oversight is delivered through multiple, overlapping institutions and tools rather than a single,  fraud-enforcement process. It explains how independent Inspectors General, GAO, DOJ enforcement, bid protests and eligibility challenges, and disclosure and whistleblower mechanisms operate in parallel, each with distinct evidentiary thresholds, procedural protections, and remedies. It notes that oversight discourse frequently blurs critical distinctions among fraud, improper payments, ineligibility, documentation deficiencies, waste, abuse, and mismanagement. Those categories are not interchangeable: “fraud” is a legal conclusion that typically requires adjudicative determination, while many integrity problems reflect non-fraud control failures, administrative error, or weak monitoring. The testimony also places these classification problems in a broader environment of weakened oversight capacity and contested independence for key watchdog institutions. It notes the practical compliance constraints facing small businesses, warning that rapid, standardized documentation demands can end up measuring administrative capacity as much as misconduct. It closes by urging Congress to focus on implementing outstanding GAO recommendations on certification controls and monitoring and to require transparent classification standards before using audit outputs to support sweeping fraud claims.

detail.abstract: Since the outbreak of conflict in 2015, Yemen has been engulfed in one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with the education sector suffering devastating consequences. This paper examines the multifaceted collapse of the Yemeni education system, characterized by the destruction of infrastructure, the non-payment of teachers’ salaries, politically manipulated curricula, and the forced withdrawal of millions of children from school. Citing data from leading international organizations, the paper illustrates the scale of the crisis, including alarming dropout rates and rising illiteracy. Amid this devastation, the paper highlights a glimmer of hope through a 2025 case study by Al-Qadri and Al-Jarrah on the implementation of web-based learning journeys in Sana’a. The study demonstrated that basic, low-cost technology can significantly improve cognitive skills, such as spatial reasoning in geometry, even in conflict zones. This paper argues that technology, despite its limited use in Yemen, represents an effective, scalable, and cost-effective solution for mitigating the educational crisis. The research paper concludes by calling for increased investment and support from government agencies, NGOs, and international partners to harness digital platforms, mobile learning, and AI-based tools as a practical path toward restoring education and ensuring the country’s long-term development prospects.

title: U.S. Government Intervention in Venezuela: Game Theoretic Analysis -From the Perspective of Complete Information Games and Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium with Detailed Mathematical Formulation

detail.title: U.S. Government Intervention in Venezuela: Game Theoretic Analysis -From the Perspective of Complete Information Games and Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium with Detailed Mathematical Formulation
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the political crisis in Venezuela based on publicly available information as of January 4, 2026, assuming three players: the U.S. government (US), Maria Corina Machado (M), and Delcy Rodriguez (R). In the context of the capture of President Nicolas Maduro by U.S. forces, we estimate each player's payoffs and examine the U.S. government's response in two settings: a complete information game and an incomplete information game (Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium: PBE). The results show that in the complete information game, the U.S. government's negotiation strategy leads to a subgame perfect equilibrium, while in the PBE under incomplete information, belief updates adjust Rodriguez's cooperation probability, maximizing the U.S. government's expected payoff. This discusses the mathematical implications for U.S. foreign policy. Additionally, robustness analysis of payoffs confirms that the settings have low arbitrariness and the conclusions are stable.

detail.abstract: CO2 capture and sequestration is widely considered an option for decarbonizing integrated iron and steel production. This study estimates the levelized cost of mono-ethanolamine (MEA) CO2 capture, transportation, and sequestration for integrated steel mills in the U.S. and evaluates the associated air quality impact based on the AP4 Integrated Assessment Model. We find the discounted CO2 avoidance costs are $42-$62/tCO2. SO2 and NOx emissions are projected to increase due to the energy consumption required for CO2 capture. However, wet flue gas desulphurization can decrease SO2 emissions from reference levels by 94%-95%, while NOx selective catalytic reduction can reduce NOx emissions from reference levels by 23%-75% or at least ameliorate the negative impact of CO2 capture on air quality. The estimated costs and benefits of CO2/SO2/NOx emissions changes show that MEA CO2 capture with gas pretreatment increases the net social benefits of CO2 capture industry-wide from -$382 million to $2.9 billion.

title: Nonlinear Performance Effects of Competitive Market Signalling Strategies: Agent-Based Evidence from a Hypercompetitive Oligopoly

detail.title: Nonlinear Performance Effects of Competitive Market Signalling Strategies: Agent-Based Evidence from a Hypercompetitive Oligopoly
detail.abstract: Competitive market signalling is the study of how firms intentionally send announcements of future behaviour with the knowledge that such 'signals' are received and responded to by competitors. Research methods thus far have been largely void of both observation of signals within a real competitive setting and complexity. This study engages with those missing methodological approaches to provide insights into the ways in which non-linear signalling behaviours (tipping points) and their respective counterparts (equilibria) are generated within the context of a real empirical system. To do so, an agent-based model is developed to investigate the combined effects of signalling timing, vagueness of language and bluffing. The outputs of the model are a set of tipping points and equilibria that are then tested for observability against an empirical system. The observed subset is then analysed to determine what signalling behaviours most explain the change across observed phenomena. The intended contribution is to show, within the context of real industry behaviour, how a complex systems lens can be extended into competitive market signalling by investigating the non-linearities of performance change. Doing so highlights the leverage points within a strategic system by which signalling behaviours can be adopted or modified for gaining advantage over competitors.

title: Heterogeneous Effects of Macroprudential Policies on Credit Volatility: Evidence from Composite Measures

detail.title: Heterogeneous Effects of Macroprudential Policies on Credit Volatility: Evidence from Composite Measures
detail.abstract: We construct composite indicators of macroprudential policies (MaPPs) using a novel dimension-reduction approach and apply them to a panel of 119 countries over 2000–2015. Our empirical analysis evaluates the effectiveness of MaPPs in stabilizing private credit while explicitly accounting for unobserved cross-country heterogeneity. The results show that MaPPs do not exert uniform effects: depending on the macro-financial environment, they may either dampen or amplify credit volatility. Borrower-targeted measures are generally effective in low-income and moderate-leverage economies, while financial-intermediary-targeted measures display context-dependent, and occasionally procyclical, effects. Overall, the findings indicate that the success of macroprudential interventions depends critically on country-specific structural and financial conditions rather than on the mere adoption of policy tools.

title: Fiscal Deficits and Current Account Imbalances: Stabilization Policies and Long-Run Equilibrium

detail.abstract: Debates on the macroeconomic effects of fiscal policy on consumption and demand continue to centre on the relevance of the Twin Deficit Hypothesis (TDH), reflecting tensions between frameworks grounded in myopia, income uncertainty, and borrowing constraints (Feldstein, 1982, 1988; Bernheim, 1987, 1988), and the rational expectations framework associated with Barro (1974, 1989), which assumes perfect foresight, perfect capital markets, consumption smoothing, and operative intergenerational transfers. Under the Ricardo-Barro rationale, fiscal effects are deemed neutral, thereby challenging the government's capacity to stabilize the external balance through fiscal consolidation. This paper proposes the Long-Run Fundamental Balances Hypothesis (LFBH) as a unified framework to accommodate these competing views on fiscal policy effects and the macroeconomic linkage. Building on Engle and Granger (1987), Stock and Watson (1993), and Pesaran et al. (2001), the LFBH examines whether a stable long-run relationship exists between the current account balance (CAB) and the overall fiscal balance (OFB). The cointegrating vector is normalized on the external component (CAB); therefore, the fiscal component is treated as weakly exogenous. As uncertainty and unstable time preferences weaken the consumption-smoothing mechanism-by altering the consumption path consistent with uninsurable income risk (Feldstein, 1988) and precautionary saving motives (Caballero, 1990)-fiscal policy may exert real effects, rendering strict Barro-Ricardian neutrality unlikely. Within the LFBH, this is captured by a robust long-run coefficient, β ̸ = 0, which governs both the magnitude and the direction of adjustment. Key Policy Implications. The LFBH delivers three main theoretical results for the macroeconomic linkage: it defines the steady-state level, provides a closed-form adjustment path, and predicts the current account's response to a one-off, permanent fiscal shock. Moreover, the sign of the robust-to-endogeneity long-run coefficient β is economically informative regarding the internalization of the intertemporal budget constraint: β > 0 supports the Twin Deficit Hypothesis and reflects myopia or binding constraints, whereas β < 0 indicates partial forward-looking behaviour.

title: No Blood in my Mobile: Regulating Foreign Suppliers
affiliations: EU Tax Observatory

detail.title: No Blood in my Mobile: Regulating Foreign Suppliers
detail.abstract: Can developed countries ensure that the goods they consume are not linked to human rights violations in the developing countries where they are produced? I study the U.S. Dodd-Frank Act Conflict Mineral Rule (2010), a due diligence policy limiting the use of conflict minerals extracted in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and adjoining countries in supply chains of U.S. downstream eletronic firms. The law increased administrative costs of complying firms by 4.2%, showing that subtantial regulatory constraints were created. I show that these firm-level adjustment changed global exports of minerals: exports of conflict minerals from DRC and neighbours decreased by 76.5%. Around one fifth of this change comes from circumvention through legal havens, which then re-export more intensively where foreign suppliers of U.S. firms are located.

title: Climate-Induced Internal Displacement in Pakistan: Human Rights Gaps, Legal Fragmentation, and Policy Pathways
affiliations: University of Sindh

detail.title: Climate-Induced Internal Displacement in Pakistan: Human Rights Gaps, Legal Fragmentation, and Policy Pathways
detail.abstract: Despite contributing minimally to global greenhouse gas emissions, Pakistan ranks among the countries most severely affected by climate change. Recent extreme weather events-most notably the catastrophic floods of 2022 that inundated nearly one-third of the country and displaced millions-have laid bare critical weaknesses in Pakistan's legal and policy frameworks for protecting populations uprooted by climate-related disasters. This article examines Pakistan's domestic laws and international obligations relevant to climate-induced displacement, identifies systemic protection gaps affecting displaced communities, and evaluates the extent to which existing human-rights guarantees are realised in practice. Adopting a policy-oriented and rightsbased lens, the study proposes targeted legal and institutional reforms to strengthen protection, ensure equity, and promote durable solutions. Key recommendations include the enactment of a dedicated legal framework on climate-induced internal displacement, the integration of displacement risk into federal and provincial planning, improved access to remedies and civil documentation, and the expansion of social protection and resettlement programmes grounded in human-rights standards.

title: A Texas Practitioner's Guide to Tax Foreclosures of Mineral Interests
affiliations: Texas Tech University School of Law

detail.title: A Texas Practitioner's Guide to Tax Foreclosures of Mineral Interests
detail.abstract:
Texas serves as the primary hub for oil and gas production in the United States, driven largely by its unique system of privatized mineral ownership. This ownership model allows mineral interests to be severed from the surface estate, yet leads to rapid fractionalization over generations as interests are divided among heirs. This extreme fragmentation often results in "missing" owners who are unaware of their holdings or their property tax obligations, ultimately leading to tax foreclosure suits and sheriff’s sales.
    This Article examines the legal tension between the state’s taxing power and the constitutional due process rights of mineral owners. A central issue is the use of "notice by posting" or publication. Within this process, if a taxing authority fails to conduct a "diligent inquiry" to locate an owner whose identity is readily ascertainable in public records, the resulting foreclosure judgment may be deemed void. Such void judgments create significant title instability, as they can be challenged through collateral attacks that are often immune to standard one-year statutes of limitations.
    This Article provides a comprehensive analysis of how these legal vulnerabilities impact four major stakeholders: (1) original claimants seeking to recover divested interests, (2) tax sale purchasers relying on sheriff's deeds, (3) oil and gas operators managing royalty payments, and (4) title examiners tasked with verifying the chain of title. By exploring recent Texas Supreme Court jurisprudence regarding equitable defenses and the requirements for diligent inquiry, this Article aims to equip practitioners with the tools necessary to navigate the contentious landscape of mineral tax foreclosures while also supporting the state’s policy of promoting energy development.

title: The Soil of Underdevelopment: Land in Haiti

detail.title: The Soil of Underdevelopment: Land in Haiti
detail.abstract: This chapter examines Haiti's unique land distribution following its independence in 1804 and its potential impact on the country's long-run development. Unlike much of Latin America and the Caribbean, Haiti became a nation of smallholder farms due to institutional choices made after independence. Using newly assembled microdata on over 17,000 plots from 1920 to 1959, the chapter provides new insights on Haiti's farm sizes and land inequality. The data show that the 1950 census underrepresents the prevalence of the smallest farms. They also show evidence for declining farm size over time. Finally, the data provide the first calculations of Haiti's farm size inequality that include large farms. While they show inequality was higher than implied in the census, it was much lower than comparable countries. By highlighting the institutional roots of Haiti's land tenure system, this study offers new insights into the relationship between property rights and economic development.

title: When Breaking Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) is a Piece of Cake Linearizing secp256k1 through Midpoint Symmetry
affiliations: My Digital Truth

detail.title: When Breaking Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) is a Piece of Cake Linearizing secp256k1 through Midpoint Symmetry
detail.abstract: Standard cryptographic security relies on the assumption that discrete points on an elliptic curve lack a visible causal connection, rendering brute-force attacks impossible. This paper challenges that paradigm treating the Generator not as a static point, but as a dual-coordinate gear defining rotation and descent. By establishing a "Sovereign Midpoint" as an absolute reference, the perceived complexity of the secp256k1 curve is reduced to a linear measurement. Using a stylized 11-unit model and empirical proof for secp256k1, the author demonstrates that every private key functions as a simple index number in a symmetric field. By mapping the "Minimum Pulse" of the Y-coordinate horizon, the search space is transformed into a "Double-Sided Ruler," where any public key can be identified as a specific offset from the center. This approach effectively converts the discrete logarithm problem into a straightforward task of surveying and counting, rendering traditional ECC encryption as simple as a "straight line.

detail.abstract: Which poverty context matters for long-term outcomes—family or community, economic or social? We construct a measure of poverty along these dimensions and analyze individual-level longitudinal data spanning 21 years in Indonesia to examine the long-term outcomes associated with different types of deprivation experienced in childhood. We find that adverse outcomes in adulthood are associated not only with growing up in a poor family but also in a poor community. Family poverty generally has a stronger influence than community poverty, except for health and life satisfaction, which are shaped more by the community. We also find that both economic and social domains matter, with the economic domain’s influence being stronger. Girls’ education suffers more from exposure to early deprivations, whereas boys’ health is hit harder. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for different dimensions of childhood deprivation, and they have strong policy implications for addressing inequality of opportunity.

detail.abstract:
Rulers in premodern states faced severe constraints from domestic elites, religious authorities, and foreign powers. Standard accounts in historical political economy explain their responses in terms of fiscal capacity, coercion, and institutional
bargaining. Yet some of the most puzzling episodes do not fit this pattern: emperors “becoming monks,” kings “selling” their kingdoms to the Church, or rulers voluntarily accepting vassal status under external overlords. This paper argues that such acts are not mere expressions of piety or weakness but instances of reverse-hostage strategies. Instead of seizing hostages from powerful groups, rulers strategically offer themselves as hostages to religious or external patrons in order to change elite incentives and increase their probability of survival. A simple two-stage model formalizes this logic and links the choice among status quo sovereignty, religious reverse-hostage, and external reverse-hostage to observable parameters. The argument is illustrated with Emperor Wu of Liang and King John of England.

detail.abstract: In the transition from fossil energy to renewable energy, innovation and thus the patent system, plays an important role. Using the solar PV industry as an example, the article shows how a coherent approach to energy policy and innovation policy is necessary, because of the externalities of the technology neutrality of patent law. Patent law inadequately incentivizes innovation in renewable energy technologies over fossil technologies. Furthermore, patent law does not stimulate sustainability in the renewable energy industry as such, evidenced by the reliance on coal-fired utilities in production of solar PV systems. Energy or environmental policies that support sustainability in the dynamics of the market will indirectly include sustainability in patent law, as market dynamics are integrated in the normative rationale of patent law. The article discusses how such policies can support the functions of patent law, driving innovation in renewable energy technologies and contributing to ensure that energy and industry markets are sustainable.

title: A Two Kernel Model for Climate Strategy: Mitigation as Closed Optimization and Adaptation as Stochastic Resilience

detail.title: A Two Kernel Model for Climate Strategy: Mitigation as Closed Optimization and Adaptation as Stochastic Resilience

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Two-Kernel Model, a structural framework for understanding why national climate strategies succeed or fail. Traditional climate planning relies on linear policy or technology pathways, but this approach often collapses when applied to real-world economic, social, and financial conditions.
The Two-Kernel Model separates climate strategy into two interacting kernels: a Stability Kernel, which determines a country’s structural readiness (infrastructure, fiscal capacity, political continuity, and technological absorption), and a Trajectory Kernel, which shapes the dynamic pathway of emissions reduction, investment allocation, and market response.

By separating these two kernels, the model explains why countries with similar policies achieve vastly different results, why decarbonization paths diverge after initial success, and why investment-driven climate transitions frequently stall despite strong policy ambition. The framework integrates economic structure, behavioral incentives, national risk systems, and climate-finance architecture into a unified strategy function.

The paper demonstrates how the Two-Kernel Model can be used to diagnose structural bottlenecks, predict decarbonization outcomes, and redesign national climate strategies. It provides a generalizable method for linking policy, finance, and infrastructure within a coherent analytical system, offering practitioners and researchers a new tool for understanding and improving climate transition performance.

title: The Impact of Economic Reforms on Welfare and Conflicts in Post-Soviet Eastern Europe

detail.title: The Impact of Economic Reforms on Welfare and Conflicts in Post-Soviet Eastern Europe
detail.abstract: This paper investigates leading indicators of successful reform in former Soviet republics and satellite states in Eastern Europe by analysing political and economic reform indicators from 1990 to 2025. The study focuses on nine countries divided into two groups. The successful reformers consist of Czechia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland, and the group of unsuccessful reformers consist of Armenia, Georgia, Moldova, and Ukraine. Using GDP per capita and monthly salary as measures of economic success, this study analyses the trends and causal relationship between human rights, economic freedom, political rights, civil liberties index, control of corruption, government effectiveness, political stability/absence of violence, and rule of law. Quantitative analysis found that political reformers that improve rule of law and control of corruption are key to successful economic reforms and prosperity. Furthermore, qualitative analysis found that economic prosperity positively correlated with participation in international institutions such as the EU and WTO because it incentivised and guided transitioning countries. These findings are important for the lagging economies in Eastern Europe, especially postwar Ukraine, showing that they must first conduct political reform in order to improve economic welfare.

detail.title: Export Promotion: What is Missing? (Identification of Gaps and Policy Options)
detail.abstract: (This paper intends to figure out the factors, both of structure and policy, responsible for the stagnation of Pakistan's exports. For doing so, a critical analysis of the structure of exports and export-oriented schemes is conducted. The export structure is analyzed in the light of data of the Atlas of Economic Complexity of Harvard Growth lab and World Integrated Trade Solution (WITS) trade statistics while for the analysis of export-oriented initiatives, relevant data of FBR is used for the period 2020-21 to 2024-25. A critical evaluation of export structure shows that exports are characterized by low complexity, low tech-content, and low value-added. Pakistan's revealed comparative advantage (RCA) lies in goods like textile, raw hides and skins, food items, and agricultural products. Its export value index has not witnessed a sharp increase over time in comparison to those of India, Bangladesh, and Vietnam. Analysis of export-oriented schemes suggests that they are biased in favour of the big exporters. Low utilization of these schemes by the small and medium-sized exporters amply vindicates the said assertion. The findings of this paper suggest that anti-export bias, low productivity, and policy neglect of small and medium-sized exporters are the main factors behind the stagnation of exports. It is suggested that exemption of input goods, meant for export, from import-stage tariffs should be given through tariff code and not schedules with strings attached or sector-specific SROs. This policy shift would induce the small and medium-sized exporters in particular to avail exemptions. Gradual phasing out of import tariffs to reduce anti-export bias, a well-coordinated industrial policy, prioritization of innovation and productivity, SME-based export strategy and transforming the existing natural clusters into clusters of exports, besides granting exemption of inputs through tariff code, are recommended as public policy prescriptions to meet the challenge of low exports.) title: The Behavioral Physiology of Reproduction: A Control-Theoretic Account of Fertility Collapse under Modern Contraceptive Environments

detail.title: The Behavioral Physiology of Reproduction: A Control-Theoretic Account of Fertility Collapse under Modern Contraceptive Environments
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a new endogenous dynamical theory of fertility decline based on a single modification to standard behavioral assumptions. Specifically, we introduce the hypothesis that the immediate suppressive signal governing sexual behavior-modeled as homeostatic inhibition-does not reference realized fertility outcomes or anticipated childrearing costs, but instead depends solely on experienced sexual reward. Modeling human reproductive behavior as a closed-loop control system, we show that under modern sexual environments characterized by low-cost contraception with negligible attenuation of sexual reward, fertility-suppressive behavior is maximized as an immediate consequence of quasi-static individual optimization, without requiring any temporal evolution. By further introducing the dynamic accumulation of chronic anxiety as a downstream state variable, together with the long-run degradation of behavioral control, the model endogenously generates multiple empirically observed phenomena. Representative implications include withdrawal from romantic relationships, paradoxical fertility responses to simulated childrearing experiences, short-term fertility rebounds followed by long-term collapse under coercive pronatalist policies and increasing aversion to passive exposure to sexual content. Unlike existing economic, institutional, or cultural explanations, the proposed framework yields structural temporal predictions and articulates a clearly falsifiable central hypothesis. The theory provides a unified perspective for understanding fertility decline across diverse institutional and cultural contexts, ranging from liberal democratic societies to historical cases of authoritarian intervention.

detail.abstract: Contemporary sustainability and environmental governance frameworks rely heavily on proxy metrics, optimisation models, and compensatory mechanisms that often obscure irreversible ecological change and long-term loss of future options. While tools such as environmental impact assessment, cost-benefit analysis, and offsetting regimes support comparative evaluation, they frequently treat ecological impacts as substitutable, deferrable, or reversible within administrative or market-based logic. This paper argues that a central governance blind spot lies in the inadequate treatment of irreversibility. It proposes a conceptual governance perspective that treats irreversible ecological commitments and the foreclosure of future option space as non-negotiable constraints shaping decision admissibility, rather than as variables to be balanced or optimised. Building on insights from ecological economics, resilience theory, and systems thinking, the paper introduces the Entropic Governance Framework (EGF) as a pre-standard, procedural discipline for examining decisions under constraint. EGF does not propose new metrics, optimisation models, or policy prescriptions. Instead, it reframes sustainability as a governance problem of how irreversible commitments are surfaced, justified, and owned within decision processes. The framework emphasises transparency, accountability, and escalation of justification when actions create long-lived ecological lock-in or constrain future adaptive capacity. This paper offers a conceptual positioning of EGF intended to support critique and interdisciplinary dialogue. A detailed applied case study demonstrating implementation of the Entropic Governance Framework is currently under peer review. The present paper focuses on conceptual positioning and theoretical grounding, intended to support interdisciplinary dialogue and critique while the applied work proceeds through formal review.

detail.abstract:
This research provides a comprehensive, forward-looking evaluation of the global AI infrastructure cycle, assessing the financial sustainability, energy feasibility, and long-term economic viability of hyperscale AI investment across NVIDIA, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and OpenAI. Leveraging comparative financial modeling, industry capex trajectories, semiconductor supply constraints, and cost-per-inference economics, the analysis highlights a structural imbalance between current AI infrastructure spending and the monetization capacity of existing AI products. Results show that hyperscalers are deploying unprecedented levels of debt-funded and cash-funded capex to acquire GPUs, expand data centers, and secure energy supply, while AI-derived revenue remains between 1-3% of topline which is far below the 15-20% threshold required to sustain multi-year AI buildouts. Energy limitations, including regional power scarcity and grid lead-time delays, further reduce the scalability of AI clusters and increase the risk of infrastructure stagnation.

Scenario modeling identifies the 2023-2026 period as an early-cycle hypergrowth phase in which AI chip orders may grow at 100%+ annually, followed by a normalization window in 2027 onward where demand stabilizes at 20-40% of peak volumes. In this maturing phase, companies unable to close monetization gaps face structural risk. OpenAI emerges as the system’s critical weak link due to limited revenue diversification, no profitability, and dependence on external funding. Meta faces commoditization risk, while NVIDIA’s long-term growth becomes exposed to demand decay once hyperscaler saturation peaks. Meanwhile, Microsoft, Google, and Amazon maintain relative resilience due to diversified revenue bases, though they remain vulnerable to delayed AI adoption, energy shortages, persistent high interest rates, and reduced cloud expansion.

The study concludes that the AI sector is currently overbuilt relative to economic output and resembles the early dot-com period with rapid infrastructure expansion without proportional monetization. Unless enterprise AI adoption, consumer willingness to pay, and breakthrough automation accelerate meaningfully, the sector will face a correction driven by the convergence of financial tightening, energy constraints, and monetization inefficiency. This paper emphasizes the need for top-down AI infrastructure planning, realistic TAM calibration, and insights on Energy & AI Compute analysis to extrapolate path towards sustainable AI Infra expansion enforcing market stability and prevent a sector-wide downturn.
