detail.abstract: Autonomous AI systems collapse the historical separation between producing a capital asset and operating it. Once deployed, such systems can perform operational functions autonomously, eliminating the need for continuous human operating labor to generate returns on the capital investment in the system. Because the production of these systems does not require sustained use of firm-internal resources, there is no structural necessity that their development occur within the deploying firm. While builders can produce these systems externally, their economic value is realized only upon integration into the deploying firm's infrastructure, controls, and workflows. These conditions enable a new production model in which bespoke, self-operating systems are developed externally by specialized builders and transferred to firms as exclusive capital assets. Yet no standard contractual framework governs such transactions. Firms, therefore, initiate these acquisitions through employment or services arrangements, bargaining structures optimized for coordinating and controlling human labor, rather than for acquiring self-operating capital. This misalignment at the level of the initial bargain produces predictable structural failures: unintended IP expropriation, accounting distortions arising from improper capitalization, incentive misalignment between builders and firms, and ongoing contractual obligations that outlast the asset's deployment. This paper introduces the Capital Asset Formation Agreement (CAFA), a contractual framework governing asset formation and the transfer of autonomous systems as capital assets. We identify the conditions under which external asset formation becomes viable, demonstrate why labor-based contracts fail structurally when applied to autonomous system acquisition, and present CAFA as a market-clearing mechanism that aligns legal form with economic substance. The framework separates asset transfer from integration labor.

title: Autonomous Capital: Production Theory and Contract Design for Self-Operating Systems
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Autonomous Capital: Production Theory and Contract Design for Self-Operating Systems
detail.abstract: The standard Cobb-Douglas production function relates output to two inputs: capital (K) and labor (L). Capital amplifies productivity, but labor supplies the operative function, the human effort that activates capital and generates output. If labor goes to zero, output goes to zero. This paper introduces synthetic labor (S) as a third input in the Cobb-Douglas framework, a non-human factor that occupies the operative role historically assigned to human workers. By incorporating S into the production function, we show that autonomous AI systems do not merely augment labor; they perform the operative function itself, thereby allowing output to persist as human operating labor approaches zero. This modification to production theory carries a direct implication for the theory of the firm. When operational intelligence is embedded in capital rather than supplied by labor, the firm's function shifts from Coasean labor coordinator to capital allocator, acquiring and capitalizing externally produced autonomous systems rather than organizing workers to operate passive assets. These theoretical claims have immediate institutional consequences. Firms seeking autonomous systems currently acquire them through employment and services agreements, instruments designed for labor coordination rather than asset transfer. This misclassification produces predictable failures: IP expropriation, accounting distortions, incentive misalignment, and structural debt (legal and organizational errors made upstream that become embedded in the system's architecture, yielding implementations that function in research settings but fail under operational conditions). The paper introduces the Capital Asset Formation Agreement (CAFA) as the contractual framework that operationalizes the shift from labor procurement to capital acquisition. CAFA separates asset transfer from integration labor, platform from implementation, and capital consideration from service fees, aligning legal form with the economic substance that production theory now requires.

title: The Option Value of Work: Life-Span Uncertainty and the Geometry of Taxation
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Option Value of Work: Life-Span Uncertainty and the Geometry of Taxation
detail.abstract: This paper develops a new microfoundation for the Laffer curve by modeling labor supply as the exercise of a real option with stochastic maturity. Individuals are interpreted as holding an American call option on future consumption, while taxation places the government in the corresponding short-call position. As remaining lifetime becomes shorter or more uncertain, the option’s time value collapses and the curvature (gamma) of the utility function rises. This sharply increases labor-supply sensitivity to marginal tax rates and compresses the Laffer curve. The framework provides structural explanations for why aging economies face declining fiscal capacity, why health shocks trigger strong labor-supply responses, and why redistributive preferences vary systematically with demographic composition. The model unifies insights from public finance, life-cycle theory, and option pricing, and suggests new avenues for optimal taxation and policy design.

title: AI-Driven Structural Speed Mismatch and Systemic Failure in Socio-Technical Systems: Toward a Multi-Layer Learning Paradigm

detail.abstract:
Why do socio-technical systems increasingly exhibit persistent instability even as their technical components demonstrate rapidly improving learning and adaptive capacity? This paper addresses this question by reframing systemic failure as a structural coordination problem rather than a collection of isolated technological or institutional deficiencies.

 

The central argument is that AI-driven acceleration intensifies pre-existing asymmetries in learning speed across cognitive, technical, and institutional layers. While each layer continues to adapt according to its own internal logic, their characteristic temporal dynamics diverge, progressively undermining cross-layer consistency. Under such conditions, localized optimization or governance adjustments remain structurally insufficient to restore system-wide stability.

 

To analyze this dynamic, the paper introduces a Multi-Layer Learning Paradigm (MLLP), which conceptualizes socio-technical systems as coupled learning structures composed of heterogeneous layers with distinct rates of adaptation. System stability is defined in terms of the sustained alignment of these layers over time. The analysis identifies recurring structural failure patterns that emerge when learning speeds remain persistently misaligned, including cognitive fragmentation, diminishing effectiveness of technical interventions, and institutional lag in absorbing accumulated deviations.

 

The contribution of this paper is to provide a unified structural explanation for why the expansion of AI-related capabilities may coincide with systemic instability, by interpreting such failures as endogenous outcomes of asymmetric learning dynamics across layers.

detail.abstract: I examine how the economies of scale in credit card lending affect mortgage lending via the spillover of information gathered from credit card operations. I find that a one standard deviation increase in the number of credit cards per capita increases mortgage origination by 10.2% and decreases interest rates by 16.6 bps. Collectively, my results are consistent with the hypothesis that information gathered from credit card operations reduces the uncertainty faced by lenders and thereby increases the supply of credit in the mortgage market.

detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of multi-cloud architectures has transformed the way organizations manage their IT infrastructure, offering scalability, flexibility, and cost efficiency. However, this shift introduces significant security challenges, particularly concerning data protection, threat detection, and access management. Traditional security models often fall short in multi-cloud environments, where data is spread across various providers and platforms. This paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies into multi-cloud security architectures. We examine how AI and ML can enhance the detection of security threats, improve risk management, and automate responses across disparate cloud platforms. detail.abstract: Advances in generative AI have ushered sophisticated tools into tax and legal practice. These tools can hallucinate, fabricating citations, quotations or factual assertions that appear plausible yet are entirely false. In Mata v. Avianca, U.S. attorneys relying on ChatGPT filed a brief containing fictitious case law and were sanctioned. Such incidents expose significant risks for professionals who rely on AI without thorough verification. By late 2025 a survey of court records and disciplinary actions documented nearly 800 AI‑related citation errors across at least 25 countries. These cases include filings by lawyers and pro se litigants as well as orders drafted by judges. This article examines how courts and administrative bodies worldwide have responded to AI‑generated hallucinations in tax and legal submissions and decisions. It compares sanction regimes and remedial measures in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, India, Israel and other jurisdictions. The analysis highlights emerging verification standards under existing procedural rules and professional‑conduct codes. It assesses how courts treat different actors, lawyers, self‑represented parties, experts and judges, and how tax and legal doctrines are adapting to the challenges posed by unreliable AI outputs. The paper also considers legislative reforms and bar‑association guidance aimed at mitigating AI risks.

title: Unethical Factors Contributing To Nigeria's Economic Underdevelopment: Analysis From An Islamic Perspective

detail.abstract: If the human and natural resources a country is endowed with are the yardsticks for its greatness and development, it is undisputable that Nigeria is destined to be great. However, in the global economy system today, Nigeria is conspicuously located in the periphery of the periphery despite its abundant resources. This is attributed to various unethical factors like mismanagement of resources and large-scale embezzlement that have hindered its development and contributed to its economic backwardness. This paper explores these factors. It relies on both primary and secondary sources of data. Viewing ethics and  unethical practices from an Islamic perspective, it argues that unethical practices which Islam strongly prohibits have been normalized in Nigeria's economic and sociopolitical milieu. This consequently worsens the country's economic woes with little prospect for redemption. It observes that serious attention has not been paid to how these factors undermine development. Drawing on some verses of the Qur'an and prophetic traditions, this paper analyzes how revenue should be generated, utilized, and geared towards economic development. It concludes that economic practices in Nigeria are, in most cases, a departure from Islamic ethical principles of economics despite the fact that, demographically, the Muslims are the majority. These ethics, if observed, benefit not only the Muslims but the country. To liberate the country from the clutches of underdevelopment, this paper strongly recommends that Islamic ethics should be mainstreamed in government activities - particularly in law making, budgeting, policy formulation, and policy execution. This consideration will greatly help to revamp the economy and enhance development.

detail.abstract: This analysis examines the OECD’s Pillar Two framework, which establishes a global 15% minimum corporate tax to address tax competition and profit shifting. It traces the evolution of international tax governance from pre-globalisation physical presence rules to the rise of intangible asset mobility, and explores the shift from BEPS 1.0 to BEPS 2.0. The paper discusses theoretical justifications rooted in economic rent theory and details the structure and mechanisms of the Global Anti‑Base Erosion (GloBE) rules, including model rules, safe harbours, identification of multinational enterprise groups, and effective tax rate calculations. It analyses the unified fiscal subject approach and policy‑based exclusions and assesses their impact on tax sovereignty. The study addresses special considerations for U.S.‑parented MNEs, adjustments from accounting income, and the influence of covered taxes on effective rates. It examines the allocation of taxing rights through the ordering of Qualified Domestic Minimum Top‑Up Taxes (QDMTTs), Income Inclusion Rules (IIR), and Undertaxed Profits Rules (UTPR), and evaluates risks of enforcement fragmentation. The paper compares residence and source jurisdiction interests, highlighting revenue distribution disparities and fiscal autonomy constraints, particularly for developing economies. It concludes by discussing potential reforms and long‑term sovereignty trade‑offs, stressing the need for broad participation and robust enforcement to sustain global tax cooperation.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the OECD’s Pillar Two global minimum tax initiative, anchored in the GloBE Model Rules that ensure multinational enterprises pay at least a 15 percent effective tax rate. It examines key mechanisms including the income inclusion rule (IIR), undertaxed profits rule (UTPR), and qualified domestic minimum top‑up taxes (QDMTTs), as well as the carve‑outs such as the substance‑based income exclusion and incentives like qualified refundable and marketable transferable tax credits. The paper reviews the EU’s Directive 2022/2523, U.S. legislative proposals, Asia‑Pacific QDMTTs, and the Subject to Tax Rule multilateral instrument signed in September 2024. It discusses implementation challenges, including integration with domestic laws, divergent adoption across jurisdictions, compliance complexity, and long‑term threats posed by tax‑credit schemes. The paper concludes that broad participation and robust enforcement are critical for the sustainability and effectiveness of Pillar Two.

It argues that Pillar Two replaces the traditional benefit principle with coordinated fiscal cartels, and analyses key administrative developments in 2024‑2025 such as the OECD’s June 2024 guidance on securitization vehicles and deferred tax liabilities, and the September 2024 signing of the Subject to Tax Rule multilateral instrument. detail.abstract: When plaintiffs seek preliminary injunctions, courts provide early signals about case merits that shape settlement negotiations. I analyze how the accuracy of these signals affects litigation outcomes. Denial and grant both affect settlement, but asymmetrically. Denial weakens the plaintiff's bargaining position and increases settlement-the plaintiff accepts less favorable terms. Grant strengthens the plaintiff's position and decreases settlement-the plaintiff rejects settlement. The denial effect dominates, so more informative preliminary rulings promote settlement overall. This creates a tension with social welfare, however. False denials are locked in by settlement; false grants are self-corrected at trial. Courts focused on clearing dockets may deny preliminary injunctions too often, accepting higher error costs to achieve marginal gains in settlement. When defendant care is endogenous, denial-heavy standards also undermine deterrence. The framework provides guidance for ongoing debates about preliminary injunction standards in patent, antitrust, and other areas.

detail.abstract:
Taxpayers have six wins and zero losses in cases that grant nonrecognition to exchanges that occur in proximity to tax-free business transactions (contributions to and distributions from entities) of the exchanged property. Those six cases (the proximate-exchange cases) were decided between 1983 and 1989. From those cases emerged the proximate exchange principle: “[a] trade of Property A for Property B, both of like kind, may be preceded by the tax-free acquisition of Property A at the front end, or succeeded by a tax-free transfer of Property B at the back end.” Despite the explicit declaration of the proximate-exchange principle and the almost four decades since the last proximate-exchange case was decided, lawyers and other tax advisors continue to caution property owners against doing the transactions that have explicitly been sanctioned by the courts and lead them to alternative structures.

One reason advisors may caution against doing proximate exchanges is that proximate-exchange cases and their resulting transactions have been heavily scrutinized over the years. Such analyses appear to disregard the proximate-exchange principle. An equally problematic result of advising against court-sanctioned structures is the advice to engage in one of several pre-packaged alternative structures. Despite their popularity, these alternative structures appear to have escaped scrutiny over years. This Article fills that gap by recounting the overwhelming authority supporting proximate exchanges and turns a critical eye to the alternative structures. Not surprisingly, those alternative structures do not hold up under such scrutiny.

The foundation supporting proximate exchanges is the overlapping purposes for granting nonrecognition of gain provided under section 1031 and the partnership tax contribution and distribution rules. When considering structured exchanges, courts and the Internal Revenue Service deviate from traditional tax principles that elevate substance over form and apply a form-driven analysis that is a unique part of section 1031 jurisprudence. No authority applies the form-driven analysis to alternative structures. Alternative structures, which are beyond the form-driven analysis of section 1031 jurisprudence, do not stand up under judicial and other principles. This Article applies substance-over-form principles to the alternative structures and shows that such structures add complexity, transaction costs, and non-tax risks but do not reduce tax risks.

detail.title: The Impact of Foreclosure on Housing Market: Evidence from Milwaukee
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of foreclosure on housing values in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, using a property-level panel constructed by linking mortgage transaction data from Black Knight, borrower characteristics from the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA), and assessed home values from Milwaukee County's Master Property File (MPROP) over 2007-2020. Employing both static panel models and an augmented interrupted time series (AITS) event-study framework, we trace the dynamic evolution of home values before and after foreclosure. While a static specification yields an average depreciation of 8.12%, the event-study reveals that the effect peaks at approximately 13% around four years post-foreclosure, reconciling our findings with larger estimates in prior literature. Our analysis uncovers pronounced racial disparities: Black and non-Black homeowners follow similar pre-foreclosure trajectories, but Black homeowners experience substantially larger and more persistent post-foreclosure declines. We document a novel role for loan duration, with each additional year of ownership prior to foreclosure associated with a 1.71% decline in value-a finding we validate using the AITS framework as reflecting genuinely different post-foreclosure dynamics rather than a statistical artifact. Finally, homes in areas with foreclosure rates above the 90th percentile experience substantially more severe value reductions, consistent with threshold spillover effects. These findings highlight how foreclosure's consequences vary across race, ownership duration, and neighborhood context.

title: Policy Trade-Offs from Complementary Resource Consumption: PV Adoption and Residential Water Use
affiliations: University of Alabama, Department of Economics, Finance, and Legal Studies and University of Nevada Las Vegas

detail.title: Policy Trade-Offs from Complementary Resource Consumption: PV Adoption and Residential Water Use
detail.abstract: Recent rapid growth in residential solar photovoltaic (PV) adoption has spurred investigation into whether households exhibit a "rebound effect, " increasing overall electricity consumption post-adoption. Though sizable increases in electricity usage have been documented, the extent to which these rebound effects spill over onto complementary goods such as water has not been explored by prior literature. Using panel data from Henderson, NV, we provide the first evidence of spillovers. PV installation increases water usage by approximately two percent relative to pre-installation, which we attribute to a complementarity rebound effect. Our findings highlight a unique policy trade-off, as solar potential is spatially correlated with water scarcity. We demonstrate that ignoring the water impacts of residential PV adoption may inadvertently exacerbate water scarcity, particularly in regions where water conservation is most critical.

title: Central data monitoring of clinical trials: a survey of the UKCRC registered clinical trial units in the UK
affiliations: University of Southampton, , Institute of Cancer Research (ICR) - Clinical Trials and Statistics Unit (ICR-CTSU), University of Bristol, , Queen Mary University of London and

detail.title: Central data monitoring of clinical trials: a survey of the UKCRC registered clinical trial units in the UK
detail.abstract: Background: Central data monitoring is activities performed by trial staff to improve the quality, integrity, and reliability of trial processes and data collection whilst a trial is open. The aim of this research was to determine the variation in activities conducted and the barriers, roles and documentation involved across UKCRC trials units. Methods: A survey asking about the central data monitoring activities conducted by trials units was sent to all UKCRC registered trials units on 25th April 2025. We listed 16 central monitoring activities and asked about whether or not they were conducted on any, some or all trials and which staff role was responsible. Results: Responses were received from 63.5% (33/52) of CTUs between until 5th June 2025. 8 of the 16 activities: protocol compliance and deviations, patient flow (e.g., CONSORT chart), recruitment versus predicted recruitment, eligibility issues, consent issues, data completeness for primary analysis, missing CRFs, and data outliers, are conducted for all trials by at least 27/33 (81.8%) of the units and for some trials by all the trials units. 10/16 (62.5%) of the activities were done by a mixture of staff roles at the majority of units. Conclusions: Our survey shows the variety in the central data monitoring activities conducted by UKCRC trials units and the variation as to who is conducting these activities. We make recommendations to improve the consistency and quality of monitoring in UKCRC trials that includes recommending during trial set up consideration of conducting all the top 8 activities for all trials.

title: Does Gig Economy Reshape Accrual Properties? Evidence from Uber Entry
affiliations: Clarkson University, Clarkson University and Temple University - Department of Accounting

detail.title: Does Gig Economy Reshape Accrual Properties? Evidence from Uber Entry
detail.abstract: This study examines whether the emergence of the gig economy reshapes firms' accrual properties. Exploiting Uber's staggered entry across U.S. states as an exogenous shock, we find that accruals become less correlated with cash flows after Uber's market penetration. This effect is partly driven by increases in firms' human capital investments which are expensed rather than capitalized and do not necessarily translate into future cash flows. Consistent with this mechanism, the attenuation in the accrual-cash flow association is more pronounced for firms that adopt more employee-friendly workforce policies, provide greater employment insurance, and exhibit larger declines in accrual expense volatility. Collectively, our findings highlight how labor market shifts contribute to temporal changes in accrual properties, while underscoring the relevance of the SEC's 2020 amendment to Regulation S-K-which mandates enhanced disclosure of human capital investments-for financial statement users.

detail.abstract: The availability of local knowledge useful for enforcement of taxes is a common motivation for decentralized tax administration, a benefit to be traded away for economies of scale with centralization. However, there is limited empirical evidence that localized agencies are able to capitalize on this information advantage. This research exploits geographic variation in Colorado's level of government responsible for general local sales tax administration to investigate enforcement effectiveness relative to the state. Specifically, we employ data on Airbnb monthly listings from 2017 to 2019 to test for heterogeneity in the behavioral response to local sales tax increases. The results demonstrate larger reductions in Airbnb listings in response to sales tax increases where localities are responsible for tax enforcement, consistent with a model where local governments were more effective than the state at Airbnb detection. Further investigation indicates that local governments' advantage relative to the state was in detecting properties that were frequent listers on Airbnb.

title: Dao Governs All, Techniques Verify the Origin: Human Nature Institutionalism-A New Paradigm of Institutional Dynamics based on the Axiom of Myopia and Its Cross-Cultural Empirical Evidence

detail.title: Dao Governs All, Techniques Verify the Origin: Human Nature Institutionalism-A New Paradigm of Institutional Dynamics based on the Axiom of Myopia and Its Cross-Cultural Empirical Evidence
detail.abstract:
Existing institutional studies are trapped in Western-centric paradigms, flawed "homo economicus" assumptions, and failures to unify behavioral explanations. This study takes the Axiom of Myopic Human Nature as the sole and unshakable foundation—humans inherently prioritize immediate diversified interests (fame, power, morality) and avoid immediate harms, a gene-encoded essence irrelevant to morality, self-evident and unprovable. Without this axiom, all subsequent deductions (three theorems and two lemmas) collapse entirely.
Based on this axiom, we originally propose Human Nature Institutionalism (HNI), a quantitative institutional dynamics paradigm rooted in traditional Chinese governance wisdom. Three foundational theorems (Force Attenuation, Institutional Swing, Institutional Efficiency) and two derivative lemmas (Interest Path, Pendulum Effect) are logically deduced—all constructs originate exclusively from the axiom, with lemmas extending theorems to quantify institutional trajectory and swing amplitude.
Validated via triangulation (cross-temporal/cross-cultural cases, 1248 global observations, ABM simulations), HNI reconstructs institutional economics’ human foundation, modernizes non-Western wisdom into quantifiable models, and provides a universal operational framework for cross-cultural governance, perfectly responding to Journal of Institutional Economics’ call for non-Western original theorization and interdisciplinary innovation.

title: Do Narratives Crowd Out Fundamentals? Retail Investors' Response to Generative AI
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Business, Xi'an Jiaotong University (XJTU) - School of Management, Lingnan University and Singapore Management University

detail.title: Do Narratives Crowd Out Fundamentals? Retail Investors' Response to Generative AI
detail.abstract: This study examines how retail investors respond to the advent of generative AI and the ensuing capital-market consequences. Using a large language model to analyze millions of investor questions from China's Investor Interactive Platforms (IIP), we document a structural reallocation of retail investors' information demand. Following the launch of ChatGPT, firms with high prior AI engagement receive significantly more AI-related questions, while questions about non-AI topics decline. This shift in information demand is associated with higher trading volume and volatility but, paradoxically, weaker price informativeness. Our findings suggest retail investors' AI information demand introduces speculative noise and crowds out their attention to non-AI fundamentals, providing a novel perspective on how generative AI transforms financial markets.

title: The Option Value of Work: Life-Span Uncertainty and the Geometry of Taxation
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Option Value of Work: Life-Span Uncertainty and the Geometry of Taxation
detail.abstract: This paper develops a novel microfoundation for the Laffer curve by modeling labor supply as the exercise decision of a real option with stochastic maturity. Individuals are interpreted as holding an American call on future consumption, while taxation places the government in the corresponding short-call position. Uncertainty about remaining lifetime reduces the time value of labor, increases the curvature (gamma) of the indirect utility function, and amplifies labor-supply responsiveness. The Laffer peak emerges precisely when utility gamma equals the tax-scaled cross-derivative, linking revenue maximization to the geometry of preferences. The framework provides structural explanations for why labor-supply elasticities rise sharply with age, health shocks, and demographic transition, and why aging economies face declining fiscal capacity. The model unifies insights from public finance, option theory, and life-cycle labor economics, and suggests new avenues for optimal taxation and policy design.

title:
Beyond the Trade
My Journey Building an Industry

detail.title:
Beyond the Trade
My Journey Building an Industry
detail.abstract:
Time has a peculiar way of compressing and expanding, depending on the weight we bear and the contexts in which we act. In the world of technology and finance, a month can feel like a decade; in moments of forced stillness, a day can stretch far beyond its hours. As I write these words, a new chapter of my life is beginning, but its foundations reach deep into decades of curiosity, risk, challenge, and recalibration.

I was raised amidst the backdrop of China’s rapid transformation—my early childhood hauntingly marked by a country’s journey from rural poverty to a surging engine of global ambition. My parents, both educators, instilled in me a simple discipline: be curious, work hard, aim to leave things better than you found them. When our family emigrated to Canada, I encountered a new set of codes—social, linguistic, technological. With relatively little in monetary terms, but a world of possibility ahead, the seeds of independence and resilience took hold.

This book is the product of over twenty years spent building, learning, failing, and—occasionally—thriving at the intersection of finance, technology, and entrepreneurship. My journey took me through writing code for trading systems in New York and Tokyo, launching startups that nearly ran out of cash, and ultimately, gambling everything on the then-nascent world of cryptocurrencies. I’ve experienced bull runs and bear winters so extreme they seemed almost theatrical, regulatory crackdowns that crashed market capitalizations overnight, and, most recently, a period of literal confinement that forced me from the pace of hypergrowth into a state of radical reflection.

title: Nonattainment under the Clean Air Act: Tracking Designations and Modeling the Timing of Attainment

detail.title: Nonattainment under the Clean Air Act: Tracking Designations and Modeling the Timing of Attainment
detail.abstract: This paper examines how political partisanship shaped both the designation and resolution of county-level nonattainment (NA) status for total suspended particulates under the Clean Air Act. Logistic models show that adding emissions, industrial composition, political leadership, and EPA regional effects to pollution measures increases in-sample accuracy from 81% to 88%, indicating that designations reflected more than air-quality metrics. Among 1978 NA counties, Cox models with time-varying coefficients show that Republican-led states attained earlier in the mid-1980s, while counties with larger annual exceedances transitioned more slowly; both effects diminished over time. These results highlight evolving political and scientific drivers of NA decisions.

detail.abstract: The prohibition of ribā ‫(رِبَا)‬ in the Qur'an is traditionally interpreted as a categorical ban on interest. This interpretation, while historically grounded, becomes increasingly strained when applied to modern fiat monetary systems characterized by systematic debasement, inflation uncertainty, and state-backed credit institutions. This paper argues that ribā is not reducible to a timeless numerical prohibition, but is a moral category aimed at preventing domination through obligation under conditions of stable money. By combining Qur'anic textual analysis, historical monetary context, and formal economic reasoning, the study demonstrates that (1) the Qur'anic ribā prohibition presupposes measurability of principal, (2) fiat debasement fundamentally breaks this measurability, (3) modern interest functions primarily as an uncertain estimation of purchasing-power erosion rather than guaranteed surplus extraction, and (4) the collapse of principal measurability demands a reconceptualization of ribā as a moral category rather than a mechanical rule. The paper concludes that insisting on literal equivalence between ribā and modern interest produces internal contradictions that the Qur'an itself does not demand.

title: The Crisis of Faith in Western Civilization: Law, Meaning, and the Search for Moral Order

detail.title: The Crisis of Faith in Western Civilization: Law, Meaning, and the Search for Moral Order

declarations.declarationOfInterest: My research and writing focus on the intersection of law, faith, history, leadership, and global development, with particular emphasis on how legal systems, spiritual traditions, and moral philosophy shape civilizations during periods of crisis and transition. Drawing from over three decades of practice in international law, constitutional law, immigration, and human rights, my work explores how law functions not merely as policy, but as a moral architecture for society. A central theme of my scholarship is the crisis of faith and meaning in Western civilization, and how this crisis influences democratic stability, justice, migration, war, and economic inequality. I engage in comparative religious traditions - including Judaism, Christianity, Islam and Eastern spiritual thought - as sources of ethical reasoning relevant to modern governance and public life. My current projects include: -Law and spiritual ethics in times of civilizational transition -Leadership theory grounded in moral philosophy and historical memory -Space law and American leadership in emerging frontier domains -Global development, migration, and post-colonial legal frameworks -Interfaith dialogue as a stabilizing force in fractured societies

detail.abstract: Western civilization is experiencing a crisis of faith unlike any in its recorded history. This crisis is not limited to declining religious observance or institutional distrust-though both are visible symptoms. It is, more fundamentally, a crisis of meaning itself. The moral and metaphysical assumptions that once undergirded Western law, politics, education, and social life have eroded, leaving behind a powerful legal and technological machinery increasingly disconnected from any shared vision of ultimate purpose or moral truth. The structures of order remain, but the spiritual and philosophical foundations that once gave them coherence are increasingly brittle.¹ For nearly two millennia, Western civilization rested on a synthesis of Jerusalem, Athens, and Rome-biblical faith, Greek reason, and Roman law. From Augustine and Aquinas to Grotius and Blackstone, law was never merely procedural. It presupposed a moral universe: truth existed, justice was real, power was accountable to conscience, and the human person possessed inherent dignity.²

title: The Dialectics of Fate: The Ethics of Actualization
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Dialectics of Fate: The Ethics of Actualization
detail.abstract:
The theoretical trajectory of this research project has evolved from a structural analysis of socio-political mechanics in Anatomy of Chaos to a fundamental redefinition of reality itself in The Ontology of the Observer. Having established in the preceding metaphysical framework that Consciousness serves as the fourth fundamental coordinate of existence—the necessary mechanism for collapsing potentiality into actuality—we must now address the profound ethical implications of this cosmology. This paper, The Dialectics of Fate, serves as the final integration of the physical and the metaphysical, deriving a system of human conduct directly from the ontological premises of our model. We posit that if the human agent is the functional instrument through which the "Metaphysical DNA" of the universe resolves probability into history, then ethics is no longer a matter of social convention or religious dogma, but a strict protocol of navigational responsibility.

Central to this framework is the translation of our ontological reinterpretation of the Cartesian cogito—"I observe, therefore I actualize"—into a practical philosophy of action. We argue that the structural tension between the inertia of Matter and the teleology of Consciousness creates a tragic dialectic, presenting the individual with two distinct, mutually necessary existential strategies: the Path of Fusion and the Path of Actualization. The former represents the choice to reintegrate with the biological flow, providing the system with essential stability and mass; the latter represents the choice to inhabit the "Empty Throne" of the Observer, providing the system with its vector and capacity for transformation. This paper demonstrates that neither path offers a moral high ground or an escape from the systemic costs of existence. Instead, we offer a rigorous demarcation between the functional necessity of these roles and the pathology of gratuitous violence, arguing that the ultimate ethical duty is not to save the world from its inherent thermodynamics, but to bear witness to its unfolding with a clarity that precludes self-deception. Thus, we conclude the system not with a promise of salvation, but with a definition of dignity compatible with a deterministic universe.

detail.title: Bank Governance: Lessons Still Not Learned

detail.abstract: Policymakers learned the wrong lessons about bank governance from the 2008 financial crisis—and the response to Credit Suisse's collapse demonstrates that these misconceptions persist. Post-crisis commentators blamed agency conflicts between shareholders and management, focusing on short-term behaviours. The real culprit was risk-shifting: shareholders, boards, and management together transferring risk to debtholders and taxpayers. The policy response was counterproductive: say-on-pay provisions, deferred equity compensation, and enhanced shareholder engagement do not reduce risk-taking—they amplify it. Supervision failed to prevent risk-shifting because regulators operate reactively, intervening only after problems materialise. Credit Suisse exemplifies this dynamic: despite repeated regulatory interventions, its shareholder value-oriented board continued to pursue ever riskier strategies. Concrete solutions exist, but they require fundamental reform of managerial compensation and of the role of boards and supervisors. Instead of exclusive equity-based compensation, regulators could impose pay that aligns with creditors' interests and financial stability. More boldly, banks could adopt structures giving creditors and supervisors governance powers commensurate with risk exposure. The point is to move from reactive supervision—which attempts to constrain risk-shifting after the fact—to prophylactic governance: restructuring the incentive environment so that risk-shifting cannot operate effectively, rather than treating its symptoms after they have manifested themselves.

detail.abstract:
Background: Universal models on community response to disasters, such as the Zunin and Myers model have guided global psychosocial support systems, including in India. Such universal models may overlook cultural nuances and contemporary hazards, particularly in diverse Majority World contexts like India with distinct collectivist ethos and kinship networks. 
Research Objective: This paper critically examines limitations of universal disaster response models in addressing diverse cultural settings, emphasizing the need for culturally-sensitive and data-driven frameworks that reflect India's unique socio-cultural landscape and evolving hazard profile. 
Methods: A two-stage mixed-methods design was employed. Stage 1 comprised a historical literature review of the Zunin and Myers model's development. Stage 2 involved content analysis augmented by directed content techniques, applied to in-depth interviews with 12 disaster responders (volunteers, NGO members, officials) who operated during the 2018 floods through 2024 landslides in Kerala. Coding combined a priori themes from the original model with inductive discovery of novel patterns. 
Major Findings: Seven clusters emerged. The heroic phase was validated but manifested through collective leadership and informal networks. The honeymoon phase was prolonged by extended family and community support, suggesting renaming to "collective solidarity." A disillusionment phase was largely absent due to sustained state and community support. Reconstruction proceeded with strong community-government collaboration. Three additional themes of responder mental health and preparedness, socio-cultural contextual factors, and institutional learning that were not captured in the original model were also suggested. 
Conclusion: Uncritical use of universal models risks misinterpreting local realities and hindering recovery. Kerala’s experience reveals culturally specific adaptations that challenge key assumptions of universality in disaster response, particularly around disillusionment. Incorporating extended family systems, collective agency, and continuous institutional evolution is essential for developing indigenous, data-driven disaster response frameworks in India. Future research should compare across regions and include community perspectives to refine culturally grounded models.

title: Sequencing Stability: A Developmental Framework Explaining why Mis-Timed Ethical and Spiritual Governance Produces Social Disorder

detail.title: Sequencing Stability: A Developmental Framework Explaining why Mis-Timed Ethical and Spiritual Governance Produces Social Disorder
detail.abstract: Why do moral, ethical, or spiritual governance frameworks often failand sometimes intensify violencein fragile societies? Existing political and development theories explain instability through economics, institutions, or ideology, but rarely address the sequencing of societal readiness. This paper proposes a three-stage developmental framework arguing that societies must pass through material stabilization, psychological regulation, and ethical-spiritual integration in sequence. The central claim is that ethical or spiritual abstractions, when imposed prematurely on materially insecure societies, function not as moral guidance but as ideological instruments, increasing polarization and collective violence. Drawing on comparative historical cases, the framework explains recurrent policy failures across revolutionary, post-conflict, and fragile states. The paper contributes a diagnostic tool for policymakers, conflict analysts, and development planners, emphasizing that ethical governance is not universally stabilizing but context-dependent and sequence-sensitive.

detail.abstract:
Humanity is confronting climate change — a crisis undeniably rooted in the environmental externalities of industrial civilization. Yet the global distribution of responsibility and vulnerability remains structurally asymmetrical. Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and Small Island Developing States (SIDS), despite contributing minimally to historical emissions, face the most severe climate impacts. Paradoxically, these nations risk becoming the last entrants into a high-emission development pathway, not by choice but due to infrastructure deficits and delayed access to low-carbon systems. This dynamic creates a persistent attribution conflict between developed and developing economies:
Who is responsible for emissions embedded in modern infrastructure? Who benefits from emission-reducing systems that others still lack? While the Greenhouse Gas Protocol defines Scope 1–3 boundaries, current accounting methods remain ambiguous in causal allocation and incomplete in capturing infrastructure-enabled decarbonization. They measure who emits, but not who reduces emissions by enabling low-carbon civilization.
This paper introduces Scope 0 — a causality-based accounting layer that quantifies emission reduction enabled by systemic infrastructure, social functionality, and avoided-emissions pathways. We propose a mathematically tractable and repeatable logic for quantifying decarbonization impacts driven by access to electrification, digital services, mobility, and public goods infrastructure. The framework addresses the structural gap between emitters, beneficiaries, and infrastructure enablers, enabling a fair, verifiable, and reproducible attribution system.
By grounding climate accounting in causal inference rather than static boundary definitions, Scope 0 establishes a  foundation for equitable mitigation incentives and global climate justice — especially for late-transition economies.

title: Dynamic Weighted Voting System (DWVS): A Framework for Fair and Accountable Political Participation

detail.title: Dynamic Weighted Voting System (DWVS): A Framework for Fair and Accountable Political Participation
detail.abstract: Traditional electoral models suffer from critical flaws: universal suffrage (one person, one vote) often produces irrational outcomes due to uninformed voters and delayed accountability, while classical elite systems breed rigidity and inequality by granting static privileges. This paper proposes the Dynamic Weighted Voting System (DWVS)-a novel framework where political influence (voting weight, maximum 20 points) is earned and maintained through two independent dimensions: Knowledge Weight (up to 10 points, assessed by standardized civic exams every five years) and Moral Weight (up to 10 points, adjusted in real time based on verifiable misconduct). Unlike elitebased meritocracy or capital-weighted systems, DWVS ensures procedural fairness: every citizen has equal opportunity to gain maximum influence, but neglecting to re-test or failing to uphold ethical standards automatically reduces their weight. By combining recurrent re-testing, strict ceilings, and immediate moral accountability, DWVS addresses the irrationality of mass democracy and the rigidity of static privilege, establishing a system of efficient, fair, and continuously accountable governance.

detail.abstract: Why do "impossible trilemmas"-from monetary policy to AI safety-appear structurally persistent? We propose the Means-Limitations-Purposes (MLP) framework, grounded in a triadic Resources-Capital-Information (RCI) constraint model, as a dynamic alternative to static trilemma thinking. Rather than inherent contradictions, such tensions arise under specific RCI configurations where available means cannot jointly satisfy multiple purposes. Across six governance domains (e.g., climate, health, education), our analysis shows how targeted interventions-technological (R), institutional (C), and informational (I)-can reconfigure constraints and relax trade-offs. Artificial intelligence provides a critical test case: its computealgorithm-data structure maps directly onto RCI, while AGI's "non-overlap" problem elevates information to a meta-constraint. We formalize MLP-RCI in symbolic logic, establishing it as a computable system model amenable to simulation and policy design. The framework does not claim universal resolution, but suggests that when R, C, and I evolve in synchrony, previously intractable trilemmas may become tractable. For scholars and practitioners, MLP-RCI offers a structured, cross-domain language to diagnose roots of conflict-and design coordinated pathways toward dynamic multi-objective balance in the AI era.

title: Blessing of Order Crossover for Inventory Systems
affiliations: Institute of Operations Research and Analytics, NUS and

detail.title: Blessing of Order Crossover for Inventory Systems
detail.abstract: We investigate the effect of order crossover in inventory systems with stochastic leadtimes. In systems with sequential supplies, the optimal cost grows linearly with the demand rate 𝜆, failing to achieve economies of scale. In contrast, while order crossover renders parallel supply systems generally intractable, it facilitates a significant reduction in the optimal cost to Θ(𝜆^{1/3})-a phenomenon we term the blessing of order crossover. To exploit this benefit, we propose simple policies that achieve this optimal rate by leveraging only two base-stock levels. Our results highlight the fundamental difference between sequential and parallel supply systems, and provide quantitative insights into the impact of order crossover. We also extend our analytical framework to account for different unmet-demand assumptions, demonstrating the universal rate-optimality of our proposed policies when unmet demands are backlogged, lost, or have stochastic patience. With a simple modification, our proposed policies remain rate-optimal even when unmet demands are censored from the inventory manager.

detail.abstract: In apex and constitutional courts, decisions are typically taken by a panel. If the panel decides per curiam, decisions can at most be explained by the fraction of panel members that share some demographic marker. Using this approach, in the German Constitutional Court outcomes are not significantly explained by the policy preferences of the political party that has nominated the majority of the justices on the panel. This paper puts the non-result to a harder test. It exploits the fact that justices have fixed dockets, defined by subject matter. It uses a hybrid approach, combining a rich dictionary of keywords with a large language model as the umpire for the residual uncertainty, to infer the identity of the justice referee. As, for a small number of cases, the court publicizes the name of the referee, the accuracy of the method can be evaluated, and is acceptable (78.26%). Yet also the preferences of the political party that has nominated the justice referee only explain success with a request for a preliminary ruling, not success on the merits.

title: Stopping Shopping at Stop and Shop? How Temporary Disruptions Affect Store Choice *
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School and

detail.title: Stopping Shopping at Stop and Shop? How Temporary Disruptions Affect Store Choice *
detail.abstract: Shopping patterns in retail markets are highly persistent, with households patronizing the same stores over time. Whether this persistence reflects unobserved heterogeneity or a causal effect of past choices through state dependence remains an open question. We study an 11-day strike that effectively closed 240 Stop & Shop grocery stores, using a novel identification strategy to isolate the strike's long-term effects on consumer demand through state dependence. We find that the strike caused households to make 9.9% fewer trips to S&S after the strike's resolution, simply by displacing planned visits during the strike. The reduction is observed immediately in the period after the strike's resolution and attenuates only gradually over time. The effect of trip displacement is larger for households who, during the strike, visit a store that they had not previously visited, suggesting that state dependence in store choice is partially driven by search and learning frictions. These results support an economically meaningful role of state dependence in grocery store choice, suggesting that temporary supply disruptions, and marketing tactics that induce consumer switching, can have long-term effects on profitability.

detail.abstract: We leverage Becker's time allocation theory to examine consumer demand and market competition for time-intensive goods. The Beckerian model predicts higher diversion ratios for goods with substantial time shares and those with high time costs relative to monetary prices. Applying this model to data from two field experiments, we analyze demand for Facebook and Instagram, focusing on substitution patterns across online activities and offline time use. detail.abstract: Many temporary foreign worker programs issue "closed" visas that effectively tie workers to a single employer, restricting worker mobility and weakening bargaining power. We study the labor market return to temporary foreign workers (TFWs) gaining permanent residency (PR), which loosens this mobility restriction. Using administrative data linking matched employer-employee data in Canada to temporary and permanent visa records from 2004-2014 along with an event-study design, we find that gaining PR leads to a sharp, immediate, and persistent increase in the job switching rate of 21.7 percentage points and an increase in earnings of 5.7 percent three years after PR. Workers also sort into high-wage firms after gaining PR, and the increase in the firm pay premium is roughly 56 percent of the total earnings gain. We find larger earnings gains for job switchers across industries, low-skilled workers, and workers from low-income countries. To guide and interpret our reduced-form results, we develop a search-and-matching model featuring heterogeneous workers and firms. Permanent residents and native-born workers search for jobs in the same labor market and engage in on-the-job search, while TFWs search separately within a segmented labor market and do not receive outside wage offers. We calibrate the model to match our reduced-form results, and we use it to simulate the long-run effects of PR and consider two counterfactual policies: (1) increasing the cost to firms of posting a TFW vacancy and (2) allowing TFWs to switch employers freely under "open" visas. We evaluate how these policies affect output, wages, profits, and overall social welfare.

detail.abstract: Why do people sometimes overreact to new information and other times underreact? We develop a model in which the strength of a signal-how much one should update their beliefs with new information-depends on multiple features of the information environment. Limited attention to these features leads to misperceptions of signal strength: people approach a problem with an experience-based prior, which they adjust only partially based on how much attention they pay to different features. This mechanism explains a wide range of belief-updating patterns. Insensitivity to a single feature generates underreaction to strong and overreaction to weak signals, and more neglected features amplify this. Insensitivity to multiple features can instead break that pattern: insensitivity to one feature can generate excess sensitivity with respect to another, leading to overreaction to both weak and strong signals. A series of experiments provides support for the model and its underlying mechanism.

This working paper examines how trust, reciprocity, and cooperation shape the prospects of adopting the Ecosystem Approach (EA) to coastal and environmental governance in the Niger Delta, with a focus on Ogoniland, Nigeria. Originally prepared as a Return-to-Work Report for the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade following training in Ocean Governance and Sustainable Fisheries (2017), the study provides an empirical snapshot of the social capital conditions underpinning community–state–industry relations in one of the most environmentally degraded regions of the world.

Using an adapted version of the World Bank’s Social Capital Assessment Tool (SC-IQ), survey data were collected from 190 residents across the four Local Government Areas of Ogoniland. Descriptive analysis reveals a marked contrast between strong bonding social capital (high trust and reciprocity within communities) and weak linking social capital (low trust in government agencies and oil companies). While internal cohesion supports mutual aid and collective problem-solving, vertical distrust undermines cooperation with institutions essential for implementing ecosystem-based management.

The findings demonstrate that social capital asymmetries—particularly low institutional trust, perceived injustice, and limited accountability—constitute structural barriers to the operationalisation of the Ecosystem Approach. Strengthening cross-scale cooperation, rebuilding state legitimacy, and creating inclusive governance arrangements are essential prerequisites for effective coastal management in the Niger Delta.

The report offers a historical baseline for understanding contemporary environmental governance challenges, and remains relevant for debates on ecosystem management, political ecology, and post-petroleum transitions in Nigeria.

detail.abstract: We compare the lending technology of direct lenders, banks, and finance companies using a unique data set on secured borrowing by the universe of U.S.-based private middle market firms. The borrowers of direct lenders are distinct relative to those of traditional lenders; they are younger, more likely to be in intangible capital industries, and more likely to be located in the biggest cities in the United States. These differences reflect the focus of direct lenders on private equity-owned firms; direct lenders have negligible impact in industries and cities with low private equity presence. The lending technology of direct lenders is distinct from banks: they have almost no branch network, they are geographically distant from borrowers, they write collateral claims more focused on the continuation value of firms after a default, and they have a higher degree of specialization in certain industries. Direct lenders and private equity sponsors match on industry specialization more strongly than geographic proximity. The findings suggest that direct lenders are not a general substitute for traditional lenders in middle market business lending, but they are instead specialized lenders focused on a particular segment of the U.S. economy with a distinct lending technology.

detail.title: The Impossibility of Deflation: Why Monetary Contraction Remains Structurally Temporary in Fiat Systems
detail.abstract: Popular discourse frequently invokes "deflation" as both an economic threat and, paradoxically, a desirable characteristic of certain assets like Bitcoin. Yet a careful examination of how modern monetary systems actually function reveals a fundamental misunderstanding: true deflation—a sustained, permanent reduction in the money supply—is structurally impossible within fiat currency regimes absent sovereign default. What observers commonly identify as deflation represents, at most, temporary withdrawals of currency from active circulation, inevitably reversed by the maturity cycles of government debt instruments. This analysis examines the mechanics of central bank balance sheet operations, the distinction between deflation and disinflation, and why the only genuine deflationary shock possible within the current system would require the politically catastrophic scenario of sovereign insolvency.

detail.title: Sovereignty at Speed: Constitutional Liquidity, Market Hierarchy, and Crisis Stabilisation CLP / ICL Framework for Measuring State Capacity in Financial Crises

declarations.funderStatement: Independent Researcher

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the concept of Constitutional Liquidity Power (CLP): the capacity of the modern state to stabilise financial markets at speed through balance-sheet interventions. CLP is constitutional because it depends on institutional permissions and judicial non-interference. It is liquidity because it manifests through market repair, collateral provision, and refinancing. To make this capacity empirically tractable, we develop the Index of Constitutional Liquidity (ICL), which measures three conditions: (1) the existence of stabilisation instruments, (2) political and legal permission to use them, and (3) the speed and scope of execution. CLP is a capacity, not a guarantee. It explains why some states stabilise in days, while others require months or fail.We test the theory across major crises: the United States in 2008, 2019, and 2020; the
Eurozone from 2008 to 2020; the United Kingdom in 2022; and Switzerland in 2023. These cases show that modern sovereignty rests on the ability to mobilise liquidity before financial markets collapse. Judicial silence, or active deference, emerges as a crucial constitutional condition. The results reveal a hierarchical structure. The United States operates at the apex of a triangular system, supplying global dollar liquidity. China stabilises internally through credit control, while Japan stabilises duration through balance-sheet absorption. Other states adapt to this hierarchy. This is not a currency war, but a capital war, in which the scarce strategic resource is refinancing, not exchange rates. The conclusion is straightforward: sovereignty today is balance-sheet capacity at speed. Time is constitutional. Those who can intervene fastest govern those who cannot. CLP measures that power. ICL makes it visible.

title: Corporate Wealth Distribution Coefficient (CWDC): A Multidimensional Measure of Inequality

detail.title: Corporate Wealth Distribution Coefficient (CWDC): A Multidimensional Measure of Inequality
detail.abstract: Rising income inequality and corporate wealth concentration have become pressing global challenges. While top executives and shareholders capture disproportionate gains, employees, communities, and innovation often receive limited benefits. Existing measures, such as CEO-toworker pay ratios or CSR/ESG ratings, provide partial insights but fail to capture the multidimensional nature of corporate wealth allocation. This study introduces the Corporate Wealth Distribution Coefficient (CWDC), a novel metric designed to assess wealth distribution at both firm (CWDC-F) and national (CWDC-N) levels. CWDC-F integrates wage inclusiveness, CSR/ESG, R&D investment, and normalized stock buybacks, while CWDC-N captures broader patterns of inclusiveness, responsibility, and innovation across economies or trade blocs such as BRICS or the G7. By combining internal equity, external responsibility, and long-term investment, CWDC provides policymakers, regulators, investors, and labor groups with a robust framework to evaluate whether corporate growth fosters broad-based prosperity or perpetuates concentration. The CWDC thus offers a multidimensional, actionable measure of corporate wealth distribution with implications for research, regulation, and stakeholder decision-making.

Crafting Your Brand Identity:A Guide to Positioning Statements and Messaging Pillars

In today's saturated market, brands succeed by clearly defining who they are and why they matter. Successful brands don't leave their messaging to chance—they establish a strategic foundation that guides every aspect of their communication. This starts with a clear positioning statement, an internal document that serves as the brand's internal compass, shaping how the brand presents itself to customers and differentiates itself from competitors. But a positioning statement alone isn't enough. To ensure consistency and authenticity across all messaging, brands must also develop messaging pillars—key themes that reinforce their identity and bring their positioning to life through a more detailed description. This note explores the relationship between positioning statements and messaging pillars, outlining how they work together to create a compelling and cohesive brand narrative.

Positioning Statement

Every single top brand has one thing in common: A clear definition of who it is, how it is different, and why it matters. A successful brand must first decide exactly how it wants to be perceived by the public and, most importantly, its customers. This is done through an internal document—not in advertisements, social media content, or other external channels. That document is the positioning statement, which acts as the road map for all other brand communications and other business decisions. A positioning statement is a concise description that outlines how a company, product, or service fills a specific target's need and differentiates itself from competitors.

Messaging Pillars

Messaging pillars build on the foundation of positioning statements to deepen and reinforce a brand's unique market position. As an internal document, messaging pillars are the three to five key themes that break down and expand on a brand's identity (how it wants to be perceived) and value proposition (the unique benefit it provides), written in paragraph form. These pillars act as a structured guide for further communication, ensuring that all marketing, branding, and public messaging stay consistent, clear, and aligned with brand values.

detail.abstract:
Power can be one of the most misunderstood and discomforting topics in organizational life. Yet it shapes every team and institution, and leaders who fail to grasp how it works often misread critical dynamics. This technical note synthesizes five decades of research across social psychology, evolutionary theory, management, and organizational behavior to clarify what power is, how it differs from status, and why the distinction matters. It also explains the origins of hierarchy, delineates the major sources of power in organizations, and examines two fundamental paths to acquiring power and status: dominance strategies and prestige strategies. Through evidence-based insights, this note reveals the benefits, limitations, and trade-offs of each path and shows why the most effective leaders blend both approaches. Designed to help students and practitioners navigate complex organizational landscapes, this note offers a practical framework for recognizing where real power resides—and subsequently acquiring and exercising it more strategically.

Excerpt

What Is Power? Clarifying Concepts and Controversies

Many people feel uncomfortable with the subject of power and often consider it “an organization's last dirty secret.” There is also widespread confusion about what power really is, and fierce debates rage over which strategies for acquiring it actually work. This technical note aims to cut through some of the controversies about power by reviewing 50 years of research from the fields of social psychology, evolutionary psychology, management, and organizational behavior.

Organizations as Hierarchical Contexts

Survival has been one of humanity's oldest and most enduring challenges. Early on, the need to survive propelled humans to form groups in a quest for food, protection, and safety—resources easier to secure with others than alone. Groups also helped individuals meet important psychological needs, such as the need to belong.

Yet living in groups also created challenges. Different preferences, personalities, and beliefs among group members made coordination difficult, and a group's survival largely depended on solving coordination problems. This challenge led to the formation of hierarchies—systems in which individuals occupy different ranks or relative social positions. By ranking members according to “merit,” prominence, or control of resources, groups could establish order and improve their chances of survival.

Throughout history, hierarchies have persisted and existed in groups across all cultures. Even in teams lacking formal ranks or in organizations describing themselves as “flat,” informal hierarchies still emerge. For example, at the product-design firm IDEO, nearly everyone holds the title of “engineer.” Yet some engineers, such as those who generate “cool” ideas, earn more respect and higher salaries than others.

detail.abstract:
This technical note introduces the Scientist–Artist–Judge (SAJ) framework, a practical model for understanding and improving how people think through complex managerial and leadership challenges. The framework is grounded in the observation that poor decisions often stem not from a lack of intelligence or effort, but from over-reliance on a single mode of thinking—analysis, imagination, or judgment—at the expense of balance. SAJ conceptualizes effective thinking as the productive integration of three roles: the Scientist, who seeks accurate understanding; the Artist, who imagines new possibilities; and the Judge, who evaluates what is appropriate and worthwhile. The note outlines each role, illustrates common patterns of unbalanced thinking, and demonstrates how balanced thought enhances decision quality in ambiguous, high-stakes, or emotionally charged situations.This technical note is suitable for use in MBA, executive education, and advanced undergraduate courses on leadership, managerial decision making, ethics, innovation, and professional judgment.

Excerpt

The Scientist, the Artist, and the Judge

The Scientist, the Artist, and the Judge (SAJ, pronounced “sage”) framework helps people become more reflective, strategic, and ultimately effective in their own thinking. It presumes that our effectiveness in any situation depends on how well we understand what is happening, and it is motivated by a simple observation: People often create flawed solutions not because they lack intelligence, but because they over-rely on a single cognitive function, be it analysis, imagination, or judgment. This overreliance creates otherwise predictable blind spots and leads to unbalanced thought that undermines solutions.

The SAJ framework proposes that thinking well is a matter of balance and requires holding three fundamental questions in productive tension: (1) What is truly happening?, (2) what are our options?, and (3) what is the right or best path forward? These questions correspond to the three roles—the Scientist, the Artist, and the Judge—that serve as metaphors for the kinds of thinking required to navigate life. Understanding these roles requires first expanding upon the aims and scope of each and then examining the characteristic failures when any one role dominates. From there, we can outline the path to balanced thought.

In leadership and managerial work, SAJ is particularly helpful when you face ill-structured, nonobvious, or emotion-laden concerns, such as (a) complex decisions with ethical stakes, (b) innovation and change initiatives, and (c) sticky interpersonal or political dilemmas. Since SAJ is about fundamental thinking modalities, it does not replace but rather enhances other frameworks (e.g., ethics, decision trees, innovation processes). For instance, decision trees are more effective the more one can envision desirable end states (an Artist–Judge relationship), discover all the options and dependencies (Artist–Scientist relationship), and skillfully characterize the trade-offs (Scientist–Judge relationship). To illustrate this framework in practice, we begin by examining each role in turn—starting with the Scientist, then discussing the Artist, and finally considering the Judge. We'll examine what each adds, what it overlooks, and how it shapes real-world decisions.

detail.abstract: Economic exclusion has a measurable price-and for vulnerable groups in Turkey, the 32-point gap between the highest and lowest scoring groups is associated with approximately 2,120 TRY per month in observed income differences. Yet no standardized metric exists to quantify and compare these losses across marginalized populations. This paper introduces the Belonging Cost Index (BCI) to the Turkish context, a composite framework measuring exclusion costs across labor markets, financial systems, and housing stability. Using original survey data from nine vulnerable groups (n=102)-including undocumented immigrants, Syrian and Afghan refugees, Kurdish minorities, disabled adults, and foster youth-we demonstrate that belonging costs vary substantially, with scores ranging from 36 to 68 points on a 100point scale. The 32-point gap between the highest and lowest scoring groups is associated with approximately 2,120 TRY per month in income differences. Labor market exclusion drives 65% of these costs, while financial and housing barriers compound losses. A one-point BCI increase is associated with 160 TRY ($4.70 USD) lower monthly income (p<0.001). The BCI enables targeted policy design: scenariobased projections suggest housing-first programs could be associated with 18-26 point BCI reductions for housing-precarious groups, while credential recognition could yield 12-15 point reductions for refugees. Turkey's minimum wage context (17,002 TRY/month) provides a critical benchmark, as most vulnerable groups earn 30-90% of this threshold. The BCI offers a replicable tool for equity-focused policy in Turkey and other middle-income countries facing similar integration challenges.

detail.abstract: This paper presents findings from practice-based research across more than sixty organisations in Europe, investigating patterns of dysfunction in leadership and organisational management. Drawing on interviews with managers, executives, coaches, and organisational development specialists, supplemented by survey data from close to one hundred managers, the research identifies recurring patterns across industries and contexts. The findings suggest a fundamental mismatch: management approaches designed for stable environments applied to conditions of complexity and rapid change. Observed patterns cluster into five types: fragmentation, measurement gaps, rigidity, capability atrophy, and accumulation effects. A critical finding is that theoretical frameworks addressing these dysfunctions, including systems thinking, organisational learning, and complexity science, have existed for decades yet remain largely unapplied. Management as a system, despite its decisive influence on organisational outcomes, operates as an unmanaged function. This neglect may pose greater risk to organisations than the external disruptions currently commanding attention.

It argues that legitimacy, not pressure, must return to the center of global diplomacy. The article integrates three JSTOR sources to support its analysis and proposes a model for identifying structural coercion as a threat to credibility and participation in international relations.

detail.abstract: The paper analyses the relationship between bank competition and stability, with a specific focus on the Middle East and North Africa. Price competition is positively associated with bank liquidity, as it induces self-discipline incentives on banks for the choice of bank funding sources and for the holding of liquid assets. On the other hand, price competition may have potentially negative implications on bank solvency and on the credit quality of the loan portfolio. More competitive banks may be less solvent if the potential increase in the equity base-due to capital adjustments-is not large enough to compensate for the reduction in bank profitability. Also, banks subject to stronger competitive pressures may have a higher rate of nonperforming loans, if the increase in the risk-taking incentives from the lender's side overcomes the decrease in the credit risk from the borrower's side. In both cases, country-specific policies for market entry conditions-and for bank regulation and supervision-may significantly affect the sign and the size of the relationship. The analysis suggests implications for policy reforms designed to improve market contestability and to increase the quality and independence of prudential supervision.

detail.abstract: Among the various institutional layers that shape the structure and function of regional innovation systems (RIS), the network of research universities (RU) stands out as a principal component, constituting the hubs and channels that facilitate knowledge creation, technology transfer and skilled workforce development. Here we analyze the contributions to regional scientific competitiveness associated with regional versus cross-border collaboration, as well as the prestige signaling associated with the flagship institutions located within a particular region. By applying hierarchical regression models with institutional fixed effects to research profiles constructed from ∼ 800,000 publications affiliated with 28 RU in California (CA) and Texas (TX), in particular including all University of California and University of Texas campuses, we find that research co-produced with a premier regional university that also extends across international borders features a 21% (CA) and 25% (TX) citation premium. We also show that the citation premium attributable to institutional prestige and international collaboration have both increased over time, reflecting the growing influence of these factors in relation to institutional and regional competitiveness. These findings underscore the importance of balancing investment in regional integration with crossborder engagement, as prestige spillovers can enhance RIS competitiveness by attracting elite scientists, fostering impactful collaborations, and integrating distant regions within global research networks. Managing RIS competitiveness thus requires strategic investments in both regional collaboration and flagship institutions to optimize local benefits while leveraging the capacity to attract external research expertise and capabilities. Our results also lend support to increasing prevalence of multi-institutional consortia and RU satellite campuses, which identify institutional and regional synergies in order to strategically amplify institutional competitiveness.
