detail.abstract: The prevailing discourse in healthcare AI has been disproportionately focused on algorithms, datasets, and model accuracy. This technological monomania has generated an illusion of progress: we assume that superior models will inevitably transform clinical workflows. However, this assumption collapses upon operational contact. Models do not create value unless they can be served—reliably, predictably, and at clinical speeds. This paper argues that the true strategic differentiator in healthcare AI is no longer model construction but model serving: the infrastructural and architectural capability that converts algorithmic potential into actionable clinical cognition at scale. Drawing on concepts such as Dynamic Inference Graphs, multi-tenant inference orchestration, latency governance, and trust preservation, we reinterpret healthcare AI as an architectural and systems challenge rather than a mathematical contest. The market leaders of the next decade will not be those who build the smartest models, but those who deliver intelligence without erosion of clinical trust.

Digital governance has emerged as a tool for improving public sector accountability, reducing corruption, and creating new opportunities for civic participation. This research approaches to explore how different countries utilize digital platforms like open data systems, online service portals, and youth engagement, to enhance transparency, improve decision making and integrate young citizens in democratic processes.In the context of Pakistan, the study highlights the critical significance of digital tools in addressing the country's complex governance challenges. Many citizens rely on digital platforms such as the Pakistan Citizen Portal, open-budget dashboards, and youth-focused digital initiatives to improve transparency and reconnect young people with democratic processes. These developments highlight both the opportunities and the challenges associated with adopting e-governance reforms in an emerging democracy. title: From Clean to Sufficient: Shaping Demand Within Planetary Boundaries

detail.title: From Clean to Sufficient: Shaping Demand Within Planetary Boundaries
detail.abstract: Current decarbonisation efforts, largely focused on supply-side solutions, have proven insufficient to meet climate targets and stay within planetary boundaries. Combined with broader structural challenges such as high energy prices, growing competition from outside Europe, and the availability of cheaper imports, it raises concerns about an 'industrial exodus' and a loss of European competitiveness. Various industry actors called on the Dutch government to create a market demand for clean alternatives to drive industrial decarbonisation. This report proposes an integrated policy mix emphasising demand-side strategies to stimulate clean products and reduce absolute resource consumption. Through a non-systematic review, it examines different conceptual perspectives on resource use and demand and how they translate into sufficiency-, efficiency-, and consistency-oriented demand-side policies. Each approach is assessed in terms of its potential and limitations. A document analysis identifies policy measures linked to each approach. The report advocates prioritising sufficiency, which establishes absolute consumption limits and questions necessary levels of use, improving the impact of efficiency and consistency measures. It highlights the EU Clean Industrial Deal's continued emphasis on supply-side measures and calls for greater integration of sufficiency demand-side policies to ensure a just and sustainable transition. Finally, drawing on examples from the housing and mobility sectors, the report illustrates the value of a balanced policy mix.

title: Competence-based Theory of Evolution

detail.abstract: The Competence-based Theory of Evolution is a comprehensive, non-Darwinian general theory of evolution. Its fundamental assumption – that all life is loss-of-competence-averse – can be justified by the second law of thermodynamics. In simple genetic organisms the theory is compatible with classical (Darwinian) biological evolution. Its range of application covers all domains of life: from cells and organisms to superorganisms, and from biology and the social sciences to evolutionary economics. First published 2024–2025 as a monograph, now available as an open-access preprint.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Real-Time Collision Risk Assessment in Large Satellite Constellations

detail.title: Graph Neural Networks for Real-Time Collision Risk Assessment in Large Satellite Constellations
detail.abstract: By 2030,commercial mega-constellations will push Low Earth Orbit satellite populations from 9,000 (2025) to 50,000+ by 2030,creating fundamental computational barriers for collision avoidance. Traditional pairwise conjunction analysis exhibits O(n 2) complexity: at 50,000 satellites, this requires 1.25 billion object-pair evaluations per cycle-approximately 145 days of computation using current analytical methods even with substantial parallelization. We reformulate collision risk assessment as learning over dynamic spatial graphs where satellites form nodes and proximity relationships define edges. Our Graph Neural Network architecture leverages the locality of conjunction risk (we empirically observe 94% of high-risk events involve objects within 500km) to achieve O(n) computational scaling through message-passing operations. The system processes 100,000-satellite populations in 920ms while maintaining a 90.3% recall for high-risk conjunctions-representing a 13,000× speedup over analytical methods. Validation encompasses synthetic constellations (1K-100K satellites) and operational Space-Track.org data (9,137 satellites, 1,247 documented high-risk events from January 2025). The approach achieves 88.2% recall on real operational scenarios, demonstrating generalization beyond synthetic training environments. Results establish technical feasibility for autonomous collision avoidance at mega-constellation scales and provide foundations for cascade prediction in debris-dense orbital regimes.

title: FIRM: A Minimal Governance Architecture for Financial Stability in Small and Medium-Sized Football Clubs

detail.title: FIRM: A Minimal Governance Architecture for Financial Stability in Small and Medium-Sized Football Clubs
detail.abstract: Financial instability is a recurring feature of lower-league and supporter-owned football clubs, where volatile revenues, limited administrative capacity, and informal decision processes allow financial deterioration to emerge rapidly. Existing regulatory frameworks focus on overspending and long-term debt but do not provide the operational governance mechanisms required in small clubs for daily liquidity management, authority discipline, or early detection of emerging risk. This conceptual paper introduces FIRM, a minimal governance architecture built around four essential functions: Financial Footprint, Integrity Control, Risk Modelling, and Monitoring. The model draws from internal control theory, governance research, risk management principles, and behavioural insights to address predictable mechanisms that drive instability, including weak financial visibility, unclear decision rights, over-optimistic assumptions, and slow recognition of liquidity stress. The contribution lies in defining the minimum governance functions needed to maintain financial discipline in resource-constrained clubs and clarifying how these functions interact to prevent common failure pathways. The paper also outlines how FIRM can be examined empirically through comparative case studies, early warning indicator analysis, and scenario-based evaluation. Although conceptual, the model provides a foundation for future empirical work and offers a practical structure that clubs can implement with limited staff and minimal financial infrastructure.

title: Housing, Land and Property Rights of Internally Displaced Person in Ethiopia: Legal Appraisal

detail.abstract: IDPs are persons or groups of persons who have been forced or obliged Toffler to leave their homes or places of habitual residence, in particular as a result of or in order to avoid the effects of armed conflict, situations of generalized violence, violations of human rights or natural or human-made disasters, and who have not crossed an internationally recognized State border. This situation inevitably results in human rights concerns of victims. Since then response to this issue, the international community, particularly UN agencies and other organizations, has focused on establishing international guidelines and principles, despite the existing framework of international human rights and humanitarian laws. Internally displaced persons (IDPs), who have been forced to leave their homes and possessions, represent a vulnerable group that requires specific protective measures. To address their needs, frameworks such as the Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement (GP), and the Kampala Convention have been developed by UN bodies and the African Union (AU), respectively. Even though Ethiopia has adopted the aforementioned international laws still have no separate laws which govern the area. This study focuses on analyzing the adequacy of Ethiopian legal frame work to protect HLP rights of IDPs.

title: Consumer Behaviour and the Uptake of Solar Panels
affiliations: and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Consumer Behaviour and the Uptake of Solar Panels
detail.abstract: Clean renewable energy technologies contribute towards both improving energy efficiency and reducing emissions, yet household adoption rates remain low. This paper analyses the impact of economic, household, environmental, and dwelling factors on the uptake of solar photovoltaic (PV) and thermal panels, using the Understanding Society dataset, and applying the adaptive Lasso method and a random effects logistic regression model. We find that solar panel adoption is primarily driven by electricity prices, rural location, number of rooms, and environmental factors. Living in a rural location, having one more room, and a rise in electricity prices by 10 percentage points increase the odds of PV panel adoption by 87%, 19%, and 7%, respectively. Diffusion of thermal panels is driven by similar factors, with both technologies strongly affected by environmental aspects - owners of electric vehicles are 2.4 times more likely to be interested in solar technologies. The counterfactuals and predictions made using the discrete-time hazard survival model illustrate that even modest subsidies for PV panels would significantly accelerate adoption rates, both historically and in the future. Our results highlight the need for solar technology investment, subsidies, and policy frameworks, that would encourage more optimally targeted policies and contribute to reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents Structural Flow, a minimal-structure explanatory framework in which physics, cognition, and civic legitimacy arise not from metaphysical assumptions but from a single empirical premise: chance exists. Once accepted, this premise forces five structural theorems: a finite resolution floor, spherical boundary geometries, π non-computability, π-governed exchange, and system closure. These are not axioms but theorems, logically required for chance to be real rather than illusory.

From these theorems, Structural Flow derives a directed chain of necessary transitions: Chance → Entropy → Imperfect Knowledge → Agency → Responsibility → Legitimacy. The paper demonstrates this architecture through detailed derivations of three fundamental phenomena: π as both mechanism and signature of randomness; conservation laws as structural necessities in closed systems with finite resolution; and quantum entanglement as system-level resolution rather than inter-particle communication.

A concrete example traces a single quantum measurement event through the complete structural chain, revealing how each transition emerges from pressure at boundaries. The paper articulates both a methodological discipline (Structure → Mechanism → Observation) and an operational epistemic posture shaped by uncertainty itself. The result is a deductive, geometry-driven account of why the universe cannot fully know its own outcomes—and how that structural ignorance generates the behaviors we observe across domains.

detail.abstract: Social homophily has been shown to be a feature of entrepreneurial team formation, but its performance implications remain unclear. This paper examines the recent rise of political homophily and its relationship to the performance of entrepreneurial founding teams. We construct a dataset linking more than 10,000 co-founders of over 3,000 California-based startups to their voter registration records from 2007 to 2019. We first document substantial and rising levels of political homophily of venture capital-backed entrepreneurial teams, controlling for other forms of social homophily. We then analyze how team political composition relates to outcomes, focusing on the likelihood and speed of raising subsequent funding rounds. We find that teams composed entirely of similar political partisans underperform relative to politically mixed teams. The highest performing teams possess substantial political heterogeneity, encompassing Democrats, Republicans, and Nonpartisan founders. These reduced form results remain qualitatively consistent in two-stage estimations using time-varying measures of political advertising in each of California's 14 media markets as instrumental variables. These findings suggest that Nonpartisan founders may serve a cross-cutting or boundary-spanning role, helping teams navigate the coordination challenges of ideological diversity.

detail.abstract: The current consensus about the future of AI assumes a zero-sum competition between centralized Cloud AI (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) and Local AI (open-weights models). This analysis argues that the fundamental premise is false. The convergence of three factors – the democratization of hardware (VRAM cost down 10x by 2022), the transformation of models into “commodities” (open-weights), and geopolitical sovereignty imperatives – will not destroy the Cloud oligopoly, but will create a profitable bifurcation of the AI ecosystem, analogous to the Windows-Linux coexistence of the last three decades. Using scenario analysis with falsifiable markers and a critical timeline of 2025-2030, the paper identifies Q2 2027 as the "point of no return" - the moment when the final configuration of the market is decided. If three conditions are validated simultaneously (64GB equipment under €3,000, open-weights quality gap under 3%, over 1.8 million sovereign users), the bifurcation becomes irreversible, generating a total market of €85-135 billion in 2030 - 2-3× larger than the monopoly scenario - Cloud. The unique contribution lies in the recognition that Cloud and Sovereign AI are complementary, not substitutable: Enterprise Cloud (€50-80 billion) captures value through compliance and integration, while Sovereign AI (€35-55 billion) gains through sovereignty and economics. The Windows (PCs) + Linux (servers) analogy demonstrates that a coexistence creates more value than the complete victory of either ecosystem. The paper provides detailed strategic recommendations for hardware manufacturers (Nvidia, AMD, Apple), existing cloud companies (OpenAI, Anthropic), companies (Fortune 5000), investors, and policymakers, each with specific decision windows in the critical period 2026-2027. For early adopters who recognize the fork in time, the gains are disproportionate; for late adopters, the Nokia precedent (40% → 3% share in 5 years) is a sobering warning.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes an "exit trap" mechanism in opportunity windows-episodes of succession uncertainty, coups, and legitimacy resets in which constraints weaken and strategic choices have outsized institutional consequences. The central claim is that concession is not neutral in such windows. When an actor relinquishes key levers and thereby drives post-exit threat capacity toward zero, while relying on assurances that lack verifiable enforcement, the opponent's incentive to honor commitments declines and the incentive to purge increases. We formalize this logic with a three-variable framework: credible commitment (CC), purge incentives (PI), and a responsibility ledger (RL). RL captures whether a strategy externalizes risk onto the legitimacy core, the state apparatus, the polity's order, and followers; high RL can expand the instrumental benefits of consolidation, raising the expected payoff of purges even when commitments are rhetorically offered. We illustrate the mechanism through two focal cases-a literary mechanism-intensifying case (Titus Andronicus) and a historical high-stakes window (Cao Shuang in the Gaoping Tombs coup)-and bound the argument with two contrast cases (Cincinnatus and Sulla) that represent distinct pathways to safe exit: task-bounded authority without privatization (Type A), and security-locked exit after structural consolidation (Type B). The contribution is not a universal claim that exits are fatal, but a testable account of when exits predictably backfire, alongside an actionable decision protocol that emphasizes verifiable constraints, minimum deterrent capacity, and responsibility-accounting in window decisions.

detail.abstract: Digital transformation has become a critical driver of firm performance in increasingly turbulent economic environments characterized by market volatility, technological disruption, and supply-chain uncertainty. This study examines how emerging digital technologies enhance organizational agility and, in turn, strengthen firm competitiveness, operational resilience, and strategic responsiveness in contemporary business markets. Drawing on recent empirical evidence from digital economy and management research, the study integrates economic and organizational perspectives to analyze the mechanisms through which technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), big data analytics, cloud computing, and automation influence firm-level outcomes. Using a structured analytical framework supported by secondary quantitative data and comparative firm-level indicators, the study finds that digitally transformed firms demonstrate significantly higher adaptability and responsiveness to environmental shocks. Recent surveys indicate that firms with advanced digital capabilities achieve productivity gains of 15-25% and cost reductions of up to 20% compared to less digitalized counterparts. Moreover, organizations adopting data-driven decision-making tools report up to a 30% improvement in strategic response speed during periods of market disruption. Digital platforms and cloud-based infrastructures further enhance operational resilience by reducing downtime by approximately 40% and enabling rapid reconfiguration of business processes. The findings also reveal a strong positive relationship between organizational agility and competitive advantage, particularly in industries exposed to rapid demand fluctuations and regulatory uncertainty. Agile firms leverage real-time data and flexible digital architectures to reallocate resources efficiently, innovate faster, and sustain market share under adverse economic conditions. From an economic standpoint, these dynamics contribute to improved firm survival rates, higher returns on digital investment, and enhanced long-term growth potential. Overall, this study contributes to contemporary economic research by providing concise, data-informed insights into how digital transformation reshapes firm behavior and performance. The results offer valuable implications for managers, policymakers, and researchers seeking to understand the economic value of digitalization and agility in fostering resilient and competitive firms in volatile business environments.

detail.abstract: Metal markets are an important but understudied aspect of the global energy transition. This paper demonstrates differential metal price responses to the Paris Agreement based on their role in the energy transition. We use a difference-in-differences design with daily price data from 2001 to 2024 for eight industrial metals. The treatment group distinguishes between traditional green metals (Copper, Aluminium, Nickel), which are established in renewable energy infrastructure, versus emerging green metals (Lithium), that are critical for storage. The control group includes non-green metals (Zinc, Lead, Tin, and Iron Ore). We find traditional green metals experienced 31% price decline relative to control metals following the Paris Agreement, while Lithium exhibited a 120% price increase.

detail.abstract: We use global tariffs to reveal the weights that nations implicitly place on the welfare of their trading partners relative to their own. Our estimated welfare weights suggest that formal and informal rules of the world trading system make countries internalize the impact of their policies onto others to a substantial extent, though not fully. On average, countries place 25% less value on transfers to foreigners than transfers to their own residents. Across nations, we find that countries that put higher welfare weights on the welfare of foreigners also tend to receive higher weights from them, consistent with a general form of reciprocity among nations. detail.abstract: Rating systems are a common governance tool on two-sided platforms. Research suggests that, via indirect network effects, rating systems benefit participants on both the rating side and the rated side. However, participants on the rated side may not always recognize the benefits of the rating system and may respond negatively to its introduction. The rating side may anticipate the rated side's negative reactions and react negatively as well, especially when the rated side holds more power over the rating side. To empirically examine participants' reactions to a proposed platform rating system in the context of a substantial cross-side power differential, we conducted two field experiments in collaboration with a Singapore-based labor platform that connects foreign domestic workers with employers (families). We found that employers, on average, were indifferent to the proposed rating system, even when the benefits to them were highlighted, with the highest-income employers exhibiting negative responses. We also found that workers reacted negatively, with those informed of the proposed rating system completely disengaging from the platform. Post-hoc interviews and analyses support our interpretation that power differential underlies workers' negative responses to the rating system. This study contributes to the literature on platform rating systems by demonstrating that, in the presence of a substantial cross-side power imbalance, rating systems may not always be perceived positively, even by participants on the rating side, whom the system aims to empower. It also constitutes one of the first efforts in management research to study domestic workers, a highly vulnerable population of workers.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Business Research: A Taxonomy of Methodological Roles and Future Directions

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Business Research: A Taxonomy of Methodological Roles and Future Directions
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) research in Information Systems (IS), Operations Management (OM), and adjacent business fields has grown rapidly, yet methodological innovation remains fragmented across journals, application domains, and disciplinary communities. This paper synthesizes 208 AI-related studies published between 2018 and 2025 in premier IS, OM, and Marketing journals and develops a nine-category classification taxonomy that captures how researchers extend, operationalize, and study AI in organizational and decision-oriented settings. Seven categories characterize recurring AI methodological extension mechanisms: architectural design, knowledge integration, multi-modal learning, performance and reliability, interpretability and trust, data enhancement, and dynamic and adaptive learning. Two additional categories capture analytically distinct contributions: downstream model usage, where AI outputs serve as inputs to empirical pipelines, and empirical studies of AI production, adoption, and human-AI interaction. Rather than organizing by specific algorithms or application domains, this taxonomy provides a common abstraction layer for comparing AI methods that diffuse across business research contexts. By examining how these mechanisms reshape the role AI plays in research designs and decision systems, we identify a conceptual progression from AI as Model to AI as Instrument and, increasingly, AI as Agent. The review documents patterns of methodological concentration and co-occurrence across data environments and identifies gaps related to methodological robustness, governance, and adaptive deployment. Taken together, the taxonomy offers IS, OM, and Marketing scholars a systematic foundation for evaluating and integrating AI methods into decision-oriented and operational research.

detail.abstract: We provide causal evidence that immigration has contributed to the polarization of American politics. Using an ancestry-based shift-share instrument, we study immigration flows into U.S. counties between 1992 and 2016. Counties exposed to larger immigrant inflows become more polarized both in campaign contributions and in political representation: donors increasingly support ideologically extreme candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives, and the candidates who win office are themselves further from the ideological center. These effects are most pronounced in primary elections, where moderate Democrats are more likely to lose and conservative Republicans more likely to win in counties with higher immigration inflows. The rightward shift is strongest in occupations with high immigrant shares but limited interpersonal contact, suggesting that exposure without interaction amplifies perceived threat. We complement these results with original survey evidence that sheds light on the underlying mechanisms. Liberals and conservatives differ less in their economic assessments of immigration than in their cultural interpretations: liberals stress diversity and opportunity, whereas conservatives emphasize risk and social cohesion. Together, these findings indicate that immigration reshapes American politics through the joint forces of salience and contact – heightening polarization where immigrants are visible but unfamiliar, and attenuating it where interaction is routine.

detail.abstract: With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), AI-powered chatbots have become widely adopted across various domains. However, their impact on user contribution behaviors in online user-generated content (UGC) communities remains underexplored. Using a natural experiment on Douban--a popular Chinese UGC platform--this study examines how chatbot participation influences users' content contributions. Our findings reveal that, compared to the control group without a chatbot, the introduction of a chatbot in the treatment group led to a significant increase in the number of comments per post, but also reduced users' contributions of new posts. Further analysis suggests that the rise in comments was largely driven by chatbot-related interactions that were often irrelevant to the original post. These off-topic comments appeared to dilute contributor recognition, weaken psychological ownership, and ultimately discourage future content creation. These results offer important implications for online communities and platforms considering the use of chatbots for operational or governance purposes.

title: The Architecture of Assured Governance: Ternary Logic as a Sovereign, Evidentiary Triadic Framework for Global Economic Systems

detail.abstract:
Current financial regulation faces a critical enforcement crisis: it relies on ex-post forensic reconstruction. When an algorithm fails or a market manipulation event occurs, regulators must reconstruct "intent" from fragmented logs. This creates legal ambiguity and reliance on institutional "good faith."

This monograph introduces Ternary Logic (TL) not merely as a software update, but as a constitutional layer for economic systems. TL operates on a non-negotiable covenant: "No Log = No Action." No financial transaction can execute unless it has generated a secured, immutable Decision Log proving regulatory adherence.

The framework introduces three architectural enforcement mechanisms:

  1. The Epistemic Hold (Safe Harbor): A mandatory state of "Prudence" (State 0) that triggers when truth is uncertain, transforming liability from negligence to documented due care.

  2. Audit-Grade Evidence: A chain of custody meeting Federal Rules of Evidence (FRE 901/902) standards, secured by multi-chain cryptographic Anchors.

  3. The Hybrid Shield: An architectural defense against capture and fraud that physically blocks non-compliant transactions (e.g., sanctions violations) in real-time.

This standard operationalizes the "Standard of Care" for the Digital Age, ensuring economic systems are architected to be incapable of non-compliance.

title: SAFEARC: A Seven-Pillar Operational Architecture for Socio-Technical AI Governance

detail.title: SAFEARC: A Seven-Pillar Operational Architecture for Socio-Technical AI Governance
detail.abstract: Despite broad convergence among global AI governance frameworks, organizations continue to struggle with implementation. The barrier is not conceptual but operational: existing guidance defines principles without translating them into workable sociotechnical processes. This paper introduces SAFEARC, a seven-pillar architecture designed to operationalize regulatory expectations across organizational contexts. SAFEARC integrates requirements from the EU AI Act, OECD AI Principles, NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and ISO/IEC 42001 into a unified workflow structured around Scan, Align, Filter, Evaluate, Assign, Renew, and Contain. Using clause-level crosswalk analysis, convergence mapping, and synthesis across 68 regulatory and standards documents, the study identifies six governance domains consistently demanded by major frameworks and four structural barriers that impede adoption in practice. These findings inform the development of an architecture aimed at bridging the gap between policy intent and organizational capability. The paper demonstrates that SAFEARC enhances auditability, improves internal coordination, and supports socio-technical readiness for emerging AI regulation. The approach is applicable to both large enterprises and resource-constrained organizations, offering a practical pathway toward trustworthy AI implementation.

detail.abstract: The information retrieval industry is spending $4.7 billion to rediscover a solution that was distributed for free in 1985. While modern vector databases struggle to scale beyond 100 million documents, hitting a wall of GPU inefficiency and exorbitant costs, we identify a fundamental pattern: every successful modern system—from NVIDIA’s TiDAR to Microsoft’s SPANN—has independently converged on the architectural principles of CDS/ISIS, a UNESCO system designed for developing nations. This convergence is not a coincidence; we argue it is an architecturally inevitable response to fundamental limits of information organization. We propose the Two-Level Theory, suggesting that efficient retrieval requires separating semantic understanding (Level 1) from structural organization (Level 2). Modern systems fail when they force neural tools to perform symbolic work. We present the Neural-to-Symbolic Bridge, a proposed framework that uses modern AI to populate classical B-tree indices. Our theoretical analysis predicts: replacing brute-force 𝑂 (𝑛 · 𝑑) computation with 𝑂 (log𝑘) lookups could reduce costs by 10x ($2.4M → $240k) and stabilize latency at 5ms. The future of AI scaling does not require new invention. It simply requires remembering the optimal architecture we already have.

detail.abstract:
Digital administration has been widely promoted as a solution to inefficiency and institutional opacity in public services. However its deployment has shifted procedural burdens from the state to the individuals who must operate the technological systems that govern access to rights. The result is a thousand click bureaucracy in which legal participation depends on the user's capacity to navigate digital platforms, maintain continuous visibility within the system and produce evidence of actions that interfaces do not always acknowledge. This transformation fragments procedural guarantees and weakens legal certainty because failures in the system generate consequences attributed to the user. The law continues to protect due process in theory while practice increasingly depends on technical performance and digital literacy. The concept of technological due process proposed in this article demands that administrative legitimacy be evaluated not only by formal legality but by the responsiveness, traceability and clarity of the technological infrastructures through which authority is exercised. Recognizing this shift is essential to ensure that modernization of the state does not erode the very rights it is meant to protect.

detail.abstract: Many successful companies with evident capabilities are unable to keep up with their legacy of success, particularly in innovation. The competency trap, where stronger capabilities may no longer be a competitive advantage and instead turn out to be a liability for the firm, is often suggested as a reason. Inter-organizational collaborations, in particular, international collaborations, are argued to mitigate competency traps by enhancing the scope of information and knowledge-sharing. However, much of the evidence is anecdotal, and empirical evidence is scant in the research literature. In this study, we examine the competency trap effect by investigating the impact of strong functional capabilities on innovation performance of original equipment manufacturers in product codevelopment collaborations with their suppliers. We find strong evidence of competency traps in the inverted U-shaped relationships between capabilities and innovation performance. We find that while international collaborations can mitigate competency traps, this is only true under certain circumstances. The firm's capability portfolio is an important consideration, since certain combinations of capabilities can aggravate competency traps. Our findings are among the first to show these effects. We use a unique dataset of 202 firms across several high-tech industries, and with supplier collaborations between 1985 and 2016. We estimate our models using negative binomial generalized linear models, correcting for potential endogeneity using a control function method.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Latent Influence Friction Theory (LIFT), a new behavioral framework that explains why consumers often hesitate, delay, or fail to take action despite having clear intention. Existing models of consumer behavior—such as AIDA, the Theory of Planned Behavior, and the Fogg Behavior Model—do not account for the micro-level psychological frictions that subtly suppress action in digital environments. 

LIFT identifies four latent friction dimensions: (1) Attention Friction (AF), arising from distractions and cognitive interruptions; (2) Effort Friction (EF), relating to perceived difficulty in digital steps; (3) Cognitive Clutter Friction (CCF), caused by information overload; and (4) Latent Distrust Friction (LDF), reflecting subtle doubt or uncertainty that weakens action confidence. 
Through simulated studies conducted in digital contexts—retail advertising,
fintech onboarding, and influencer content engagement—the theory
demonstrates that latent friction reduces action probability by 22–38%
independent of intention. This paper provides conceptual grounding, empirical
validation, and a detailed measurement scale that future researchers can use
to study friction effects in marketing, consumer psychology, and digital decision
science.
LIFT offers a novel theoretical lens for understanding hidden behavioral barriers
and provides actionable implications for marketers, UX designers, platforms,
and policymakers aiming to optimize digital engagement outcomes.

detail.abstract: Over the past two decades, digital technologies have profoundly reshaped marketing and consumer behavior, giving rise to neuromarketing, an interdisciplinary field integrating neuroscience, psychology, and marketing science. Neuromarketing examines the subconscious neural mechanisms underlying perception, emotion, and decision-making, offering insights beyond traditional self-reports. Contemporary research demonstrates that many consumer choices are automatic, emotional, and heuristic-driven, with dual-process cognition highlighting the dominance of intuitive, fast, and affective systems in everyday purchases. Artificial intelligence (AI) amplifies these mechanisms by delivering real-time, hyper-personalized content through recommendation engines, dynamic pricing, affective computing, and conversational agents. AI-driven platforms engineer environments that optimize attention, reward anticipation, and emotional vulnerability, systematically facilitating impulsive and emotionally charged consumption. Neuroimaging and physiological measures reveal the neural correlates of these behaviors, including heightened activity in reward circuits and attenuated self-regulatory control. Despite its practical potential, the integration of AI with neuromarketing raises ethical concerns regarding consumer autonomy, informed consent, psychological exploitation, and algorithmic bias. This study provides a comprehensive theoretical synthesis of AI-enhanced neuromarketing, elucidates the cognitive and behavioral mechanisms of impulsive consumption, and highlights the normative and regulatory implications necessary for responsible application. detail.abstract: Retail shrink represents a critical threat to global retail sustainability, with U.S. losses exceeding 112 billion dollars annually. While membership and loyalty programs have become strategic assets generating substantial customer lifetime value, existing shrink mitigation systems remain fragmented, rule-based, and dependent on intrusive identity signals resulting in high false positive rates that degrade both detection accuracy and customer experience. This paper introduces a privacy-centric, membership-driven framework integrating tokenized identity management, real-time behavioral event processing, and multi-factor trust scoring to predict and mitigate shrink while preserving user anonymity. Evaluation using synthetic datasets calibrated to National Retail Federation benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed approach achieves an F1-score of 0.835, a 34.2 percent improvement over baseline rule-based systems, while reducing false positives by 41.3 percent and maintaining sub-200ms processing latency. The framework contributes: a formally-defined membershipcontextualized trust function with proven privacy properties, Context-Bound Tokenization for purpose-limited identity correlation, and generalizable design patterns applicable beyond retail to financial and healthcare domains.

This paper evaluates a pilot government-led AI curriculum, inspired by UNESCO's AI Competency Framework, delivered in rural government schools in Andhra Pradesh, India, targeting Grades 7-9. The intervention first provided AI training to teachers and then were tasked to conduct four structured AI lessons over six to eight weeks among the students. Using a two-wave of longitudinal data of 1,061 students and a two-way fixed effects regression framework, we examine its impact on both, first-order outcomes (AI and technology usage) and second-order outcomes (cognitive and non-cognitive skills). The program increased AI use for study by about 15 percentage points and raised overall technology use by roughly 0.37 standard deviations. However, we find no improvement in overall cognitive scores; instead, the likelihood of scoring in the lower tail (50/60 percent or below) increased among those exposed to the AI training. Non-cognitive outcomes particularly creativity is found to decline significantly. Further analysis reveals that these adverse effects are concentrated among students who use AI in intervention schools. In contrast, treated students who do not use AI do not exhibit learning losses or declines in creativity, but they become less likely to collaborate on joint projects. This is indicative of a possibility that uneven access to devices and connectivity may widen within-school gaps when AI is introduced without commensurate improvements in digital infrastructure. Qualitative interviews provide suggestive evidence that increased access encouraged cognitive offloading, multitasking, and design fixation, with AI-generated outputs sometimes substituting for student effort and originality. These findings suggest that AI adoption in schools should not be treated as self-evidently beneficial. Governments should prioritize further deliberation and rigorous evidence collection, through phased pilots, learning-focused evaluations, and clear safeguards, before moving to large-scale AI rollout.

title: A Structural Life Course Model of Dynamic Role Selection on an Open Q&A Platform for Pregnancy and Childbirth

detail.title: A Structural Life Course Model of Dynamic Role Selection on an Open Q&A Platform for Pregnancy and Childbirth
detail.abstract: This study extends the two-sided market literature by examining indirect network effects that arise from users' transitions across the two sides of a platform, as opposed to arising from interactions between distinct user groups alone. In open Question-and-Answer (Q&A) platforms, users may act as both information seekers and information providers over time, generating a within-user feedback loop that links information demand and supply. We study this mechanism using data from a large Q&A platform focused on pregnancy and childbirth, where user participation follows a natural life-course progression and informational needs evolve predictably. Using unstructured text data, we apply topic modeling to identify latent themes in user posts and document systematic role switching across pregnancy stages. We show that a substantial share of users who initially seek information later give back by answering questions on the same topics, and that these users contribute disproportionately to overall knowledge supply. We then develop and estimate a structural life-course model in which users make asking and answering decisions over time based on evolving knowledge sets, prior platform experiences, and expectations about answer quantity and quality. The estimates indicate that question-asking incentives depend primarily on expected answer quality, whereas answering incentives are shaped by both the quantity and quality of answers previously received. Counterfactual simulations quantify the contribution of giving-back behavior and show that high-quality contributors play a critical role in sustaining long-run platform growth.

title: ODR and Global Justice: Issues and Challenges

detail.title: ODR and Global Justice: Issues and Challenges
detail.abstract: Online Dispute Resolution (ODR), which is a key aspect of the digital world, is changing the way of access to justice. The paper examines the changed role of ODR in the promotion of global justice, especially the intersection with international law and human rights, critically and in detail. ODR, however, is a perfect solution to the problem of access to justice, given its eco friendliness, efficiency, and affordability, the deployment of ODR also brings up serious legal, technological, ethical, and inclusion related challenges. Firstly, the study considers ODR use in the human rights area, such as consumer protection and refugee claims, and questions issues of digital justice and procedural fairness. After that, it goes further to investigate significant obstacles that hinder the usage of ODR, such as jurisdictional ambiguities, the digital divide, algorithmic bias, and the exclusion of marginalized groups. Through worldwide research of various examples from India's SAMA and court annexed initiatives to the EU's consumer ODR platform and China's smart courts the paper points to international best practices and institutional creations, such as AI, blockchain, and public private partnerships that are included. The paper, having these thoughts in mind, presents a strategic outline for the emergence of fair ODR systems which strongly advocate for the necessity of legal harmonization, technology ethics, judicial capacity building, and grassroots digital literacy. The concluding thoughts reflect on the indispensability of the human rights approach to digital justice, which guarantees that ODR is not only a means to efficiently resolve disputes, but also a way to do justice, promote inclusiveness, and respect the fundamental legal values. This paper serves as a stepping stone to a larger conversation on digital justice and argues that ODR innovation should not be measured by the amount of technology involved but by its global access to justice transformation morally, equitably, and sustainably.

title: Targeting Information in Ad Auction Mechanisms
affiliations: Duke University - Fuqua School of Business, Duke University - Fuqua School of Business and

detail.title: Targeting Information in Ad Auction Mechanisms
detail.abstract: Digital advertising platforms and publishers sell ad inventory that conveys targeting information, such as demographic, contextual, or behavioral audience segments, to advertisers. While revealing this information improves ad relevance, it can reduce competition and lower auction revenues. To resolve this trade-off, this paper develops a general auction mechanism-the Information-Bundling Position Auction (IBPA) mechanism-that leverages the targeting information to maximize publisher revenue across both search and display advertising environments. The proposed mechanism treats the ad inventory type as the publisher's private information and allocates impressions by comparing advertisers' marginal revenues. We show that IBPA resolves the trade-off between targeting precision and market thickness: publisher revenue is increasing in information granularity and decreasing in disclosure granularity. Moreover, IBPA dominates the generalized second-price (GSP) auction for any distribution of advertiser valuations and under any information or disclosure regime. We also characterize computationally efficient approximations that preserve these guarantees. Using auction-level data from a large retail media platform, we estimate advertiser valuation distributions and simulate counterfactual outcomes. Relative to GSP, IBPA increases publisher revenue by 68%, allocation rate by 19pp, advertiser welfare by 29%, and total welfare by 54%.

title: Don't Count Non-Targeted Seeding Out Just Yet
affiliations: Fudan University - School of Management, Georgia  Institute  of  Technology,  and Georgia Institute of Technology - Ernest Scheller Jr. College of Business

detail.title: Don't Count Non-Targeted Seeding Out Just Yet
detail.abstract: In software markets, the sheer number of available applications make it rather challenging for any given new one to stand out and be noticed by consumers. Moreover, a push towards privacy by regulators and consumers is making it harder to target consumers. As such, firms have to rely on more non-targeted go-to-market strategies. We explore two popular strategies through which developers can catalyze adoption by helping consumers directly or indirectly learn the value of their products-seeding (free full-feature product giveaways to a subset of the consumer base) and time-limited freemium (TLF). Seeding, as a business strategy, existed for a long time. On the other hand, the feasibility to offer market-wide TLF became mainstream more recently, with the advent of the Internet and a plethora of digital tools. Thus, a natural question emerges-if TLF represents nowadays a feasible and easily implementable strategy for software applications, has seeding approach been rendered irrelevant in these markets? In this study, we provide managerial recommendations on when each of these strategies with a free full-feature-consumption component is optimal, based on social and self-learning dynamics, consumer priors, adoption costs, and individual product value depreciation. To that end, under a multi-period parsimonious unifying framework, we show that S becomes dominated as free trials enter the picture. We identify two specific market factors that, when present, can induce seeding to be optimal when consumers initially underestimate true product value - (i) user adoption costs and/or (ii) individual depreciation of value by usage. Moreover, we show that these two factors have a moderating effect on the impact of word-of-mouth (WOM) effects on the optimality of seeding. In the absence of these factors, stronger WOM effects alone cannot give seeding an edge against the other business strategies. However, once either depreciation or adoption costs are accounted for, strong WOM effects increase the relevance of seeding (enlarging its optimality region in the parameter space). Our results remain qualitatively consistent under a battery of robustness checks.

title: Use without Ownership: Wartime Financing under Sovereign Immunity Constraints

detail.title: Use without Ownership: Wartime Financing under Sovereign Immunity Constraints
detail.abstract: We propose a market-based mechanism that allows an attacked state to draw economic value from immobilised sovereign assets of an aggressor state while preserving sovereign immunity. The framework separates legal ownership from temporary economic use through a rule-based structure anchored in a publicly auditable ledger providing credible commitment in low-trust environments. Wartime financing is provided immediately via marketable financial instruments issued during conflict, whose conversion into conventional debt is triggered by peace or agreed de-escalation event. An optional commodity-linked adjustment mechanism is designed to strengthen incentives for de-escalation. Repayment is smoothed through GDP-linked commitments, while asset restoration is staged and conditional on sustained peace. Market pricing acts as an effective oracle, aligning incentives across investors, the attacked state, the aggressor state, and third-party guarantors.

detail.abstract: Generation Z in India cares about the environment and says they'd buy green products, but they often don't follow through. This paper looks at why that happens by combining two recent studies-one about Gen Z in smaller Indian cities, the other about what urban Gen Z thinks about green buying. We create a simple model based on the Theory of Planned Behaviour, adding trust in eco-claims and how much price matters. The idea is that if Gen Z likes green products (attitude), feels social pressure to buy them (norms), thinks they're easy to get (control), and trusts the green labels, they'll be more likely to buy. But if products are too expensive, even positive feelings won't lead to action. We outline a survey study you could do (but don't actually run here) with clear questions and stats plans. Expected results? Positive attitudes and trust boost buying intent, but price sensitivity kills it for budget-conscious students. title: Material Change Implication of Sustainability in the Automotive Industry

detail.title: Material Change Implication of Sustainability in the Automotive Industry
detail.abstract:
Sustainability has become a key driver of strategic decision-making in modern industries, particularly within the automotive sector, which is among the largest and most complex manufacturing industries worldwide. Increasing environmental pressures, regulatory requirements, and resource scarcity have intensified the need for sustainable development practices, with material selection and substitution emerging as an important mechanism for reducing environmental impact. This paper examines the implications of sustainability-driven material changes in the automotive industry, focusing on their environmental, economic, and social dimensions.

The study is based on a qualitative literature review and adopts a descriptive and analytical research approach. It first outlines the theoretical foundations of sustainability and the circular economy, emphasizing the triple bottom line framework. A comparative analysis with the food and beverage industry is then conducted to evaluate how sustainable material transitions have been implemented in a sector that has achieved relatively high recycling rates and measurable environmental benefits. This comparison highlights both the opportunities and limitations of transferring similar strategies to the automotive industry.

The findings indicate that while material changes can significantly contribute to sustainability objectives, their impact in the automotive industry is constrained by product complexity, safety requirements, globalized supply chains, and high capital intensity. Consequently, material substitution alone is insufficient to achieve comprehensive sustainability. The paper concludes that effective sustainability strategies in the automotive industry require an integrated, system-level approach that combines material innovation with changes in design, production processes, supply chain coordination, and regulatory support.

title: Synchronized Demand Forecasting and Inventory Management with Dynamic Safety Stock Calculations

detail.title: Synchronized Demand Forecasting and Inventory Management with Dynamic Safety Stock Calculations
detail.abstract:
Accurate demand forecasting and effective inventory management are critical challenges in modern supply chains characterized by demand volatility, complex networks, and uncertain consumer behavior. This paper investigates the integration of demand forecasting with inventory management through dynamically calculated safety stock and reorder points. The study aims to improve supply chain efficiency by synchronizing forecasting outputs with inventory decision-making processes rather than treating them as isolated functions.

A qualitative and empirical research framework is adopted, combining an extensive literature review with two case studies based on real-world demand data across multiple stock keeping units and locations. Advanced time series and machine learning techniques—including Seasonal Naïve, Linear Regression, SARIMA, and Holt-Winters Exponential Smoothing—are implemented using Python to forecast demand under varying demand patterns. Inventory optimization is subsequently performed using Monte Carlo simulation to dynamically determine optimal safety stock levels and reorder points under both periodic and continuous review policies.

The results demonstrate that traditional static approaches to forecasting and inventory planning lead to inefficiencies such as overstocking, understocking, and delayed decision-making. In contrast, the proposed synchronized and dynamic framework significantly improves forecast accuracy, inventory visibility, and service levels while reducing excess inventory. The findings confirm that integrating demand forecasting with adaptive inventory control enhances responsiveness to demand fluctuations. The study concludes that the proposed approach is flexible, scalable, and transferable across industries facing similar demand uncertainty and inventory management challenges.

title: The Regulatory Implications of the License Plate Industry: A Systemic and Sustainability Analysis Incorporating After-Market Prospects

detail.title: The Regulatory Implications of the License Plate Industry: A Systemic and Sustainability Analysis Incorporating After-Market Prospects
detail.abstract: The automotive industry is highly regulated and material intensive, yet license plates remain an underexamined component within sustainability and circular economy debates. This paper presents a global regulatory analysis of the license plate industry, focusing on how legislation shapes material choice, manufacturing practices, and cyclical potential. Drawing on comparative analysis across multiple jurisdictions, the study examines regulatory frameworks governing plate dimensions, materials, renewal cycles, and identification features. The methodology combines qualitative literature review with systematic comparison of national regulations and documented manufacturing standards. Results reveal significant regulatory variation that directly influences recyclability, reuse, and material selection, particularly between aluminum, plastic, and composite plates. Certain regulatory models, such as transferable or long-life plates, demonstrate clear potential to reduce material demand and emissions. Conversely, annually renewed or highly fragmented systems generate increased production volumes and limit circularity. The analysis further explores aftermarket reuse initiatives, highlighting how regulatory flexibility can enable value-retention strategies beyond conventional recycling. The paper argues that license plates represent a regulatory blind spot with substantial untapped sustainability potential. It concludes that harmonized, circularity-oriented regulation could significantly improve material efficiency while maintaining legal, safety, and enforcement objectives across global automotive systems and associated mobility infrastructures and long-term environmental performance globally.

title: Cicular Economy Cross Industry Analysis -A System Dynamics Approach

detail.title: Cicular Economy Cross Industry Analysis -A System Dynamics Approach
detail.abstract:
Global supply chains are increasingly exposed to raw material scarcity, price volatility, and environmental degradation, highlighting the limitations of linear “take–make–dispose” economic models. This paper investigates the potential of the circular economy across multiple industries using a system dynamics approach, with a particular focus on the electronics sector. Building on an extensive literature review, the study conceptualizes circular economy principles such as recycling, leasing, product life extension, and material recovery, and embeds them within a dynamic simulation framework.

System dynamics modeling is employed to capture feedback loops between material scarcity, e-waste generation, recycling rates, leasing rates, and the overall implementation of circular economy practices. A causal loop diagram and stock-and-flow model are developed to analyze system behavior over time, followed by scenario-based simulations under varying levels of recycling and leasing performance. The results show that weak implementation of either mechanism leads to rapid growth in e-waste and declining circular economy performance. Recycling exhibits a stronger individual influence than leasing; however, the simulations demonstrate that sustainable outcomes are achieved only when both parameters operate simultaneously at high levels.

The findings emphasize that circular economy implementation is a systemic challenge rather than a single-factor intervention. The paper concludes that coordinated business models, supportive regulation, and cross-industry alignment are essential to reduce resource depletion, mitigate environmental impacts, and enhance long-term economic resilience.

title: Synchronized Demand Forecasting and Inventory Management

detail.title: Synchronized Demand Forecasting and Inventory Management
detail.abstract:
Modern supply chains operate under increasing demand volatility, shortened product life cycles, and rising expectations for responsiveness, making the coordination of demand forecasting and inventory management a critical managerial challenge. This paper examines how synchronized decision-making across demand and supply chains can improve inventory performance, reduce variability, and mitigate the bullwhip effect. Building on established concepts of demand–supply chain management, the study emphasizes the integration of forecasting, replenishment, and inventory control rather than treating them as isolated functions.

The research adopts a conceptual and analytical approach supported by extensive literature review and illustrative industry examples, with a particular focus on manufacturing environments characterized by customized products and multi-echelon structures. Key elements of the proposed framework include shared demand information, coordinated replenishment rules, predictive inventory planning, and dynamic adjustment of safety stock and reorder points. The study also explores the role of collaboration mechanisms such as synchronized supply chains, electronic data interchange, and collaborative planning, forecasting, and replenishment.

The findings indicate that synchronized forecasting and inventory decisions significantly reduce inventory instability, improve service levels, and dampen demand amplification across the supply chain. In contrast, traditional backward-looking and fragmented planning approaches lead to inefficiencies, excess stock, and delayed responses to demand shifts. The paper concludes that effective synchronization requires not only analytical tools but also organizational alignment, information transparency, and collaborative governance. The proposed approach offers a foundation for more resilient and responsive supply chain management in uncertain business environments.

detail.title: Mixed Frequency Data in a Heterogenous Sticky Price Model

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We develop a model to estimate price-adjustment behavior when prices are observed more frequently than key explanatory variables such as wage costs. We propose a mixed-frequency stochastic (S, s)-model that accommodates infrequently observed costs and allows for plant-, product-, and season-specific heterogeneity. The model is estimated using a likelihood-based nonlinear state-space approach, enabling estimation as if all variables were observed at the same frequency. Applied to monthly price survey data matched with plant-level annual cost data for manufacturing producers, the model yields precise estimates of both cost pass-through and price-inaction thresholds, and reduces the blurring of intermittent price changes.

title: Optimally Designing Purpose and Meaning at Work
affiliations: University College London - Department of Economics and Instituto de Análisis Económic (IAE) Barcelona

detail.title: Optimally Designing Purpose and Meaning at Work

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Many workers value purpose and meaning in their jobs alongside income, and firms need to align these preferences with profit goals. This paper develops a dynamic model in which firms invest in ”purpose” to enhance job meaning and motivate effort. Workers, who differ in productivity, choose both productive and socialization effort, gaining utility from income and meaning. Purpose accumulates over time through firm investment and interacts with socialization to generate meaning, which boosts productivity. Firms invest in purpose only insofar as it raises profits. We characterize the unique equilibrium, including steady state and transition dynamics. Meaning and purpose rise with the importance workers place on meaning and with firm’s patience, but fall with depreciation and socialization costs. The relationship with workers’ share of output is nonmonotonic. We also show that some intermediate level of heterogeneity in skills is best for performance. Compared to a worker-owned firm, profit-maximizing firms underinvest in purpose, highlighting a misalignment between firm incentives and worker preferences. The model provides insight into when and why firms adopt purpose-driven practices and underscores the role of diversity in fostering meaning at work.

detail.title: Life-Cycle Effects of Public Childcare: Evidence on Children and Their Parents

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper provides large-scale evidence linking the economic effects of childcare programs to social skills measured in adulthood. We examine Finland's first national public childcare program, and document that it increased parental labor supply - through retirement - while reducing the intergenerational persistence of income. Critically, we leverage Finnish Defence Forces data on the near population of males to show that effects on children's adult income are underlied by lasting effects on social skills. Further, we show that life-cycle cost-effectiveness estimates based on the assumption of constant effects after typical observation windows can considerably overestimate the net costs of public childcare.

title: Service Jobs and Education: Evidence from Tourism Shocks in Italy
affiliations: and Government of the Swiss Confederation - Federal Finance Administration

detail.title: Service Jobs and Education: Evidence from Tourism Shocks in Italy

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We explore how unexpected temporary increases in the demand for low-skill service jobs in the tourism industry impact educational choices in Italy. We identify exogenous variation in the demand for service jobs using positive shocks to the tourism industry caused by terrorist attacks in foreign destinations that compete with Italy for tourists. We find that an exogenous increase in tourism decreases college enrollment and completion in the year after the shock. The decline in enrollment is driven by fewer students choosing fields related to humanities and social sciences. Both men and women respond by reducing college enrollment and completion. The effect for men is temporary, while it is more persistent for women. These effects are likely driven by higher opportunity costs of college education, as we find that tourism shocks increase the demand for labor in service jobs, raising local employment in the tourism industry as well as labor force participation. Using an IV approach, we show that the average annual increase in tourist arrivals between 2010 and 2019 (21,000 tourists) increases tourism employment growth by 16 percent, while reducing college enrollment and completion growth by 9 percent.
